file: A BREAKTHROUGH FOR NERVOUS HU NA.txt
text:
ï»¿
She played her first match of the 1982 Federation Cup tournament on a July evening in Santa Clara, Calif., and wasn't seen again in public for eight months. 
Hu Na hid in the homes of sympathetic Chinese families on the West Coast during that time, hoping one day to be granted asylum in the United States. 
Her second wish was to pursue a professional tennis career.
Miss Hu's defection caused an international incident and her whereabouts had all the intrigue of a spy novel. 
The Chinese Government suspended several cultural exchanges with the United States, which eventually granted Miss Hu asylum on April 4, 1983, in Washington. 
She played her first professional match two months later.
Hu Na, who defected to United States from China in 1982, defeats Annabel Croft of Britain in first-round match at Wimbledon; photo (M)
But Miss Hu was not to become another Martina Navratilova, who defected to the United States from Czechoslovakia when she was already one of the highly ranked players in the world. 
Miss Hu was a champion in China but only a qualifier on the women's tour.
''It was very hard because the players were so good,'' she said. 
''I got discouraged because every time my game went up, I'd get injuries.''
Miss Hu is ranked 150th in the Women's Tennis Association rankings but has made the biggest tournament in the world the site of her professional breakthrough. 
She qualified for Wimbledon by winning three difficult matches last week and today became the first Chinese-born player to win a match in the main draw, defeating Annabel Croft of Britain, 6-3, 7-5, in a first-round match.
Â 
'Cracks Under Pressure'
Although Miss Croft may not be well known herself, she is ranked 40th and was the favorite of the hometown crowd. 
It earned her a place on Court One, which is adjacent to Centre Court and usually draws the second- biggest crowd. 
''I was nervous,'' Miss Hu said. 
''There were so many people who came out to see us.''
Miss Hu is 22 years old but her game is just developing. 
The lack of top quality competition in China is one reason, and the customary slow progress made by serve-and-volley players is another. 
At times, it seems as if she has disappeared once again. 
''I think she's improved a lot,'' Miss Croft said. 
''I've been told by other players that she cracks under pressure.''
Any pressure she may face on the tennis court, however, would not begin to compare to what she encountered when she defected. 
She received letters that were reportedly written by her parents, pleading for her return to China. 
She was homesick and did not speak English.
''My English wasn't very good,'' Miss Hu said. 
''I watched 'Three's Company' and 'The Love Boat.'
Jack Tripper was my first teacher.''
Â 
Potential in Question
Jack Tripper is the character played by John Ritter in the television show ''Three's Company.''
Miss Hu has since had other instructors. 
She is attending the United States International College in San Diego, where she lives in a Chinese community with several families, spending a few months with each. 
She speaks English well enough to face her interviews without the aid of an interpreter.
She said she never questioned her decision to leave China. 
Newspaper accounts at the time said that Miss Hu was reluctant to join the Communist Party, as her coach in China requested. 
She said she preferred not to talk about those things today.
Her potential as a player remains in question. 
She has been tutored by such notable coaches as Vic Braden, Harry Hopman and Nick Bollettieri, but has advanced as far as the quarterfinals only three times in 23 tournaments, and those were on the satellite tour. 
She has earned $7,000.
At this point, however, she appreciates some things that most players take for granted. 
It was a thrill for her, she said, to be able to play a match without braiding her hair.

text:

A Foreign Ministry spokesman said today that a 19-year-old Chinese tennis player who defected to the United States last summer would not be prosecuted if she returned home.
The player, Hu Na, said last week that threats from Chinese Communist Party officials frightened her into seeking asylum.
PEKING, March 25 (AP) - A Foreign Ministry spokesman said today that a 19-year-old Chinese tennis player who defected to the United States last summer would not be prosecuted if she returned home.The spokesman said that if Miss Hu returned to China, she would be sent soon to play in an international tournament in Switzerland. 
Miss Hu is still awaiting formal United States approval of her application for political asylum. 
She said earlier this week that just before she left China to play in the Federation Cup tournament in Santa Clara, Calif., last summer, high-ranking party officials told her she was ''embarrassing'' the Communist Party by refusing to join.
The Foreign Ministry spokesman said in a statement: ''In recent years Hu Na frequently went abroad to take part in international competition after she was trained as a tennis player. 
The Chinese Tennis Association has declared that so long as Hu Na makes up her mind and returns home, the association will still send her to participate in an international tournament to be held in Switzerland in June this year. 
Therefore the question of prosecuting her did not exist in the past nor will it arise after her return to China.''

There were only 11 tricks in sight, and a squeeze was needed for the 12th.

West won and fell into the trap by leading the diamond jack.

The most dedicated lover of the game to compete in the recent Fall Nationals in San Francisco was surely Dr. C.P. Chang of Shanghai, a physician of great professional distinction. 
For almost half a century he has been the only resident of the Chinese mainland to be a member of the American Contract Bridge League. 
He learned the game in 1924 as a student at the Peking Union Medical College. 
His medical career took him to the United States in the 30's, where he played with success in Philadelphia and Chicago.
He has been a principal force in keeping the game alive in Shanghai during the past 30 years, in the face of official discouragement. 
As a result, the switch three years ago, which gave bridge not only tolerance but encouragement, left Shanghai in the lead, and their players are now by far the best in China.

At the age of 76 this cheerful and indomitable man, brushing aside the handicap of two artificial legs, traveled from Shanghai to San Francisco to take part in the Nationals.
The diagramed deal, played in Shanghai, is an example of his considerable ability. 
He sat South and had a difficult rebid when his partner responded one spade; one d iamond would have been better and would not have created a problem. 
The two-club rebid was not entirely sati sfactory, but neither was anything else.
When North continued by bidding two diamonds, Dr. Chang took a shot at three no-trump, satisfied that he was well-armored in the unbid heart suit.
Dummy's second suit is often the one for the defense to attack, and West decided to lead diamonds. 
But instead of the three he selected the queen, a mild eccentricity that came close to luring South to defeat.
The diamond queen was captured with the ace, and the club queen was led for a finesse. 
West held up his king, and did so again when the ten was led around to him. 
But he naturally took his king when a club was led to the jack. 
Meanwhile, East discarded two hearts.

The large group of American players, including many internationally known stars, competing in China's first international tournament that began last week are due for some surprises.

For the following information I am indebted to Dr. Steven Fox of the Beijing Children's Hospital, Peking.
When the game of bridge became not only legal but officially encouraged in China two years ago, the result was an explosion of team play with hundreds taking part in each major city. 
Foreigners are barred, however, and there are no women players.
Bridge column discusses style of play used by Chinese bridge players as China hosts its first international tournament
There are no pair games, perhaps because the necessary organization and scoring are relatively sophisticated. 
One Chinese player offered a different explanation: ''No international competitions are matchpoint events, so why bother?''
This half-truth suggests that China will not be represented in the world pair championship in Biarritz, France, next year, and we may have to wait until 1984 to discover how well they can do in a world championship.
Since manufactured boards were not available, the first competitions were organized with an expedient used by many before: four small envelopes, one for each hand, in a large envelope. 
Now there are boards made of wood, with rubber bands holding the cards in place. 
In Shanghai there will be ''written bidding,'' a concept that will be new to the Americans.
This will take care of the language problem in bidding, but it will not help when explanations are needed. 
Chinese players do not 'alert' and consider it ungentlemanly to ask for explanations, so there is likely to be confusion and difficulty.

file: CHINESE CREW IS FIRST IN DRAGON BOATS.txt
text:

China, to no one's surprise, captured first place today - for its fifth consecutive victory - in the 11th annual Hong Kong international dragon boat races. 
But to everyone's surprise, the False Creek Canoe Club of Vancouver, British Columbia, placed second.
The Canadian team, with Olympic canoeists among the crew of its dragon-headed racing canoe, handled the choppy water of Victoria Harbor's waterfront course easily, which allowed it to beat a fast-closing Indonesian team by five-tenths of a second. 
The Indonesians were slowed when their portside No. 2 paddler missed two strokes and lost control of his paddle in the final few yards of the race.
''It was a killer of a race,'' said Mike Flesher, one of the Canadians. 
''We were flat out in the end with nothing left. 
It's a good race when it goes like that.''
The Chinese, with their 20-man crew employing a choppy stroke, drove their cadence - kept by a drummer aboard the canoe - to 110 beats to a minute at various stages over the 640-meter distance of the race. 
The Canadians used only 19 paddlers in an effort to lighten the boat.
Don Irvine, another of the Canadians, believed that with calmer water and an equally manned canoe, his team could beat the Chinese. 
''The Chinese are well disciplined and fine athletes, but not unbeatable. 
With 20 people we could have a really good race with the Chinese. 
As it was, it was primo close.''

file: Christmas in China For Hockey Team.txt
text:
ï»¿
Harbin, Manchuria, is an unlikely place to spend a Christmas vacation.
An industrial city of 2.5 million people in northeastern China, Harbin is also China's winter-sports capital. 
The Brown University hockey team spent its Christmas vacation there, playing five games in nine days. 
The last game signaled the formal opening of China's National Ice Festival.
Brown had accepted the invitation extended by the New York-based People to People Organization on behalf of the Chinese Government. 
China has a national hockey team, which has had limited international exposure to date, and is looking for more.
Â 
Captain Lost to Injury
Brown won 2, lost 2 and tied 1 game during the team's stay. 
Two of the games, a 7-6 loss and a 3-3 tie with the Chinese national team, were televised throughout China. 
Three others were against club teams, sprinkled with players from the national squad. 
Brown also lost its captain, Tom Wallack, for the rest of the season with a knee injury suffered during one of the games.
Coach Herb Hammond, now in his fourth year at the Providence school, compared both the city and the hockey to his visit to Moscow in 1972.
''They've had 25 years of hockey in China, but only recently have they gone in an Olympics direction,'' he said. 
''They have a couple of coaches from Czechoslovakia in to help out. 
They want to go to Calgary in 1988 and play in the B or C pool.
''The Chinese play a noncontact type of hockey. 
They were very impressed by our desire to win. 
They called a lot of penalties, and we played short-handed almost all the time just because they haven't been exposed to our kind of play.
''Their equipment was really inferior, too, much like the Russians had 10 or 15 years ago. 
But they'll improve. 
They were all interested in trading pieces of equipment with us.''
Â 
Impressed by a Goalie
The Chinese national team was roughly comparable to a mediocre major United States college team, according to Hammond. 
Four or five of its players, including one of the goalies, would be capable of playing at that level, he said.
The cultural differences were striking and unforgettable. 
''We all lost weight,'' joked Hammond, recalling banquet dishes such as bear claw, sea slug and moose nose. 
As the only Westerners in the city, team members drew curious onlookers wherever they went. 
The Chinese were particularly intrigued by the Western modes of dress of Hammond's and the wife of an assistant coach, Mark Trivett.
Hammond said the crowds were quiet. 
''There was no emotion, no cheering at our games, even though there were 6,600 fans at each one,'' he said.

file: FIGHTING THE ODDS IN TABLE TENNIS.txt
text:
ï»¿
After a long climb out of the American basement rec room, the game of Ping-Pong is spinning toward acceptance as a sport in this country.
The impetus is the decision to include table tennis as a game in the 1988 Olympics. 
The American effort to compete against the two national teams that dominate the sport, China and Sweden, will be helped by a $1.2 million grant from the United States Olympic Committee, one of 37 full shares of the profits from the Summer Games last year in Los Angeles.
As the United States Open Table Tennis Championships got under way in this resort's cavernous convention hall this week, with more than 600 players from 30 countries rocketing shots at each other across dozens of green tables, promoters were savoring the chance to boost the game from summer-camp obscurity to the hot-ticket mass following it enjoys in other nations.
China's 'Most Popular Sport'
One of the first things the United States Table Tennis Association did with the Olympic money was to hire a Chinese couple to coach the American men's and women's teams.
Ai Liguo moved to the United States last year from Peking with his wife, Li Henan. 
Ai, 43 years old, was a player on the Chinese team that won the world championship in 1961. 
Miss Li was the coach of the world championship Chinese women's team.
''We had good jobs and high social position in China,'' Ai said during a break from his scrutiny of the strokes of the hundreds of American players participating in the Open. 
Ai was chief editor of Sports News, which he described as the leading sports publication in China.
''My wife was very famous because table tennis is the most popular sport in China,'' he said.
Â 
Second Behind Soccer
The top-rated American player is Eric Boggan, a 21-year old New Yorker who is ranked 33d among the best male players in the world.
''Our problem in America,'' said Tim Boggan, Eric's father and a vice president of the International Table Tennis Federation, ''is that there are something like 19 million Americans who play table tennis, but only a few thousand take it seriously. 
In China there are two million officially registered players - players who compete seriously at the sport - and the unofficial figure is probably more like 12 million.''
The game is the only livelihood of about 40,000 Chinese players, he said.
By contrast, he pointed out, only a few American players are able to squeeze a living from it. 
Eric Boggan plays for a club team in West Germany, said his father, a professor of English at Long Island University whose other son, Scott, 23, is ranked the third-best American player.
Ping-Pong is estimated to be the second most popular participatory sport in the world behind soccer, but it has never attracted much of a following in the United States, even though most Americans have played the game.
Until the 1950's, when Europeans dominated the game, table-tennis competition was seen as battle between players with special offensive or defensive skills. 
Long battles over points tended to pitch two players ranging far from the table, one killing the ball while the other returned the smashes with unerring, looping shots. 
Or else the opponents engaged in an exchange of chopping, spinning shots and single points could involve dozens of individual strokes.
''Now techniques have changed and the game is much faster,'' said Tim Boggan. 
''The Japanese introduced a racket in the 1950's with a sponge layer that rocketed the ball. 
In the 1960's the Chinese used a sponge paddle with a layer of rubber that gave their shots both speed and spin.
''With the new rackets the day of long rallies came to an end and now the game is attack, attack, attack,'' said Boggan, smiling. 
''The quality of the rubber paddles allows for so much speed and hop on the ball that the defensive player doesn't have a chance.''
The International Federation is studying ways to slow down the game, he said. 
One proposal is to raise the net by a half-inch; another is to force single players to serve cross-court as doubles players are made to do.

file: FIVE AMERICANS AND A CHINESE REACH FINALS IN CLIBURN PIANO COMPETITION.txt
text:
ï»¿
Six pianists, all males, five of them Americans and one from China, were chosen last night as the finalists of the Van Cliburn International Piano Competition. 
They are the survivors of the 39 pianists from 17 countries who started competing on May 17 for the richest prize that any musical competition in the world has to offer - a $12,000 cash award, a recording contract and two years of solo and concerto appearances in the United States, Europe and the Far East.
The judges, aided by a computer, selected the finalists shortly before midnight last night. 
They are: Zhu Daming, 29 years old, from China. 
Jeffrey Kahane, 24, from Piedmont, Calif. 
Andre-Michel Schub, 28, from New York. 
Santiago Rodriguez, 29, from Columbia, Mo. 
Christopher O'Riley, 25, from Jamaica Plain, Mass. 
Panayis Lyras, 27, from New York. 
Over a hundred people waited patiently at the Ed Landredth Auditorium
Eighth in series on Van Cliburn International Piano Competition notes 1981 finalists and briefly describes their playing styles
This is the eighth of a series of occasional articles on the Van Cliburn International Piano Competition. 
The world-famous piano contest will end Sunday with the winner on the way to a major career.
of Texas Christian University until John Giordano, chairman of the jury, read the names of the finalists. 
In the audience were all 39 of the competing pianists and their host families. 
The families were more excited than the contestants, who received the news of success or failure with stoic professionalism. 
The six finalists were brought to the stage, where they embraced one another. 
A photo session followed, climaxed by pictures of the contestants in Texas hats. 
Mr. Zhu, for one, was obviously amazed at this example of American folk ways.
In reading the names of the finalists, Mr. Giordano emphasized that the order in which the pianists were called to the stage had no relation to the actual scores the jury had given. 
The pianists were called forth by the number that they originally had drawn, starting with the lowest. 
Before the competition started, each pianist had drawn a number, giving him the order in which he would play. 
Mr. Zhu had the lowest number of the finalists (No. 5) and Mr. Lyras was highest (No. 36).
Â 
How Judges Operated
Each of the 11 judges had submitted a ballot with a numerical rating for each contestant, with 100 being the top score. 
The computer averaged the scores, breaking down the results to four decimal places. 
When the printout was studied last night, it was clear that four pianists were well above the other eight semifinalists. 
But for the fifth and sixth places there was a triple tie. 
According to the rules of the competition, a less than twopoint difference between two contestants is considered a tie. 
Three pianists were within two points of each other for the last two places.
Thus a vote was taken and fed into the computer. 
The judges were asked to list the three names in order of preference, No. 1 being the highest rated. 
''Don't forget,'' Mr. Giordano emphasized. 
''No. 1 is the best, No. 3 is the worst.''
When the votes were put into the computer, the last two finalists emerged. 
It was close. 
Each of the three was within a single vote of the others. 
The two-point rule does not apply to a tie-break.
The selection of the finalists was greeted by the public and the professionals around here with general approbation. 
It is when the winner is named on Sunday that there may be howls of outrage. 
Each of the three leading contestants has a fervent following.
Among the young pianists in the competition who did not make it to the finals, the favorite by far is Mr. Kahane. Seven or eight of them were discussing the level of talent in the competition the other day, and it was unanimously agreed among them that Mr. Kahane is the most poetic and elegant of all. 
They will be terribly disturbed if he does not win first prize.
Â 
Judges Leaning Toward Two
But it is believed, on very good authority, that the judges are leaning toward Mr. Shub and Mr. Rodriguez, who are neck and neck. 
The next three days will of course decide the issue. 
With solo recitals and chamber music out of the way, the finalists now have to play concertos. 
With the Texas Little Symphony, all will be heard in a concerto by Mozart or early Beethoven. 
With the Fort Worth Symphony, they will play a major 19th-century concerto. 
Leon Fleisher will conduct.
Each of the finalists has a sharply etched style, and they differ considerably from one another. 
Mr. Zhu, trained entirely in China, does lack experience in Western music, but his instincts are remarkably sure and he learns with incredible speed. 
He has a blazing technique, draws a resonant sound from the piano and approaches music in a very serious manner.
Mr. Kahane is indeed the poet that his colleagues believe him to be. 
A prize-winner in the 1977 Clara Haskil International Piano Competition in Vevey, Switzerland, and high up in the 1980 American National Chopin Competition in Miami and the Chopin International Piano Competition in Warsaw, Mr. Kahane studied at the San Francisco Conservatory and the Juilliard School. 
He does not rely on powerhouse technical effects, though he has a glittering technique. 
It was characteristic of his style that in his recital he played a perfect performance of Chopin's Variations Brillantes (Op.12), and later he received a deserved standing ovation for his performance of the Dvorak Piano Quintet. 
But he did have a bit of trouble with the big sonorities of the Schumann Fantasy. 
Many believe him to be the most sensitive, refined pianist in the finals.
Â 
Self-Described Romantic
Mr. O'Riley has been a finalist in the 1975 Three Rivers Competition in Pittsburgh and second-prize-winner in the 1980 Montreal International Piano Competition. 
He grew up in Pittsburgh and was trained at the New England Conservatory. 
He describes himself as a Romantic pianist. 
Mr. O'Riley likes big sonorities, and attacks the keyboard energetically. 
When he played the Brahms F-minor Piano Quintet, he all but made a little concerto out of it. 
He is a pianist with temperament and a big style.
The one pianist who went out of his way in his programming was Mr. Lyras. Greek-born, he came to the United States when he was 12, and attended the High School of Performing Arts in New York and the Juilliard School. 
He has won first prizes in the 1976 University of Maryland International Piano Competition and the 1978 Three Rivers Piano Competition. 
In 1980 he won the Silver Medal at the Arthur Rubinstein International Piano Competition in Tel Aviv. 
Where everybody else stuck close to repertory staples for their recitals, Mr. Lyras played such things as three Medtner ''Fairy Tales'' and the ''Islamey'' of Balakirev. 
His inclusion of the Balakirev piece suggested a pianist with virtuoso instincts, and Mr. Lyras did play the old warhorse with technique to burn. 
He is a well-schooled, utterly dependable pianist who brings logic and power to his playing.
Of the two front-runners, it is a classic case of Apollo and Dionysus. 
Mr. Schub was born in Paris but came to the United States as an infant. 
He started to play the piano at 4, studied at Princeton University and the Curtis Institute of Music, won the 1974 Naumburg Competition and was awarded the Avery Fisher Prize in 1977. 
Mr. Schub is an Apollonian player. 
He is an elegant pianist and, as his performances of two of the Paganini-Liszt etudes showed, a supreme technician. 
His fingers have been well brought up and have been taught never to associate with a wrong note.
Â 
Plays With Immense Authority
He plays with clarity, intelligence and immense authority. 
Yet he is a cool pianist. 
Proportion to him is more important than color. 
He refuses to make a play for the audience, and he performs miracles of virtuosity in a detached, aloof manner.
Mr. Rodriguez is the Dionysian pianist. 
He was born in Cuba, came to the United States at 9, received a degree from the University of Texas at Austin, and studied at Juilliard. 
In 1976 he won the Maryland International Piano Competition and took second place in the Naumburg Competition. 
In 1977 he was a finalist in the Leventritt Competition.
Mr. Rodriguez is a crowd-pleaser, a virtuoso, a colorist, a dashing, cocky performer who has thought out every element of his interpretations. 
Fortunately he is much more than a technician. 
His interpretations have had taste at all times, and his virtuosity is always employed for legitimate musical devices. 
In the Preliminaries, he played the first book of the Brahms ''Paganini'' Variations, and it was a stunning performance, one of the best this listener has ever heard. 
He was also remarkably effective in the Stravinsky ''Petrushka.''

The live coverage is part of a 90-minute special on the competition, made possible by International Business Machines Corporation. 
In New York, the telecast will start at 7:30 P.M.

file: OLYMPIC PROFILE_CHINA_S MASTER TECHNICIAN OF THE ART OF HIGH JUMP.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's best prospect for the Olympic gold in track and field hardly looks like a world- class athlete. 
With his Nike shirt worn inside out, wire-rimmed spectacles and hunched back, 21-year-old Zhu Jianhua is plugged into his Sony Walkman, nonchalantly watching a pre-Olympic competition from the bleachers, as he waits for his event.
Nicknamed ''Bean Pole'' in his native Shanghai, Zhu's frail, long- legged 6-foot-4-inch, 152-pound frame marks him as a high jumper. 
In a backward flop style that combines the agility of a gymnast with the speed of a runner, his featherweight body sails across the 7-7 1/4 (2.33- meter) bar with the ease of an airplane at takeoff.
Profile of Zhu Jianhua, China's master technician of art of high jump, who is competing in Olympic games; photo (M)
Though he has set the world record three times - at 7-9 1/4 (2.37 meters) and 7-9 3/4 (2.38) in China's preliminaries and national championship last year, and 7-10 (2.39) at a West German track meet in Eberstadt in June - the ultimate test of Zhu's athletic prowess will be the men's finals in the high jump on Aug. 
11.
Can he handle the pressure of international competition, particularly against the two-time United States Olympic bronze medalist, Dwight Stones?
As the leading athlete of the first full Chinese team to join the Olympic Games, Zhu bears the additional pressure of ''winning for the motherland.''
For a nation with a weak sports tradition, once dismissed as the ''sick man of Asia,'' Olympic medals carry the symbolic weight of China's struggle for recognition as a world economic power.
''We have three objectives,'' Hu Hongfei, Zhu's 59-year-old coach, said in his native Shanghai dialect. 
''First, to bring in at least the bronze, second, to bring in the gold, third, for Zhu to break his own world record.''
Â 
Has Stones's Respect
According to Stones, now 30, Zhu is ''technically the best high jumper around; he'll probably be the first to clear 8 feet.''
But, Stones added, world-record high jumpers don't necessarily perform well in the Olympics.
''The Olympic record was significantly below the world record in 1972 and 1976,'' Stones explained. 
''Every time Zhu broke the world record, the competition was held under ideal conditions. 
Eberstadt was a synthetic environment with only 4,000 spectators; a fantastic facility, where high jumping was the only event. 
The Olympics is a one-time competition with special pressures. 
There will be distractions - the 1,500 final, 400 relay final and other premier track events that same day, the crowds; it will be a long competition that could last five hours.''
Stones emphasized the importance of mental preparation in managing the lengthy hours between jumps.
''Zhu is 21 years old; this will be his first Olympics,'' Stones said. 
''This is my third Olympics on the facility where I made my best mark - 7-7 3/4.''
Â 
Zhu's 'Bad Luck'
Once before, Zhu buckled under pressure. 
At the first international track and field championship in Helsinki last year he finished third, clearing 7-6. 
Only two months before he had set his first world record on his home turf in Shanghai.
''It was bad luck,'' Zhu said of the world championships. 
''I was nervous and did not know how to handle the psychological pressure of international competition.''
Â 
Is he nervous about the Olympics?
''No. I've paid my dues,'' he said in a conversation conducted in his Shanghainese dialect.
''Comparing oneself to others increases anxiety,'' Hu said. 
''When Zhu was a child, I told him that the goal was to raise his own personal record among the best high jumpers in his age group; I never pushed him to be first in competition. 
I tell Zhu that he must aim high, keeping in mind his own record and the world record. 
The opponent is the bar, not the competitor.''
Â 
'Long Lower Limbs'
Hu, a former middle-distance runner who describes himself as a ''so-so athlete determined to succeed as a coach,'' first spotted the 10-year-old boy's ''long lower limbs, the stuff of a high jumper,'' at a school playground, and has been training Zhu since.
''The unity of their coach-athlete relationship is remarkable,'' said Harry Sneider, Stones's coach, who also has plaudits for Zhu's technique. 
''Zhu's speed conversion, the ability to convert horizontal speed into vertical lift, and his use of the swing leg are marvelous. 
He's also got the best flexibility of any jumper. 
Zhu has maximized the use of his physique to achieve extraordinary results.''
''Zhu needs to develop endurance, though, through weight lifting,'' said Stones.
''Stones has his technique and I have mine,'' said Zhu, who only takes 10 rapid-fire steps to the bar, before his speedy flight up and over.
The competitive styles of both Zhu and Stones are as dissimilar as their personalities, perhaps a reflection of the dichotomy between East and West. 
Stones is outgoing and talkative, with a reputation for ''psyching out'' his competitors, whereas Zhu appears introspective and mellow as he competes against his own standard.
Mobbed by reporters after he had won the pre-Olympic competition, Zhu handled the press with aplomb, and simply walked away when he'd had enough.
''For every half-hour I speak, Zhu only says two words,'' said Hu.
Fans come up to Zhu and say ''Youre No. 1,'' or ''Good luck,'' and Zhu understands and looking genuinely pleased, murmuring a humble ''thank you,'' the only two words he knows in English.
Zhu's public reserve masks the determination of a professional athlete, which was evident at a young age. 
At one time suring his childhood, Zhu continued to high jump, despite a painful wound from a splinter on the sole of his foot. 
Zhu was a sickly youngster who suffered from frequent fevers and respiratory problems, and as the pampered youngest son of five children, he was discouraged from sports by his parents.
He also suffered from ''fear of height,'' ducking the bar instead of going over it, whenever the height was raised, not an uncommon phobia among high jumpers, said Hu. 
How Zhu performs on that one day of the Olympic competition, however, will depend on his ability to handle the distractions and his detractors; how he manages his energy level; whether he can endure the August heat, all while carrying the weight of Chinese and world expectations.

text:
ï»¿
Before the Olympic Games began, many gold medals were predicted for China in men's gymnastics. 
The Chinese were favored to win the team gold medal; their star, Li Ning, was favored to win the individual all-around gold medal; and Li, Tong Fei and Lou Yun all were expected to win medals in various of the individual apparatus finals.
Once the competition began, the raves for China were tempered by the entirely unexpected performance of the men of the United States team. 
They not only won the team gold medal, but their Peter Vidmar took the lead, just ahead of China's Li, in the preliminary standings for the individual all-around medals.
Profile of Japanese gymnast Koji Gushiken, who has won gold medal in all-around individual competition despite fact that he placed fifth before start of event; Gushiken's career and background traced (M)
With all the hubbub about Vidmar and Li, not much notice was paid to the little man with the ancient-looking face who stood in fifth place as the all-around competition began Thursday night. 
Koji Gushiken of Japan was known as one of the world's best gymnasts, but there were four other world-class performers ahead of him - not only Vidmar and Li, but Tong and Bart Conner of the United States.
And in this sport where thousandths of a point can make a difference, there is very little margin for error for someone in fifth place trying to move up. 
So Gushiken gave six very nearly error-free performances, scoring a 10 on his vault, 9.95 on his horizontal bar and rings routines, and 9.90 on the other three events, and overtook Conner, Tong, Li and Vidmar to win the gold medal.
Â 
Vidmar Not Surprised
Most observers were astonished. 
They thought that if anyone was going to overtake Vidmar in the finals, it would be Li. 
But Vidmar wasn't surprised.
''No, no,'' said Vidmar, whose silver medal was the first medal for an American in Olympic all-around competiton. 
''I remember at the '81 world championships, everyone was talking on and on about the Russians and the Chinese, and Koji got third in the all-around. 
At the '83 world championships, everyone was talking about the Russians and the Chinese, and Koji got second in the all-around.
''He just moved up to the right spot today,'' Vidmar said. 
''He has good timing.''
Gushiken might dispute that. 
He is 27 years old, aged by the standards of his grueling sport. 
And good timing hasn't been a highlight of his 16-year career, judging by what he said, through a translator, in the interview session after his victory.
Gushiken, who is from Osaka and now lives in Tokyo, where he teaches at the Nippon Physical Education College, would have been at a prime age for Olympic competition during the Montreal Games, in 1976. 
But in each of the two years before those Olympics, he suffered a serious injury - first a ruptured Achilles' tendon, then a broken ankle. 
Each time, he said, it took him six months to recover, and another six months to reach top competitive form.
''I was only ranked 13th in Japan when the Montreal Olympics came,'' he said. 
''So I could not go.''
Â 
Disappointment in 1980
When it was time for the Moscow Games, he was back at the top, but his country joined the boycott led by the United States.
''I was very disappointed in Japan's boycott of the 1980 Olympic Games because I was a member of that team, and I had trained so hard and perservered through so much for that,'' he said.
''I left Japan this time with determination to win sort of double gold, making up for the one I missed in Moscow.''
He also made up a bit for the lost glory that once belonged to Japan in men's gymnastics. 
After winning their first team medal, a silver, in 1956, the Japanese went on to dominate Olympic gymnastics from the 1960 Games, in Rome, through the 1976 Games in Montreal. 
Japan won each of those five team gold medals, and Japanese men won 10 of the 15 individual all-around medals - three golds, four silvers and three bronzes.
Since then the Soviet Union, which had been Japan's closest competitor ever since 1956, has dominated men's gymnastics. 
The Russians won the team gold in Moscow and were heavily favored to win the world championships last October, although the Chinese slipped past them by a fraction of a point.
In those world championships, Gushiken took the silver all-around medal behind the Soviet Union's celebrated 17-year-old, Dmitri Bilozerchev. 
But the relative youth of the Chinese men, and the relative old age of Gushiken, were considered strikes against him here.
And fifth place after the preliminary scores (computed from each individual's scores in the team competition) was not the best place from which to launch a medal run. 
''I knew I was in fifth place but the difference was only 17-hundredths of a point,'' he said. 
''So if I take each exercise very carefully and do it my best, I knew I could win.''
Gushiken did not edge into first place until the fifth rotation, when he earned a 9.95 on the horizontal bar while Vidmar earned a 9.90 for his vault, putting Gushiken .025 of a point into the lead.
Either man could have won on the sixth and final rotation. 
Up first on the floor exercise, Gushiken scored a 9.90, which meant that Vidmar needed a 9.95 or 10 on the parallel bars to beat him. 
Bit Vidmar bobbled his dismount slightly and got a 9.90.
As soon as he saw that score, Gushiken burst into tears, knowing he had won.

Peter V. Ueberroth, the president of the L.A.O.O.C., said Friday that he had received ''reassurance'' on the sensitive question from Secretary of State George P. Shultz at a meeting in Washington Thursday. 
During the course of his visit, Mr. Ueberroth said he had also had met briefly with President Reagan (''It was a social thankyou visit''), whom he described as being ''very helpful'' with plans for staging the first Summer Olympics in the United States since the 1932 Los Angeles Games.
No Federal funds are being used to assist Los Angeles's $500-million effort, but Mr. Ueberroth said the Reagan Administration had assigned Michael K. Deaver, deputy chief of staff in the White House, to work with the organizers on law enforcement.
The State Department has assured the Los Angeles Olympic Organizing Committee that foreign athletes and officials traveling to the 1984 Summer Olympic Games will be allowed into the country without visa problems.
The biggest expense problem to be resolved between now and the opening ceremonies on July 28, 1984, remains negotiating contracts with 54 independent police departments and protecting thousands of athletes, officials, members of the media and visitors, Mr. Ueberroth added.
Â 
Several Topics Addressed
During a luncheon meeting with editors and reporters of The New York Times, Mr. Ueberroth answered questions on a variety of sports and political issues related to the Los Angeles Olympics. 
Some of the more significant were these:
- China's decision to cut off all cultural and sports exchanges with the United States for the remainder of this year in response to the United States having granted political asylum to the Chinese tennis player, Hu Na, had left the Los Angeles organizers ''vulnerable'' to a possible Chinese boycott in 1984. 
''The Olympics are a political event,'' Mr. Ueberroth said, describing the Chinese situation as ''very sensitive.''
He said he is hopeful that the People's Republic of China and Taiwan, which is to send athletes and officials to the Games under name Chinese Taipei Olympic Committee, would both compete. 
From an original plan to send only 30 athletes, mainland China's most recent estimate for 1984 is now at 385, Mr. Ueberroth said.
- The international governing body for soccer, the Federation Internationale de Football Association (FIFA), last week approved the sites proposed for the Olympic soccer tournament (including stadiums at Harvard University, Annapolis, Md., Stanford University and the Rose Bowl in Pasadena). 
But because of an eligibility dispute with the International Olympic Committee over the definition of amateur players in soccer, Mr. Ueberroth indicated there was still a possibility that FIFA could withdraw its sanction for soccer in the 1984 Olympics, and perhaps even stage a substitute tournament.
- A site for the shooting events still has not been found, since the I.O.C. rejected Las Vegas, Nev., as an alternative. 
''We're trying to find a solution,'' Mr. Ueberroth said. 
The possibility of the Olympic shooting events being staged outside the host country has precedence. 
''If worse comes to worse, they won't hold it anywhere,'' he said.
- The Los Angeles Raiders of the National Football League have until April 28 to decide whether they will build luxury boxes in the Coliseum, for which the Los Angeles Olympic Organizing Committee will pay the Raiders $3 million.''My guess is he won't build them,'' Mr. Ueberroth said, referring to Al Davis, the Raiders' managing partner.
- The United States is ''dead last'' in understanding that sports can influence young people in a positive way. 
''It hasn't dawned on us,'' Mr. Ueberroth said, citing the 1980 boycott of the Moscow Olympics and the reluctance to ''share our athletes'' with less developed countries as examples of recent United States negativism at the international level.
- Even without government assistance, the L.A.O.O.C. still envisions finishing in the black, with income from television ($210 million), cash ($140 million), tickets ($90 million), interest and a coin program covering its commitment. 
Mr. Ueberroth, however, has cut his original estimate of a $21 million profit to $8 million.
Mr. Ueberroth said a nationwide ticket policy that would give individuals 60 days in which to file their requests would be announced soon. 
Historically, many Olympic events are not sold out; but in the event of any sellout, a computer will select winners randomly from requests.
Appointed in March 1979, after being recruited at the last minute by the search firm of Korn-Ferry, Mr. Ueberroth left the financial comforts of the second-largest travel corporation in North America, First Travel, which he founded 20 years ago, to head the 360-member organizing committee. 
Committed to financing the games privately for the first time made Mr. Ueberroth an early target in I.O.C. circles, particularly after the administrative and financial foulups at the 1980 Winter Olympics in Lake Placid and Denver's aborted plans to stage the 1976 Winter Games.

Lake Placid Is Recalled
Foreign delegations are most seriously concerned about such matters as security, transportation and their treatment upon their arrival here. 
Some delegations had criticized the housing, transportation and services provided by the organizers in Lake Placid.
Mr. Ueberroth said his trip to Washington was designed to explain to Administration officials ''the Olympic Games and what they're about.''
''I just want to be sure as we move along we're not passing up chances for international friendship,'' he said. 
John Caulfield, of the visa affairs department, said making entry to the United States easier for foreign Olympic athletes had been discussed. 
''In general, it is quite reasonable that we would take steps to facilitate the entry of members of foreign delegations,'' Mr. Caulfield said. 
''The Olympics is different from an occasional golfer or player from the North American Soccer League.''
The success or failure of the Los Angeles Olympics, Mr. Ueberroth said, would be measured not in dollars and cents, but in how well the city embraced the games. 
''Things go better when people like it,'' he said.
''I think the best sporting event in this country is the New York City Marathon, because the people embrace that event,'' said Mr. Ueberroth, a San Jose State University graduate, who tried out for and failed to make the United States Olympic water polo team in 1956.

text:

LOS ANGELES First they made history, then they
were history. 
The American
women's volleyball team won a silver medal Tuesday night and yesterday began planning a reunion, when all of them will have scattered to the corners of the earth.
The players talked about their plans with tentative optimism, but their coach, Arie Selinger, spilled out his doubts about the future of volleyball in America, his decision to step down as American coach, and his bitterness with some people's perception of him as a tyrant.
While an all-star collection of players was celebrating America's first gold medal in women's basketball, the close, cohesive 10-year volleyball effort (''I've got 11 sisters,'' Debbie Green had said) came up one medal short.
In these Summer Games, we have seen a few Americans sulk over not setting world records and brood about silver medals, but there was no all-or- nothing bravado from Arie Selinger and his players, no cheapening of America's first volleyball medal.
''We did our best, we gave it our all,'' Flo Hyman said yesterday. 
''The competition was intense. 
We accomplished a lot. 
We're proud of our silver medal.''
Volleyball's Team America brought a beautiful sport to the public consciousness, but in the end it was defeated by a deserving Chinese team in three crushing games Tuesday night.
History will make them one of the most unusual teams in American sports history. 
They came together in a suburb of Houston nearly a decade ago, and they moved to Colorado Springs and then to Coto de Caza, Calif., becoming the Jeannie Appleseeds of a sport that flourishes in the Orient.
Since 1975, they traveled to China
and Japan and the Soviet Union,
they trained together to the exclusion of college degrees and full personal lives, and as their era ended yesterday, they proudly said it had all been worth it.
''Nobody put a ball and chain on us,'' said Sue Woodstra, the captain, who is 27 years old, has been playing volleyball 11 years, and will never wear the national colors again.
They are old now - 9 of the 12 players at least 24 years old, well into the age when the body no longer thinks it's fun to dive onto the floor, landing on one shoulder, while trying to flick a hard rubber ball back into the air with the fingertips.
''The Chinese have 10 million players,'' Miss Woodstra said. 
''You see what you're up against.''
On Tuesday night they were up against Lang Ping, the best Chinese spiker, an athletic combination of lace and steel. 
Flo Hyman, the worldly and talented American spiker, has described volleyball players as ''graceful, with strength,'' and Lang Ping and her always-positive teammates were more graceful, more strong, than the Americans.
The Chinese work 358 days a year, with a national volleyball program extending into every province, since the government decided to join the world sports powers in the mid-70's.
''Friendship first, competition second,'' the Chinese used to say, but in the regime of Deng Xiaoping they changed their motto to ''Break out of Asia and advance on the world.''
On Tuesday night they advanced on the net of Team America - more agile, more subtle, more aggressive than the home team. 
The scores were 16- 14, 15-3, 15-9.
The two teams had met last Friday in the final match of the first round, with the loser knowing it would meet Japan in the semifinal round. 
Selinger admitted yesterday that he had wanted to avoid Japan, and that he had motivated his players for the supreme effort against China the first time, ''to go at least for the silver.''
If Selinger was working with his players' minds, his counterpart from China was no ''Ned-in-the-third-reader,'' as Casey Stengel used to call novices. 
After losing to the United States, Yuan Weimin had accused his players of being ''qing xu bu wen ding'' - emotionally unstable in Mandarin.
''The players felt regret on our part,'' Miss Lang said Tuesday night through an interpreter. 
''Afterward, the coach did not criticize us. 
He told us last Friday was important but this one is the tough match.''
After the victory over Peru in the
semifinals, Selinger and Miss
Hyman said they felt an important part of their mission had been accomplished. 
They had brought volleyball to national television, they had interested new fans and even some new journalists, who hadn't known a spiked shot from a spiked drink. 
But if their mission was accomplished, a second-guesser asked, didn't that detract from their gold-medal effort?
''I didn't want to make it too hard,'' Selinger said. 
''Had we won the first game, I think the Chinese would have been in a tense situation. 
Maybe, it could be, that when we lost the first game, maybe at that particular time our players said, 'We've already won the silver,' but I doubt it.''
They were proud of their silver yesterday, the last trophy this team will win. 
The team is breaking up. 
The older players will become coaches, get their degrees, stay with the game in some capacity. 
Selinger said he would step down as coach and try to gain funding for a private, amateur volleyball base, rather than work through the United States Volleyball Association. 
He defended the ''conscious decision'' to build this team ''at the top of the pyramid'' for the 1980 Summer Games that America never attended, at the risk of not building a junior program, and he acknowledged that behind the disbanding team, the cupboard is bare.
''I think at this point, we should not maintain a national team but look for the future,'' Selinger said. 
''It will be difficult to come up with a team for four or eight years. 
I'd look to go back to basics. 
We have very little at the younger ages.''
Then some bitterness surged out of Arie Selinger, a 47-year-old Polish Israeli-American, who was rescued from a ''death train'' on its way to a Nazi camp in 1945. 
He criticized articles by one Los Angeles reporter who, he claimed, had made him sound more driven, more intense, than he deserved.
''It was working on the minds of my players,'' Selinger said. 
''They found themselves in an emotional bind.''
Yesterday the players admitted the team had willingly worked
four or five hours a day with few weeks off for the past decade. 
Sue Woodstra said: ''Arie is very determined. 
If you know his background, you know what he's been through. 
He demands a lot from his players - but no more than we can deal with.''
For Arie Selinger to be the Captain Queeg of Coto de Caza, the Darth Vader of volleyball, he would have had to show some kind of mania for a gold medal, but it never surfaced, not in victory, not in defeat.
He talked about the social value of a sport that encourages athletes to be ''graceful, with strength.''
And when the time came to accept a loss to a deserving Chinese team, in the last time these 12 women will ever be together as a unit, volleyball's Team America was graceful and it was strong.

text:

LOS ANGELES
It was a short, short time ago, the
way history is measured in China,
that sports were relegated to providing exercise and an example of social propriety. 
In the time when China was closed and turbulent, the sports slogan of the cultural revolution of 1966 was ''Friendship first, competition second.''
Such a short time later, China has brought 227 athletes to these Summer Games, and Lu Jindong, the assistant chef de mission of the Chinese delegation, was able to tell a news conference yesterday: ''If we win 10 gold medals, I'll be a happy, happy man.''
This is a great leap forward for a nation that has not participated in an Olympics since 1952 and has never won a medal, but China is one of the emerging nations of the Olympic movement. 
Its ambitions were clear yesterday when Mr. Lu revealed that China would consider applying to be host for the Summer Games of 2000.
Mr. Lu also said that athletes who win gold medals will be given a grant of approximately $2,000, hastening to add that it would be ''an award, a scholarship,'' and that ''it's more important that they not think of the rewards, however.''
From outsider to would-be Olympic host in a few decades would be a staggering turnaround, but China has questioned many other values. 
Since the reign of Deng Xiaoping began in the late 1970's, the sports slogan has been: ''Break out of Asia and advance on the world.''
In advancing on the world, they have sent a team that includes their best-known athlete, Zhu Jianhua, the world-record holder in the high jump, as well as Wu Shude, a weight lifter, Li Ning and Tong Fei, two gymnasts, Li Kongzheng, a diver who has rebounded from laser surgery for a detached retina, and volleyball and gymnastics contenders.
The Chinese appearance here is
part of the great upheaval of the
1980's that has brought in western culture and technology, including the news report from Peking the other day that blue jeans are now acceptable in China.
''Critics say that blue jeans represent the bourgeois life style,'' commented the English-language China Daily of Peking. 
''This really is farfetched because blue jeans used to be worn by hard-working American cowboys who had little to do with the bourgeoisie.''
It was only 18 years ago that intellectuals were sent into the countryside for re-education. 
At a reception for the Chinese team in General Lee's Restaurant in Chinatown the other day, Minnie Gan, a Chinese national who was educated in Christian schools and is now living in this country, recalled how she was sent to a farm in the late 60's to correct her thinking ''because I was an intellectual.''
Competitive sports was never a high priority for the Chinese yet it was further diminished during the Cultural Revolution. 
Xin Yun-Zhang, a 23-year-old physicist student from Peking who is now studying at the University of California at San Diego, drove up to cheer the arrival of the Chinese team in Chinatown last week. 
In very good English, he recalled how values had changed since he was young.
''Under the rule of friendship first, competition second, sports was a meeting, a party,'' he said. 
''That's not bad, that's good, people came together, but it wasn't encouraging the quality of sports.''
There were examples of teams or individuals being declared the winner because of superior attitude, or results being ignored for fear of embarrassing the losers.
He recalled a childhood when according to official teaching, ''the United States was imperialist and the Soviet Union was, how do you say it, revisionist.''
He only vaguely heard of the Olympics and said ''I didn't know that Chinese could send a team.''
But not long after the death of Mao Zedong in 1976, the young student recalled, ''they taught us about the Greek soldier who ran so far that he died after delivering his message'' - the origin of the marathon race.
Since rejoining the Olympic movement in 1979, China has entered world competition, learning technique and attitude. 
The other day at a workout of the Chinese male volleyball team at the Long Beach Arena, the dozen players wore varied outfits and smiled often and patted each other on the back. 
The body language was of friends or comrades, not of teammates expected to bring home a medal or face disgrace.
Every so often, Shen Keqin, an
older player at 26, gave a few
slap handshakes to teammates, and once, after plunking a serve for a point, he did a little strut and a wiggle that reminded a couple of American observers of Jimmy Connors.
''We get used to these expressions maybe more from the Japanese than from Americans,'' Shen said through a translator.
Asked whether he had yet observed an American-style high-five, he smiled and replied: ''That is the ultimate expression of a wonderful job, when you are very satisfied. 
Therefore, most of the time, we do not do it.''
Shen was asked if his view of competition had changed since his childhood in Maoist China. 
He said: ''Friendship and competition are in first place but friendship is still the most important.''
Later, after Shen had left, a Chinese journalist based in the West, who had translated the interview, offered another view of the shift in sports values: ''Friendship is still more important,'' he said, ''but the best way to show respect for somebody is to compete hard in sports.''
The role of athletes is still evolving. 
Zhu Jianhua is given larger portions of meat to sustain energy in his tall, slender frame, yet Zhu feels the need to share his rations with his fellow dormitory students. 
Zhu is allowed to train in his home of Shanghai rather than in the sports centers in Peking.
Xin Yun-Zhang, the young physicist from Peking living in San Diego, said ''all China will watch closely to see what happens here.''
He said he thought his homeland was becoming more expectant of results, but he added: ''The difference is expression. 
Here, the athletes are making more money, they are millionaires. 
In China, you are valued more that people will respect you. 
There is privilege in a different sense.''
Now there are rising expectations, the prospect of small grants for winning gold medals, and the hope from Mr. Lu, the assistant chef de mission:
''Friendship and understanding, peace through the world Olympic movement,'' he said, adding, ''This is a chance to learn from other nations.''
Also, he said, ''our athletes have been preparing in order to win glory for our nation.''

SAN FRANCISCO, March 19 - Hu Na, a 19-year-old Chinese tennis player who defected here last summer, says one of the reasons she decided to act was her feeling that Chinese officials were trying to coerce her into joining the Communist Party.
Miss Hu's case has become a serious issue in United States-Chinese relations, which have already been strained by Peking's unhappiness over United States arms sales to Taiwan, quotas on Chinese textile imports and restrictions on the sale of American technology to China.

Effect on Family Feared
Edward C.Y.

Her father is an army basketball coach and her younger brother is a star junior tennis player.
But Mr. Lau said that because of the Government's procrastination over her efforts to gain asylum, he had decided to let Miss Hu end her seclusion and tell her story. 
Last weekend he took her to Washington, where she met with several senators and represenatives who have expressed interest in her plight. 
These included Representative Stephen J. Solarz, Democrat of Brooklyn, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Asian and Pacific Affairs, who invited her to play tennis at his house with Zbigniew Brzezinski, President Carter's national security adviser, last Saturday.
Miss Hu is not sure what she will do if she is finally granted asylum. 
She says she recognizes she is not nearly as good a tennis player as Martina Navratilova, the Czechoslovak defector, and though she has been offered tennis scholarships to two small colleges she speaks only a few words of English and has not been to school since she began playing tennis full time at the age of 14.
In the interview Miss Hu said she had decided to defect after the Communist Party leader of the tennis camp where she had trained wrote her a letter virtually demanding she join the party. 
She said he had frequently advised her, ''The Communist Party has raised you and you owe your success to the party.''
Â 
'I Didn't Feel Safe'
But she was afraid he only wanted to use her as a model for other young Chinese and as a pawn in his own factional battles in the party. 
She recalled that China's world champion table tennis player, Zhuang Zedong, who had risen to be Minister of Sports during the Cultural Revolution, was sent to a labor camp after the downfall of his sponsor, Jiang Qing, Mao Zedong's widow, in 1976.
''So I didn't feel safe,'' Miss Hu said. 
''You never know when one faction is going to be replaced by another.''
Miss Hu's case presents an embarrassing situation for the Reagan Administration, which risks offending either the Chinese or the President's conservative supporters in the United States. 
Her application for asylum also raises the question of whether the United States has one standard for dealing with defectors from the Soviet Union and another for those from China.
A State Department official familiar with Miss Hu's case said it had touched off prolonged wrangling between the China desk, which opposed the request, and the Bureau of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs, which favored it. 
The Human Rights Bureau won the argument and made a favorable recommendation to the Immigration and Naturalization Service last November. 
But some officers on the China desk have continued to lobby out of channels with the Immigration Service, the official said. 
By law, the Immigration Service makes the final determination on requests for asylum, though it usually follows the recommendation of the State Department.
Mr. Lau said the Immigration Service had repeatedly assured him since early January that a decision on Miss Hu's request was imminent. 
But last week, Mr. Lau said, the Immigration Service submitted further questions to the State Department about Miss Hu, and the State Department official said the Immigration Service itself was now divided over what to do.
Â 
Other Requests Pending
The Immigration Service appears to be worried that granting Miss Hu asylum would set a precedent that could affect the more than 1,000 pending applications from other Chinese citizens now in this country. 
That figure is about 10 percent of the 10,000 or so Chinese on extended visits here, mostly students and scholars. 
So far fewer that than a dozen of these requests have been approved.
Last July, at a hearing before an Immigration Service judge in San Francisco for a Chinese meteorologist, Xia Yuren, a State Department official advised the judge that the Chinese scientist would not be in danger of persecution if he was deported to China. 
Mr. Xia, who had come to the United States to conduct research at the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, had applied for asylum after jumping out of a window at the Chinese Consulate in San Francisco, where he had been taken by the Chinese authorities.
The State Department official, Lawrence L. Arthur, chief of the Asylum Division of the Bureau of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs, said in written testimony that he was sure Mr. Xia was in no danger because the State Department had checked with the Chinese Embassy in Washington.
In response, Chalmers Johnson, a professor of political science at the University of California at Berkeley and a specialist on China, told the judge that if a Foreign Service officer gave similar assurances about a Soviet defector after getting in touch with the Soviet Embassy he would probably be ''fired on the spot.''

text:
ï»¿
A GENERATION gap has formed in diving; the age of world-class talent has been dropping precipitously, so that suddenly veterans with two decades of training - and the maturity and grace that come with it - are finding themselves upset by tiny acrobats barely half their age.
The authors of this innovation are the Chinese, who in the last two years have loosed a childrens' brigade of spinning, grinning - and winning - divers.
They include 14-year-old Chen Xiaodan, who in May at the McDonald's International meet in Boca Raton, Fla., upset the defending Olympic silver medalist, Michele Mitchell of the United States. 
The year before at the same meet, Mitchell had just barely held off two other 14-year-olds.
''When I saw these little girls for the first time I said, 'What is this?''' said Mitchell, who is 26 and on the 1988 American Olympic team. 
''Every meet we go to they send different teams.''
Diving is one of the sports in which China has made dramatic progress since returning to international sports in the late 1970's. 
The three medals - I gold, I silver and I bronze - that Chinese divers pocketed at the Los Angeles Games contributed to the 32 medals over all the nation wona fter a three-decade absence from the Olympics. 
Since 1984, Chinese divers have only grown stronger. 
The program that produces them offers a paradigm of Beijing's emergence as the newest sports power.
In the four Olympic events (men's and women's 3-meter springboard and 10-meter platform), Chinese are favorites to sweep both women's gold medals; to strongly contend for both men's golds, and to take home the majority of silvers.
When people ask how have they done it, they are usually asking, What is their secret?
As far as any one factor has made the difference, it is the sports system that Beijing has put in place since the close of the Cultural Revolution, which is similar to that in many Communist nations.
The Chinese sports system is wide-cast and elitist, designed to net promising athletes from the largest talent pool on earth - a population of more than one billion - then measure progress in training, promoting the best and rejecting the average.
In the United States, if a youngster wants to learn an ''amateur'' Olympic sport like diving, his or her parents seek out a private program, like Ron O'Brien's Mission Bay club in Boca Raton, Fla. 
As long as parents can pay, O'Brien, who is the Olympic diving coach this year, and his staff presumably continue to train a youngster.
In China, diving coaches fan out from 3,400 part-time sports schools to recruit their charges. 
It is a rigorous meritocracy, beginning with strength and flexibility tests to detect aptitude in kids who have probably never seen a swimming pool. 
There is also some preselection based on the body type coaches believe makes good divers; short, compact, perhaps with hyperextended elbows, that is, elbows that touch when the arms are raised above the head, making for a less splashly entry in the water.
''We have set up selection criteria for most sports: the average height, weight, ratio of upper body to lower body, and circumference of various limbs,'' said Dr. Gao Chongxuan of the National Research Institute of Sports Science in Beijing. 
''In the West, your primary schools have pools, a gymnasium, even their own tennis courts. 
We don't have enough facilities, so we have to select athletes who've never played sports before.''
The ultimate sign of success is that there are fresh faces among the Chinese at nearly every meet. 
It's hard to highlight the country's top candidates for Seoul (who will be chosen by coaches rather than at trials) because there's no guarantee last year's world champion hasn't been shocked in training by a youngster who only began climbing the diving tower a few season ago, Tong Hui, who won the men's 10-meter World Cup in 1987, witnessed the same year as 13-year-old named Xiong Ni move up from the provinces to joint the national team in Beijing. 
That year, Xiong finished sixth in the McDonald's International. 
This year at the same meet he upstaged American Matt Scoggin for first.
Xiong, whose dives have nearly the same degree of difficulty as those of Greg Louganis, is one of a crew of Chinese putting pressure on the double-gold medal-winner of 1984. 
Early this year, China's top springboarder, Tan Liangde, ended a six-year victory streak Louganis had enjoyed. 
And he has since beaten Louganis again.
It takes one's breath away to see 5-foot-3-inch, 105-pound Xiong in a handstand at the very lip of the 33-foot platform, as tall as a three-story building, before the plummets into a blue abyss. 
This does not seem like a sport for kids. 
In the United States it is unheard of for divers of such tender age to perform the complex somersaults and twists of top-notch dives. 
Wendy Lian Williams, a 20-year-old University of Miami junior who finished fifth on platform at the McDonald's meet and will compete in the event at Seoul, said, ''I'm young for American diving, but I get to these meets and I feel old.''
Much of the credit for introducing extreme youth to the sport belongs to Xu Yiming, the head national coach in China, whose system emphasizes fast spinning and clean entries. 
Small bodies seem to have an advantage in both areas, and small means young. 
The Chinese are masters of the ripped entry, an almost splashless finale that sounds like fabric being torn, which is created when a diver locks his wrists and hits the water with hands flat, drilling a hole through which the entire body follows.
In the late 1970's, Xu, who had been a national champion in the arly 1960's before his career was idled by the Cultural Revolution, became a fixture at international competitions, along with his video camera. 
He focused the camera on the world's top divers, as well as on modern pools, weight training gear, even locker rooms. 
Back in Beijing, Xu, an authorization, nuts-and-bolts coach, had his athletes analyze and imitate the techniques of the world's best divers.
But at big international competitions the Chinese for years did not live up to their potential. 
They lacked mental intensity, or just the confidence that comes from international experience.
The Chinese have learned from their competitive misfires. 
Beginning at the 1986 world championships, the current crop of female prodigies began maturing. 
Gao Min, then 16, won the springboard title and has remained the world's best ever since. 
In the 1987 Xu Yanmei, 16, won the World Cup platform title. 
Both World Cup women's silver medals went to Chinese.
