file: THE SEOUL OLYMPICS_The Games, From Archery to Yachting_ Diving.txt
text:
ï»¿
Gymnastics can be pretty and figure skating can be elegant, but for many people, no sport matches the esthetic and athletic beauty of diving. 
A good dive is easy to recognize, and television's slow-motion replays make a good dive even more enjoyable.
For years, the best divers were Americans. 
Now the best, or most of the best, are Chinese. 
They should dominate the four Olympic events, the men's and women's 3-meter springboard and 10-meter platform.
Of the 12 medals in the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, the United States won 8 and China 3. 
Of the 12 in the 1986 world championships in Madrid, China won 7 and the United States 4. 
Ron O'Brien, the United States Olympic coach, said he would be happy if his team won five medals in Seoul. 
Look for the Chinese to win seven or eight medals, the United Sates three or four and the Soviet Union one.
Of those American medals, two (probably gold) should come from Grey Louganis, who won both men's events in 1984. 
Now, at the age of 28, he is no longer unbeatable and his motivation and physical soundness have wavered, but he usually dives well when it counts and he remains the best diver in history. 
His main opposition will come from the Chinese: Tan Liangde on the springboard and 14-year-old Xiong Ni off the platform.
In the women's springboard, Kelly McCormick, the American silver medalist in 1984, must face 18-year-old Gao Min and Li Qing of China. 
In the women's platform, Michele Mitchell, the 1984 silver medalist, and Wendy Lian Williams, the other American, will contend for medals with Xu Yanmei of China and Elena Miroshina of the Soviet Union.
In springobard, the men do 11 dives, the women 10. 
In platform, the med do 10, the women 8. 
About half the dives are more or less basic and required.
Each diver does all his dives in the preliminaries. 
Then the 12 leaders in each event advance to the final, where preliminary scores are thrown out and all dives are repeated.
The diver tries to fill all requirements of his dive (somersaults, twists, body position, etc.) and finish with a vertical entry and minimal splash. 
Scoring is done by seven judges from different nations. 
After watching a diver's approach, takeoff, action in the air and entry, they give him from 0 points to 10 (for a perfect dive).
To minimize prejudicial scoring, the high and low score on each dive are thrown out. 
The five remaining scores are added, then divided by three-fifths, then multiplied by that dive's degree of difficulty.
The dives are clustered into six groups: forward, back, reverse, inward, twisting and (from the platform only) armstand. 
Four body positions are used; straight (body not bent, like a swan dive), pike (body bent only at the waist, like a jackknife), tuck (knees tight against the chest) and free (no restrictions).

file: TRANSLATING BASEBALL INTO CHINESE.txt
text:
ï»¿
When C. W. Post's baseball team opened a six-game exhibition series with Chinese squads here last week, something happened that the American players didn't expect: They lost.
In fact, the Pioneers, the regular-season champions of the New York Metropolitan Conference, lost twice - by 6-4 on June 3 to Peking, and by 4-3 the next day to a Sichuan Province team.
Since then, Post has bounced back with three victories. 
The final game, against Peking, will be played here Tuesday.
C W Post College baseball team, playing exhibition series with teams in China, lost first three games but bounced back with three victories; final game is to be played on June 11; American team members comment on difficulties they have in using Chinese-made baseballs; photo (M)
Aside from the surprising skill shown by their hosts, especially in base-running, the Post players have advanced many reasons for their defeats in a country where baseball is hardly the national passtime. 
These range from jet lag and overconfidence to questionable umpiring and strange ball parks.
However, perhaps the most interesting problem cited by the Americans in their first two games was a bagful of slippery, lumpy, seamless spheres of varying sizes: Chinese baseballs.
''This is a weird feeling, especially if your hands are wet with sweat,'' said Rick Wohlmacher, a C. W. Post pitcher from New Hyde Park, L.I., squeezing one of the Chinese balls in his palm. 
''I couldn't grip it, I had no control.''
Wohlmacher, one of the team's top pitchers the past two seasons, walked five and gave up four hits and five runs in 5Y innings before being relieved in the first game against Peking.
Â 
American Baseballs Used
The Chinese approved a switch to American baseballs in the third game, at Tianjin. 
C. W. Post responded by scoring four runs in the first inning on back-to-back home runs by the captain, Mike Alfano, and Joe Cioffi. 
Post went on to punch 11 hits in the 7-4 victory at Tianjin, 137 kilometers east of Peking.
The second game at Tianjin was played with a Chinese ball, which Alfano, the third baseman, said ''doesn't really carry - it''s softer.''
Nevertheless, Alfano, who has been drafted by the Atlanta Braves, hit two home runs, and his team won, 10-6.
The next day Ron Lupo, a pitcher from Commack, L.I., got a return match against Sichuan. 
In his first outing against that team, with the Chinese ball, Lupo, noted for his control, walked nine. 
The second time, with an American ball, Lupo went the distance in an 8-3 victory, walking only three and throwing five strikeouts.
Â 
Chinese Aggressive Runners
Apart from the controversy over the Chinese balls, which clearly seems to have generated more humor than hostility here, the Post players say they are highly impressed with the Chinese style of play. 
In particular, their hosts are extremely aggressive on the basepaths, and appear to get their way. 
The Chinese teams have stolen 26 bases in 35 attempts over the 5 games played so far. 
Post has stolen only three bases in nine attempts. 
In the 8-3 loss to Lupo, they stole 12 bases in 13 attempts.
''They run no matter what the score is,'' said Coach Dick Vining of C. W. Post. 
''There''ll be a man on second with no outs and they'll try to steal third.''
Post's sports information director, Bill Huffman, noted that the Chinese ''love to build runs,'' and are fond of bunting and sacrifice hitting. 
''They think of their baserunner as a resource,'' Huffman said. 
''They think, 'We've got to get this guy across the plate.'
There are no ego trips.''
Â 
Hitting Is Limited
On the other hand, the Chinese are simply not long-ball hitters. 
They have not hit any home runs in the series; their American opponents have hit six.
The fences at Peking's all-dirt Fengtai Field, one of the few baseball diamonds in China, are a Ty-Cobb distance from home plate - about 400 feet down the line and 450 feet to a billboard in left-center field that reads in Chinese, ''Friendship first, competition second.''
The games at Peking have each drawn no more than a few hundred onlookers, but this appears to be because the field is in the southwest suburbs and is difficult to reach by public transportation. 
At the more centrally located stadium in Tianjin, last Thursday's game drew 2,000 spectators.
Baseball once enjoyed some popularity in this country, but was banned at the start of the cultural revolution in 1966. 
It is now being officially encouraged, and Liang Youde, an official with the Peking Institute of Sports research, said China has ambitions to turn out a good team for the 1986 Asian Games or 1988 Olympics at Seoul, or at least in time for the 1990 Asian Games, which are being hosted by Peking.
Â 
Kuhn Is Encouraged
''You can look at the Taiwanese, the Japanese and the Koreans, and you don't have to use your imagination to think that the Chinese will do sensationally at baseball if they just hang in there for a while,'' said the former major league commissioner, Bowie Kuhn, who was sitting in the stands last Saturday with the president of the Los Angeles Dodgers, Peter O'Malley.
Kuhn said his interest in promoting baseball in the world's most populous country dates back to 1974, when the head of the United States Mission in Peking, a former Yale baseball player by the name of George Bush, saw a game and contacted the commissioner.
''George called and said, ''They're playing baseball over here,'' Kuhn said of Bush, now the Vice President.
As C. W. Post prepares for its final match, team members have alluded to one other possible reason for their resurgence after such a slow start here. 
Two Pioneer pitchers who have had problems this past season with tendinitis, Lou Burmester and Mike Juman, have experimented with acupuncture treatments here and both say they are very pleased with the results.
''It was painless and pretty effective,'' said Juman, who is from Merrick, L.I. 
''After acupuncture, I pitched pretty well, as a matter of fact.''

file: U.S. TEAM WINS GYMNASTICS IN MAJOR UPSET OVER CHINESE.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United States men's gymnastics team, alternately cautious and daring, won the team gold medal in tonight, upsetting the reigning world champions from China.
''This is certainly comparable to the U.S. hockey team winning the gold medal in 1980,'' said Abie Grossfeld, the team's head coach, as a near-capacity crowd of 9,356 at Pauley Pavilion waved American flags and chanted ''U.S.A.!
U.S.A.!'' behind him.
The startling victory capped a day of competition in which the United States continued to dominate swimming, winning all five finals including a victory by Rick Carey of Mount Kisco, N.Y., in the men's 200-meter backstroke. 
The United States also won a gold in shooting as 18-year-old Pat Spurgin of Billings, Mont. took the women's air rifle competition. 
The Americans won seven gold medals yesterday to bring their total to 16 gold - 11 in swimming - in three days. 
In addition, the American men's and women's basketball teams looked impressive in winning their second games in the round-robin competitions.
US men's gymnastics team wins team gold medal at Los Angeles Olympic Games, upsetting reigning world champions from China; photo of Mitch Gaylord and James Hartung, team members; Americans win seven gold medals on July 31, bringing their total to 16 gold in three days (M)
''It's the best feeling I ever had in my life,'' said Mitch Gaylord, who successfully completed his risky and dangerous stunt on the horizontal bar that is known as the ''Gaylord II.''
The stunt received a score of 9.95 and helped helped preserve the American victory over the the Chinese by the score of 591.40 to 590.80.
''And it's great for our sport,'' he added, ''it's a whole new era for gymnastics,.''
It was the first team medal in gymnastics for the United States since it won a silver in the five-team men's competition of 1932.
The Americans took a 1.05 point lead into the evening's competition, built in the compulsory exercises on Sunday. 
That lead had been whittled to .60 of a point by the time the teams faced their final exercise - the horizontal bar for the Americans and floor exercise for the Chinese.
The high bar is usually the Americans' best event. 
But just one fall from the bar would mean an automatic deduction of .50 of a point. 
So with such a slim lead to protect, they felt pressure to tone down the difficulty of their routines and go for more modest but more perfectly-executed performances, including less difficult dismounts.
''We saw the Chinese doing easier dismounts and gettings 10's,'' said Peter Vidmar, who had the best individual all-around score, edging China's Li Ning by .05 of a point. 
The Chinese were in the rotation just ahead of the United States team, and had scored two 10's on the rings using relatively simple dismounts, brilliantly executed.
Each of them did take out certain more difficult moves from their still rings and high bar routines, to be a bit cautious. 
But when the time came to take risks, in the last event and with the gold medal on the line, they were game.
''Jim Hartung came up to me and said, 'This is the Olympic Games - let's go for it,' '' said Vidmar. 
''and so Scott Johnson did his double-double, and Tim Daggett did his triple back, and I did my double-double and landed on my feet.''
Daggett hit his triple back somersault dismount perfectly, and got a perfect 10 as his reward. 
Vidmar hit his double-double - a double somersault with two twists - and got a 9.95 score. 
But those two were the last Americans to perform, and before they jumped onto the bar, the situaion had gotten very uncertain.
Although Johnson decided, like his teammates, to keep his tough dismount in his routine, he missed it - and his off-balance landing cost him badly, as he got a 9.50 score.
The lowest score of the six team members is always discarded. 
But that put a lot of pressure on Gaylord. 
He could not afford to get a low score, too, and he and the coach wondered if he should risk trying the Gaylord II. 
It is a supremely difficult maneuver done in midair above the bar, in which he does a one-and-a-half somersault with a half twist, then recatches the bar. 
More often than not, he misses the bar.
''And we already had one miss from Scott's performance,'' said Bart Conner, who had gotten a 10 on the parallel bars in the previous rotation, ''so Mitch was really up against the wall.''
Gaylord didn't miss. 
He soared above the bar, the crowd collectively caught its breath, he caught the bar, and the crowd gasped and then cheered. 
The score: a 9.95.
''He's been trying that move for the last six months with the intention of using it in the Olympic Games - he's not going to take it out now,'' said Gaylord's older brother, Chuck, who is also his coach. 
''It was a case of Mitch's style of gymnastics. 
He's never settled for a 9.9, he's always gone for the 10.''
Even his teammates were impressed.
''I told Mitch, 'You did the trick and you did it when it had to be done,' '' said Conner. 
''That's tough. 
My hat's off to him.''
Gaylord had given the American team a boost early in the evening, too. 
On the second rotation, while the Americans were having some problems on the pommel horse, the Chinese were wowing the judges on the rings. 
Both their stars, Li Ning and Tong Fei, scored perfect 10's, the first such scores of the evening.
Â 
A 10 on the Rings
But the Americans were on the rings next, and Gaylord earned a 10 on them, too.
''We felt like we showed 'em right there we can be as perfect as they can,'' said Vidmar.
There will always be a question about how well the Americans would have done if the Soviet Union team had been here. 
The Soviets won the gold medal in 1980 in Moscow, although they were upset by .10 of a point by the Chinese at the world championships in Budapest last October.
''The Chinese beat the Soviets and we beat the Chinese,'' said Conner, the 26-year-old veteran of this team, who has been on the American gymnastics scene for a decade and remembers the days when Americans were always at the bottom of the international heap.
''I could've been up in the stands watching, after having been part of all the momentum that built up over the years,'' he said. 
''And I'm so glad I'm here, and I'm performing, when we finally reached our goal.''
Not only is he here, he's in fourth place in the individual all-around standings. 
Each man's scores from the team competition, compulsories and optionals, are averaged to obtain a preliminary score. 
Compulsories are a set of identical routines with certain required elements, performed by all competitors. 
Optionals are routines devised by each contestant and varying in difficulty and style.
The top 36 athletes advance to the all-around finals, on Thursday, where they will do another round of optional exercises to determine the individual all-around medalists.
Vidmar has the lead in preliminary scores, with 59.275 points to the 59.225 of Li. 
Tong is third with 59.20, and Conner has 59.15 points.
For Vidmar, the excitement was so much that, as he walked away from the victory stand in the center of Pauley Pavilion after getting his medal and hearing his national anthem, he almost fainted.
''I suddenly got very, very light- headed and almost passed out,'' he said. 
''I think it was from all the shouting and yelling we were doing. 
I got real dizzy, but then I figured, so what if I pass out?
I've still got this medal around my neck.''

file: VIEWS OF SPORTS_IN CHINA, A NEW PASTIME, THOUGH NOT QUITE NATIONAL.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE North China air was a cool 55 degrees and the silver poplar trees were budding. 
A slight breeze puffed swirls of dust up from the athletic field. 
The players were already warming up, woolen winter underwear peeping out from under the cuffs of their baggy pants. 
Their movements were awkward and a constant laughter belied their nervousness.
This was the first baseball game to be played in rural Shanxi Province, several hundred miles west of Peking, since the sport was banned following the 1949 revolution. 
Some baseball equipment had been found locked in a closet in the field house of the agricultural university where I was teaching.
''Must have been left here by some American missionaries,'' said the student who had brought the equipment to my office. 
Several cloth softballs, their wrappings yellow with age, rocked gently on my desk. 
The dry climate had also preserved the stubby baseball gloves and kept the slim bats from rotting.
First we talked about getting up a game. 
But, as so often happens in China, politics threatened to get in the way. 
Baseball had been introduced to China by American missionaries in the 19th century. 
Because of this association with the West, the Chinese Communists had denounced baseball as a bourgeois and decadent sport. 
Although the Chinese government was now seeking rapprochement with the West, change comes slowly to backwater regions like Shanxi Province. 
The student hemmed and hawed, unwilling to take responsibility for organizing the game. 
And so it fell to me. 
I scheduled the game for the following Sunday, telling only selected friends. 
If threatened by the authorities for playing baseball, they could always say they did it to please me, a visiting American English teacher who could not be punished for political mistakes.
So it was that one nippy afternoon a few years ago, baseball returned to Shanxi. 
Two dozen players gathered on a rutted yellow dirt field at the back of the small campus. 
A major road cut by the field, leading to a college store and a gate, beyond which peasants sold their produce in an open market.
One elderly player, a retired gym teacher, had umpired a few games in the 1940's, and could still say ''ball'' and ''strike'' in English. 
He explained the rules, or what he remembered of them, to the other players. 
And by dribbling lime powder from a paper bag, he marked off a rough diamond on the school athletic field.
My team batted first. 
A powerful tractor driver named Zhang from Manchuria stepped into the batter's box. 
He swung hard at an inside pitch and met it squarely. 
The bat, brittle with age, split in two and rifled back over our heads. 
Zhang stared at the stump of wood left in his hand and then took off for third.
''No!
No!,'' we screamed from the sideline. 
''Run to first!''
Zhang wheeled sharply and charged diagonally across the diamond. 
He collided with the pitcher. 
But scrambling on his hands and knees, he made it to first and stood up triumphant, yellow dust billowing from his once blue clothing.
The next batter, a graduate student named Liu, sauntered up to the batter's box. 
He spat on the ground and mashed the spittle into the earth. 
Then he deliberately twisted his blue Mao cap around so the brim covered the nape of his neck. 
''I saw an American player do this on television,'' he said.
Liu hit a grounder. 
He rounded first just as the first baseman caught the ball. 
Liu headed for second, the first baseman chasing after him with the ball. 
Meanwhile, Zhang had stopped at second, probably assuming that players progress only one base at a time. 
Liu barreled into him. 
They took the first and second basemen down with them.
A wheat specialist named Mei was up next. 
He said he was an old hand, having played baseball in missionary school in the 1940's. 
He was very short, and by crouching down he practically eliminated his strike zone. 
He got to first on a walk.
By now the game was attracting quite a crowd. 
Peasants and students were swarming onto the field. 
In China, when people see a line, they stand behind it. 
So here they stood on the edge of the infield. 
When our team took the field, I played shortstop. 
I tried to explain to the hundreds of people standing between second and third that this was dangerous. 
But the sight of a tall foreigner waving his arms and speaking Chinese only caused the crowd to swell.
A line drive was hit to third. 
I dove into the crowd, knocking over bicycles and trampling on feet in a frenzy to get the ball. 
But it seemed to have vanished. 
Finally someone tapped me on the arm. 
It was an old peasant woman tottering on bound feet, her cracked lips spread wide in a toothless grin. 
Her hands were raised to me as if offering tea. 
But she was proffering the softball instead.
The old woman was luckier than a student who was beaned a short time later by a pop fly. 
As the ball plummeted down, the crowd in the outfield scattered as if being strafed by a fighter plane. 
But one student hesitated for a moment and the ball thudded down on her. 
She fell to the ground clutching her head to ward off any further attacks. 
After that, people decided that maybe it was wise to move to the sidelines.
The game continued for four more innings. 
The most dramatic play was made by a boiler repairman playing right field who stopped the ball from rolling into the outhouse cesspool. 
The final score was 10-10; all the runs scored on errors.
For several days afterward, we nervously awaited a reaction from the authorities. 
But no wall posters appeared condemning baseball. 
At the weekly political study session, the game was not mentioned. 
In China, no reaction means tacit approval. 
We began playing baseball every Sunday afternoon.
Soon, the workers in a nearby herbal-medicine factory organized a team and challenged us. 
Then a chemical fertilizer plant got up a team and joined the competition. 
By summer, 10 teams were battling each other. 
And with each game, more baseball equipment kept turning up. 
It was like the equipment I had seen on my desk in the early spring, old and worn after having been locked away, presumably forever.

file: _84 OLYMPIC EFFORT A GREAT LEAP FORWARD FOR CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
PEKING WHEN China went to its first Olympic Games, in Los Angeles in 1932, its squad consisted of a 100- meter sprinter, who was eliminated in the trials, and his coach.
Fifty-two years later, China is returning to Los Angeles with an Olympic squad of 200 athletes and 100 coaches, doctors and other officials. 
''So after a half-century, the number of people has increased 150 times,'' Wu Zhongyuan, the spokesman for the Chinese Olympic Committee, quipped recently.
The Chinese admit that they do not expect to do very well. 
But their participation in the 1984 Olympics marks the most significant step yet taken toward Peking's announced goal of developing into a major sports power by the end of the century.
China's hopes for a respectable showing, and maybe even a gold medal, are focused on the Summer Games at Los Angeles. 
Only 40 Chinese are going to the Winter Games next month at Sarajevo, Yugoslavia, to compete in the Alpine and Nordic skiing, speed and figure skating and biathlon. 
The hockey team is being kept home. 
The Chinese sports newspaper has conceded that in winter sports ''China is still a long way from the advanced world levels.''
China intends to compete in 15 events at Los Angeles, with selective strengths in track and field, weight lifting, gymnastics and women's volleyball. 
It will be the first time that the Communist mainland will be represented at an Olympics by a full contingent of athletes.
Some Chinese swimmers showed up late at the Helsinki Olympics in 1952 to put in a desultory showing. 
China was readmitted to the Olympic movement in 1979, and it sent a small team to the 1980 Winter Games at Lake Placid, but it joined the boycott of the subsequent Summer Games in Moscow to protest the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan.
With its propensity for slogans, China has coined a militant challenge for sports: ''Break out of Asia and advance on the world.''
It has already come a long way. 
China had a weak sports tradition and was debilitated by famine, war and revolution well into the 20th century. 
After the Communists took over in 1949, they began developing organized sports, but the effort unraveled when radical politics took priority during the 1966-1976 Cultural Revolution.
''Before the Cultural Revolution, we were doing quite well,'' recalled Li Pingta, an official of the All-China Sports Federation. 
''Our weight lifting, track and field and swimming were all good. 
Due to the cultural revolution, some of these were dragged back down again.''
Sports have been revived under the pragmatic regime of Deng Xiaoping, China's current leader. 
The Government claims that 300 million Chinese, nearly a third of the population of 1 billion, now engage in some kind of physical training.
Children are being selected early for their potential and sent after classes to thousands of ''spare-time'' sports schools, a less intense version of the Soviet sports-training machine. 
And the five proficiency grades for athletes, borrowed from the Russians in 1956, and dropped 10 years later, have been restored for 37 sports categories.
Li Menghua, the minister in charge of the State Physical Culture and Sports Commission, told a conference last March that the goal of China's physical culture in this century was to produce athletes with both sportsmanship and outstanding skills who would rank China among the major world sports powers by the year 2000.
Some of the sports that China does best, like table tennis, badminton and kung fu, are not yet recognized as Olympic events. 
Mr. Wu said that Chinese athletes had reached world competition levels in only a third of some 40 popular sports.
''Except for a few events, our track and field is weak,'' Li Pingta said. 
''Swimming on the whole is weak. 
Of course, everyone knows our soccer team cannot break out of the pack in Asia. 
This is something everybody is concerned about.''
Ironically, China, which has the most bicycles in the world, also does poorly in cycling. 
''In China, we take cycling as a means of transport,'' Mr. Wu explained.
The Chinese have not been hesitant about importing foreign expertise. 
An American skier quietly helped coached the ski team. 
A Bulgarian has taught rhythmic gymnastics, and a Brazilian is being brought in to coach the lackluster soccer team.
In the race to catch up, China has joined 46 international sports organizations, according to Mr. Wu. Chinese athletes began to dominate regional competition by capturing 61 gold medals at the 1982 Asian Games in New Delhi. 
China has applied to hold the 1990 Asian Games in Peking, and plans to build new sports facilities if it is chosen.
China used to denigrate the importance of winning with the old Maoist motto, ''Friendship first, competition second.''
Now its athletes are taught that victories are necessary to earn respect for China in the eyes of the world.
''We'll require our sportsmen to get the best achievements and win honor for the motherland, and our players are determined to do so,'' said Li Pingta, in discussing China's attitude toward the Summer Olympics.
China's best chance for a gold medal at Los Angeles is Zhu Jianhua, a lanky Shanghai student who broke the world record for the high jump twice in 1983. 
The 20-year-old Zhu cleared 2.38 meters (7 feet 9 3/4 inches) at the National Games last September in Shanghai. 
The Chinese press has treated the Shanghai Games as a dress rehearsal for the Olympics.
Although Zhu remains the world champion high jumper, it is uncertain how well he will do under the pressure of international competition, since he took only a bronze medal at the world track and field championships in Helsinki last August.
Another hopeful is Wu Shude, a 24- year-old weight lifter in the 56-kilo class who set a world record by snatching 128 kilos (281.6 pounds) at Shanghai. 
China also has some strong divers, like Li Yihua and Tan Liangde. 
Li Qiaoxian, a 16-year-old diver, was recently identified as a new star by the Chinese youth newspaper.
With Li Ning and Tong Fei, China is fielding its best men's gymnastic team, which beat the Soviet team to capture the team title at the world gymnastics championships in Budapest last October. 
The women's volleyball team, which took two world championships in a row, is also a serious contender. 
Its strongest player, Lang Ping, has been nicknamed The Hammer for her powerful spikes.
But the Olympic committee has played down the likelihood of a strong showing. 
Wu Zhongyuan told reporters: ''We predict that we will not get good results. 
We predict that we will do better in shooting, women's volleyball, diving, some track and field, weight lifting, fencing and gymnastics and maybe in archery. 
As for the other events, we still have quite a distance to catch up.''
China's Olympic team theoretically still has to be selected, but the principal criteria are the performances at Shanghai last September. 
Mr. Wu said that the athletes chosen would meet in Peking next April to begin final training. 
''There is a half- year left before the Summer Games, so our athletes will still have a lot of international competition,'' he said.
China expects to spend 3 million yuan, about $1.5 million, on its participation in the Winter and Summer Olympics, according to Li Guochang, the director of the secretariat of the Chinese Olympic Committee.
Mr. Li said that this covered training, accommodation and travel expenses for the athletes. 
He did not specify whether this budget included services supplied by state-run organizations such as China's airline, C.A.A.C. 
(Civil Aviation Administration of China). 
By comparison, the United States Olympic Committee budget is $80.1 million.
Chinese athletes have not been exempted from ideological obligations. 
A Peking newspaper reported not long ago that the swimming team was studying the writings of Deng Xiaoping as part of its preparation. 
Mr. Wu explained: ''Every day the swimmers will take a half hour or an hour. 
That's not the whole day.''
Mr. Wu said that the Olympic athletes would be educated in Socialist spiritual civilization, a patriotic concept of behavior that rejects Western values, before they went to Los Angeles. 
He recalled that the high jumper Zhu Jianhua has undertaken political study.
This is intended partly to discourage embarrassing defections. 
After the tennis player Hu Na was given political asylum in the United States in 1982, China angrily suspended official bilateral sports and cultural exchanges for the next year.
Mr. Wu insisted that ''we are not afraid,'' because China held the United States responsible for preventing such incidents as part of the security measures for the Summer Games.

file: A Hint of Doubt In Every Shiny Medal.txt
text:
ï»¿
Anybody who follows sports has long become inured to the-dog-ate-my-homework stories emanating from athletes whose bodily fluids have yielded a trace of one substance or another. 
It tends to make us all a tad suspicious.
Back in 1998, for example, an Olympic snowboarder from Canada who tested positive for marijuana vaguely remembered walking into a party weeks earlier where somebody might have been smoking. 
The authorities took away his gold medal -- mostly for not being able to come up with a better story than that. 
(The snowboarder, Ross Rebagliati, eventually got his medal back after it was determined the rules were not specific enough about the consumption of marijuana.)
America's career home run leader, Barry Bonds, once reportedly tested positive for amphetamines and explained that he had borrowed them from a teammate's locker. 
The teammate called him on it and, fine fellow that he is, Barry recanted.
Some soccer countries lop a few years off players' ages so they can ace a junior tournament. 
Make the guy shave three times a day and hope he doesn't get caught.
The Beijing Games have had minimal drug busts, so far -- except for the traces of illegal chili pepper on four horses competing in Hong Kong, that is -- but the big question is whether the Chinese gymnasts were under age.
The gymnastics chickens still may come home to roost. 
On Friday, the International Olympic Committee said it was looking into accusations that a few medal-winning Chinese gymnasts might have been younger than 16. 
This minimum exists to keep little children from being exploited by manipulative coaches and twisting their bodies out of kilter. 
Over 16, it's fine.
At the end of July, The New York Times reported the possibility of evidence that He Kexin and Jiang Yuyuan were really 14 and not 16. 
One could argue that they both look 12, but the documents submitted by the Chinese federation says they are 16. 
There are also doubts about Yang Yilin.
After the gymnastics competition ended, the I.O.C. requested more information from the Chinese about the gymnasts. 
This is not an inquiry or an investigation, the I.O.C. insisted. 
Just a request.
''We have asked the gymnastics federation to look into a number of discrepancies,'' said Giselle Davies, the I.O.C. spokesperson, who said the federation was cooperating in the matter.
James Scherr, the chief executive officer of the United States Olympic Committee, said, ''We believe in fairness to all athletes.''
He said he did not know if there was a statute of limitations on potential chicanery, and he said the U.S.O.C. certainly had no plans to hire a gumshoe to pull birth certificates from town halls in rural China.
From the Chinese perspective, Wang Wei, a spokesman for the Beijing organizing committee, said: ''The athletes have been cleared. 
If they hadn't been, they would not have been allowed to compete.''
All well and good, but Beth Tweddle of Britain, who finished fourth in the uneven bars final, could theoretically be given a medal if He, who won gold, or Yang, who won bronze, should ever be busted for being under age. 
Ksenia Semenova of Russia finished fourth in the all-around finals, with Yang third. 
And the United States women finished second in the team competition, behind the Chinese team, which included He, Jiang and Yang.
Meanwhile, the Olympic sport that has generated the most bans, suspension and lost medals -- track and field -- has been thrilling this last week mostly because Usain Bolt of Jamaica broke world records in the 100- and 200-meter sprints.
There is no suggestion that Bolt, who has been tested a minimum of five times, is under suspicion of having used drugs. 
But in that sport, just about anybody who improves drastically is under suspicion.
Some of the Jamaican women, who have come from nowhere in recent months, train on their island, which does not have an international testing laboratory. 
Gaps like that leave everybody, including the innocent, under suspicion.
''I think we can never stop cheating, but I think 99 percent, or 99.9 percent, are clean,'' said Frankie Fredericks of Namibia, a member of the I.O.C. and chairman of the athletes' commission. 
Fredericks, who won double silvers in the sprints at the 1992 and 1996 Games, said, ''I'm happy with the testing.''
Most definitely not happy with the testing are four riders whose horses tested positive for chili pepper at the Olympic equestrian center in Hong Kong. 
The four horses and their riders were suspended from Olympic show jumping Thursday after preliminary tests indicated the presence of capsaicin, a mild stimulant widely used in ointments for horses. 
More tests are scheduled in the next month.
The imaginative explanation -- I can see a few cyclists I know coming up with this one -- is that the horses accidentally got downwind from a large tray of curry. 
But the more prosaic excuse is that the portion of capsaicin was slightly higher than normal in ointment used on the horses.
In past Olympics, athletes have been disqualified because of asthma or cold medicine they said they had used innocently, but lately the testing has been upgraded, with the support of many of the athletes.
Ramped-up testing is a good sign. 
Skeptic that I am, I am waiting for the ramped-up alibis as well.

file: A Journeyman_s Most Harrowing Trip.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE bus was old, hot, cramped and slow as a herniated snail. 
A ride that should have taken 3 to 4 hours took a harrowing 13.
An international journey embarked on more than a quarter century ago, ignited by a young boy's fascination with round objects, mainly a basketball and the globe, took an unscheduled detour last month through a Middle East war zone.
''Only the most optimistic person alive would have called it intimate,'' that boy, now 57, said earlier this week during a telephone interview from a hastily arranged sanctuary in Amman, Jordan. 
Meet Paul Coughter, coach of the Lebanese national basketball team and citizen of the world, by way of Flatbush, Brooklyn.
Meet the American who engineered his players' escape from the mountains outside besieged Beirut, through a convoluted and imperiled passage north, to Syria, then south, to Amman, on the way to the World Championship of Basketball beginning next week in Japan.
''The crisis began five days after we started our training camp,'' Coughter said. 
''After two days, we sent the players home to be with their families. 
Then we realized if we didn't get out, we never would.
''I think we got the last bus in Lebanon. 
We were in our own mini-world, trying to block out everything, barely anything to eat, stopping at gas stations, places where people would say, 'Ten minutes ago, a bomb landed over there.'
They'd say, 'Look at that, it's still smoldering,' and then we're back on the bus, trying to convince ourselves that because one had already landed, it couldn't happen again.''
Do you think Larry Brown has had a peripatetic career?
Over 27 years, Coughter has coached on six continents, has stalked professional sidelines from Australia to Saudi Arabia to Taiwan, has also run the national teams of South Africa, Pakistan and Wales.
Do you believe Brown faced prohibitive odds with last season's Knicks?
Coughter's manager and trainer both stayed behind last month to tend to their families, and his American-born center, Paul Khoury, was marooned in Idaho, unable to renew his Lebanese visa, when the Beirut airport was bombed. 
His best player, Fadi El Khatib, wouldn't leave the country unless there was room on the bus -- which was made -- for his wife and young child.
Want to hear the N.B.A. soldiers of fortune whine about the wider lane and mysterious refs when the Lebanese are dealing with the rules of war?
For a team with aspirations normally no more grandiose than winning a game or two at the gathering of the world's basketball powers, there have been scant practices and serious sleep deprivation and incalculable stress.
Even Coughter, the globetrotting bachelor, the avowed adventurer who promises to retire soon and sail the world for the rest of his years on a custom-built yacht, called this latest chapter of A Coach's Life ''beyond bizarre.''
Lucky for him, he has never evaluated his career by the number of championships won, by the size of his paycheck. 
Ask for personal highlights and he tells of exploring an exotic island in New Zealand, of bunking with a Chinese family in Zimbabwe, of sipping coffee while gazing at the Mediterranean from the balcony of his most current address, the Zouk Hotel, 20 minutes from Beirut.
Coughter was born into a large Irish Catholic, basketball-loving Brooklyn family, his father having played at Erasmus Hall High School and his older brother for Joe Mullaney at Providence College. 
He remembers launching his first shot from his father's shoulders in Prospect Park, learning the game and using it to facilitate the ultimate road trip.
''It's like Larry Bird once said: 'Don't tell anyone, but I'd do this for free,' '' Coughter said. 
''For me, the whole thing is experiential.''
How else to describe the itinerary, from Lebanon to Syria to Jordan to Turkey to Slovenia, back to Jordan, on the way to the Philippines this week and then Japan to, as Coughter put it, ''carry the Lebanese flag at a time the country needs to be seen''?
When the United States is perceived in the Middle East to be the power behind the invading Israelis, here is an American at a helm, with an Iraqi assistant, Koussay Hatem, who is married to a Lebanese woman and said in a telephone interview that he ''must call home three, four, five times a day to see if everyone is O.K.''
In every direction is a political tinderbox that a wise and wandering Yankee, dependent on the kindness and employment of strangers, knows enough to leave alone. 
As Coughter said, ''One of my best friends in Beirut is from a family that is Hezbollah. 
We talk about basketball and women.''
On the road, the Lebanese players and even Joseph Vogel, an American who has played professionally in the country long enough to become nationalized, discuss the war, but mostly as it relates to the future beyond Japan.
''The way it's going right now, who knows if Lebanon will even be open when the world championships are over?'' said Vogel, a former player at Colorado State. 
''For me, it's a career at stake. 
For most of these guys, it's a country.''
The coach recommends focus on the task at hand, on the journey, always the journey.
Coughter, in fact, will leave Japan the day after the last game to meet the country's junior team, which he also coaches, for the Asian championships. 
He will take three flights to reach a Chinese city near the Mongolian border. 
The way things are going in Lebanon, he may not get paid, but don't tell anyone, he'd do it for free.

file: A Stumble and a Lost Opportunity for Ohno to Defend His Gold Medal.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was a lighter Apolo Anton Ohno who stepped onto the ice at the Palavela on Sunday to defend his Olympic 1,500-meter title. 
A strict diet was the tool he used to chisel his body, but in the four years since the Salt Lake Games, Ohno had also shed his bad-boy image and lost his appetite for celebrity.
He had one thing left to shed, and that was the label of disputed Olympic champion. 
If Ohno could sidestep controversy and claim another gold medal by beating a field that included the three-time world champion Ahn Hyun Soo of South Korea, his Olympic legacy would be incontestable.
It did not happen. 
In a semifinal, Ohno stumbled on the last curve before the bell lap and failed to advance to the ''A'' final.
In 2002, Ohno crossed the finish line after Kim Dong Sung of South Korea but was awarded the gold medal after Kim was disqualified for illegally blocking Ohno as Ohno tried to pass him toward the frenetic end of the 13 1/2-lap race.
The South Koreans reacted strongly to Kim's disqualification and tried to have it overturned. 
For a long time afterward, enmity for Ohno simmered in South Korea.
Ahn has succeeded Kim as the fastest skater in the world's foremost short-track speedskating nation. 
Ahn and Ohno going for the gold promised to be an intriguing storyline. 
At Salt Lake City, it was contact by Ahn that sent Ohno sprawling in the 1,000-meter final and cost him the gold. 
He slid across the finish line on his side to salvage the silver.
There would be no controversy Sunday, because there would be no showdown. 
Ohno won his qualifying heat with ease and had looked satiny smooth in his semifinal right up until the moment he jostled with Li Ye of China.
The top two finishers would move on to the ''A'' final. 
Ohno was second, behind Li, but decided not to play it safe. 
Some people thought he had skated too tentatively in the 1,500-meter final in 2002 after his spill in the 1,000. 
Determined to rewrite his Olympic history, Ohno went for broke. 
He skated wide to overtake Li, and they bumped. 
Ohno's left hand became tangled with Li's skates, and he nearly went sprawling.
''I thought I was in great qualifying position,'' he said. 
''I had a bit of contact with the Chinese skater, and it caused me to go too far forward on my skates. 
I lost a lot of speed, and that was pretty much the end of it.''
Ohno somehow regained his balance and finished fourth out of six skaters. 
Ahn went on to win the gold medal. 
Another South Korean, Lee Ho Suk, who has not finished lower than third in the event in World Cup competition this season, claimed the silver medal. 
Li JiaJun of China was third.
The 23-year-old Ohno was left to contemplate what might have been.
''I wanted to make that final,'' he said. 
''I've brought everything to the table at these Games. 
I've prepared myself physically and mentally the best I can. 
I was really looking forward to trying to get on the podium for the United States.''
Ohno's result was the final flake in a snowballing day of disappointment for the United States, which saw the skiers Daron Rahlves and Bode Miller finish out of the medals and the figure skater Michelle Kwan withdraw from the competition with a groin injury.
Ohno thought his night was over, but he was wrong. 
He was among the skaters who qualified for the ''B'' final. 
He almost missed the race, appearing on the ice as the skaters were being introduced. 
He frantically shed his blade guards and skated to a third-place finish in the ''B'' final and an eighth-place finish over all.
''I didn't even know I was racing,'' Ohno said. 
''I came sprinting out of the locker room with my skates on. 
They weren't even sharpened.''
He was held up near the entrance to the ice by an extra-vigilant security guard.
''They see some crazed skater come onto the ice, they're like, who is this guy?''
Ohno said. 
''It could have been a fan or something.''
No, just a former Olympic champion.
''What happened today doesn't change anything that happened four years ago,'' said Ohno, who will race in three more events. 
''I still feel like I'm a great skater and an Olympic champion.''
His girlfriend, Allison Baver, watched his race from the wings. 
She had just advanced to the quarterfinals of the women's 500 meters but was in no mood to celebrate.
''It really breaks my heart to see,'' she said when asked about Ohno's semifinal stumble. 
''Because I know he's the best skater in the world.''
Alex Izykowski of the United States had been eliminated in the semifinal immediately before Ohno's. 
He watched the race and felt, he said, ''the same as the whole country.''
And how would that be?
''A little disappointed,'' he said. 
''He's such a good skater, and he should be on the podium no matter what.''
He added: ''But I don't know. 
It's short-track. 
That's what they always say.''
(Photo by Goh Chai Hin/Agence France-Presse -- Getty Images)

file: A Third Chinese Gymnast_s Age Is Questioned.txt
text:
ï»¿
With the start of the women's gymnastics competition less than one week away, questions are again being raised about the age of a Chinese gymnast scheduled to compete at the Beijing Games.
Yang Yilin, a top contender for gold in the all-around and the uneven bars, could be 14 instead of the minimum age of 16, The Associated Press reported Sunday.
She is the third of six Olympians on the Chinese women's gymnastics team whose age has been questioned in the lead-up to these Olympics.
Registration lists from 2003 to 2006, previously posted on the Web site of the General Administration of Sport of China, said Yang was born on Aug. 
26, 1993, which means she will turn 15 later this month. 
Gymnasts must turn 16 during the year of the Olympics to be eligible to compete in the Games.
On the 2007 registration list, Yang's birthday changed to Aug. 
26, 1992, suddenly making her old enough for the Olympics, The A.P. said.
Chinese gymnastics officials have not yet addressed the question of Yang's age. 
Jacques Rogge, the president of the International Olympic Committee, said in a news conference Saturday that age eligibility was not an I.O.C. issue, and that the International Gymnastics Federation, known by the acronym F.I.G., is in charge of making sure gymnasts are old enough to compete.
The F.I.G.'s secretary general, Andre Gueisbuhler, told The A.P. that he would not comment about Yang's age because he had not seen the paperwork.
Just last week, questions were raised about the ages of two of Yang's teammates. 
The New York Times reported that online records listed the gymnasts, He Kexin and Jiang Yuyuan, as being too young for this Olympics, perhaps as young as 14.
A national registry of gymnasts, which had been blocked online but was viewable through Google cache, listed He's birthday as Jan. 
1, 1994. 
That date was also listed for her on a registration for an intercity competition in Chengdu, China.
Jiang was born on Oct. 
1, 1993 and is not yet 15, according to a listing of junior competitors from the Zhejiang Province sports administration. 
The list of athletes included national identification card numbers into which birth dates are embedded. 
Chinese officials have produced passports showing that He and Jiang are 16, making them old enough to compete at the Games.
Giselle Davies, an I.O.C. spokeswoman, said on Saturday that the I.O.C. had been in touch with the F.I.G. and the Chinese Olympic Committee. 
''From our perspective, this has been cleared up,'' she said.
METS MINOR LEAGUER LEADS U.S. 
The Mets minor leaguer Brandon Knight struck out 10 batters and the United States Olympic baseball team hit four home runs in a 9-1 win over Canada in an exhibition game in Durham, N.C.
Knight, who at 32 is the oldest player on the United States roster, allowed two hits in five innings. 
He struck out six in a row before Emmanuel Garcia -- the last batter he faced -- flied out to center. 
(AP)
MEMMEL INJURES ANKLE The United States gymnast Chellsie Memmel hurt her right ankle while training on the floor exercise Sunday but is still expected to participate in the Olympic team competition next weekend.
The USA Gymnastics president, Steve Penny, said in a statement that Memmel's status was being monitored daily. 
The United States women will start team qualifying Sunday. 
(AP)
BRYANT SAVES U.S. 
MENKobe Bryant provided the offense in the United States men's basketball team's first defensive struggle of the pre-Olympic season, scoring 11 of his 19 points in the third quarter of an 89-68 victory against Russia in Shanghai.
The capacity crowd of 14,523 clearly favored the United States, and Bryant was clearly was the fans' favorite player. 
They chanted ''M-V-P'' when he went to the free-throw line and booed when he was called for an offensive foul in the second quarter.
Carmelo Anthony added 17 points in what was by far the United States' most competitive tuneup for the Olympics. 
(AP)
WOMEN STRUGGLE IN WIN Sylvia Fowles scored 8 of her 13 points during a late fourth-quarter run to lead the United States women's basketball team to an 84-74 victory over Latvia in the FIBA Diamond Ball tournament in Haining, China.
Unlike past United States women's teams, this group has not had much playing time together because of injuries, overseas commitments and the W.N.B.A. season.
''We're still a work in progress,'' United States Coach Anne Donovan said.

file: Adoptee Returns to China And Helps U.S. Team Win.txt
text:

SuGui Kriss always wanted to return to China to rediscover her roots and perhaps leave her mark on the country.
She marched into the Bird's Nest last weekend for the opening ceremony of the Beijing Paralympics, representing the United States as a member of its sitting volleyball team.
Her early life in southern China was that of an abandoned infant who was raised in an orphanage in Kunming until she was adopted at age 8 by the Americans Charles and Marilyn Kriss.
''SuGui goes from a forsaken situation to marching into the Bird's Nest in front of 90,000 fans,'' Charles Kriss said. 
''It's a great testimony.''
If Paralympic organizers were looking for an exemplar among the 4,000 athletes in these games, the 21-year-old SuGui Kriss would be among them. 
She has overcome her share of problems -- and she has a powerful serve.
According to her coach and parents, the Paralympics have taken a slightly shy girl and given her confidence, a more outgoing personality and a chance to return with a Paralympic medal to her home in Albany.
The United States team finished with a 2-1 record in pool play and will face the Netherlands on Friday in the semifinals. 
The Americans won the bronze four years ago in Athens, and a victory against the Dutch would put them into the gold medal game -- probably against China. 
The Americans' only loss was to China, the defending Paralympic champions.
In Wednesday's 25-12, 25-17, 25-11 victory over Latvia, Kriss had 4 points serving, her first of the tournament.
In other action Wednesday, Britain won three gold medals in track cycling, solidifying its spot behind China, the leader, in the medal standings.
China leads the medal table with 24 gold and 77 over all. 
Britain has 21 gold and 43 over all, followed by the United States with 15 and 34.
Britain has earned 12 gold medals in cycling, the most of any team. 
Sarah Storey of Britain won the individual pursuit cycling race for her disability class, and the American Barbara Buchan won in her class.
Britain's Anthony Kappes, Barney Storey and Ben Demery won the sprint final, and Darren Kenny, Mark Bristow and Jody Cundy took the team sprint.
Of the 12 medal events in swimming, Russia, Britain and the United States each won two gold medals.
TWO BARRED FOR DRUGS The German wheelchair basketball player Ahmet Coskun failed a doping test that was conducted before the Games.
German officials said Coskun's urine test on Aug. 
23 showed the presence of the banned substance finasteride.

file: Australia_s Track Team Will Skip Ceremony.txt
text:
ï»¿
Australia's track and field authorities announced they will not allow their team to march in the opening ceremony at the Beijing Olympics because of fears the city's smog may harm the athletes.
Instead, the team will spend the first week of the Games in Hong Kong because track and field events do not begin until the second week, The Associated Press reported Monday. 
Australian authorities portrayed the decision as a logistical rather than a health issue, but nevertheless expressed their concerns about the smog.
''Anything more than five or six days and they inevitably end up with some sort of respiratory problem,'' the Athletics Australia performance manager, Max Binnington, said of his athletes.
The Chinese press, including the official government news agency Xinhua and the official Olympics Web site, has so far kept mum about Australia's decision.
Some Australian athletes are unhappy about missing the opening ceremony.
''It would have been nice to come to some intermediary solution,'' the heptathlete Kylie Wheeler told The Sydney Morning Herald.
Slow Time for Pistorius
At the German International Championships for Disabled Athletes in Berlin on Saturday, the South African double-amputee sprinter Oscar Pistorius ran the 400 meters in 49.16 seconds. 
That was more than three seconds slower than the 45.95 he needs to qualify for a provisional spot at the Beijing Games, and well short of his personal best of 46.34, set last year.
Pistorius, who uses special carbon-fiber blades, last month won the right to compete for an Olympic berth. 
He said after the race that he was not discouraged by the result.
''This is normal at this stage of training,'' Pistorius said, referring to his push to return to form after devoting several months to his successful appeal after track and field's governing body barred him from competing for an Olympic spot.
''My Olympic effort may be postponed, but it won't be ended,'' he told Reuters. 
''If I don't make it in 2008, I'll go for 2012.''
An American for Russia
The decision of the American W.N.B.A. star Becky Hammon to play for Russia at the Olympics is causing a ruckus.
The United States Olympic team coach, Anne Donovan, told ESPN, ''If you play in this country, live in this country, and you grow up in the heartland and you put on a Russian uniform, you are not a patriotic person in my mind.''
And yet, Donovan had not listed Hammon as a prospect for the United States team, even though Hammon was a runner-up for the Most Valuable Player award in the W.N.B.A. last season.
In the summer, Hammon plays for the San Antonio Silver Stars of the W.N.B.A., but in the winter, she plays for a Russian pro team, CSKA Moscow.
Earlier this year, she applied for and received dual American and Russian citizenship so that CSKA would not have to use one of two allotted ''import'' spots on its roster, a common move in international sports.
United States sports federations routinely allow foreign-born and -trained athletes to apply for citizenship and compete for Olympic spots.
Donovan said she found Hammon's switch ''unfathomable.''
Hammon told The Seattle Times: ''I know how I feel about my country. 
I'm very proud of what America represents to the world. 
But this is a basketball game. 
This is not life or death.''
Israeli Tests Positive
One of Israel's top hopes for a medal at the Summer Games, the sailor Udi Gal, faces a possible suspension from the International Sailing Federation after testing positive for finasteride, the main ingredient in the antibaldness drug Propecia. 
To receive a waiver, athletes must seek permission in advance from the World Anti-Doping Agency.
The Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth reported Gal's test result. 
If a follow-up test is also positive, Gal would face disciplinary action that could include suspension from the Games.
Gal, 29 , is also head of Israel's Olympic Sportsmen Committee. 
Although finasteride is not classified as a performance-enhancing drug, it is restricted because it can mask steroid use. 
Gal said he was taking the drug to treat hair loss.

file: Bush Puts on a New Hat_ Cheerleader for the U.S. Team.txt

President Bush always said he wanted to attend the Olympics in Beijing to celebrate sport and American sportsmanship, and on Saturday, he did so with zeal.
He hit the sand with the American women's beach volleyball team, dropped in on softball practice and took his own ride through the Olympic mountain biking course -- all before attending his first event, the American women's basketball game versus the Czech Republic on Saturday night.
''Mr. President, want to?'' said Misty May-Treanor, half of the dominant American beach volleyball team, turning her backside toward the president for the sport's traditional method of encouragement: a slap.
Bush complied, though with a discreet flick of the back of his hand on her lower back. 
Dressed in a casual blue shirt, khakis and a visor, he was even enticed to try a few volleys himself, quickly working up a sweat in the Beijing swelter (and comporting himself rather well).
The president -- college cheerleader, baseball team owner, sports enthusiast -- is clearly enjoying his immersion in the American Olympic effort.
''I wasn't exactly sure what to say to you, except to start with, God, I love our country and I love what we stand for,'' he told the team during a greeting at the Fencing Hall, where he mugged and posed for pictures for a full hour on Friday. 
(His daughter Barbara scored a picture with LeBron James.) ''And I love being with you.''
The morning after attending the opening ceremony, Bush managed his typical weekend workout on his mountain bike, only this time at the Laoshan Mountain Bike Course. 
It was his second time on the course, having ridden it with the Chinese team during a visit in 2005. 
''Biking was really, really difficult,'' he acknowledged. 
''That's why they call it an Olympic course.''
At a practice of the women's softball team, Bush expressed his support for keeping the sport in the Olympics.
''It's good for the world to have girls playing softball,'' Bush said, his back marked by a chalk handprint, a prank by the center fielder, Laura Berg, ''and these women are going to show girls how to win.''
Bush strolled into the arena for the women's basketball game about midway through the second quarter of the United States' easy victory. 
He briefly wore a navy USA Basketball hat and chatted with USA Basketball's president, Val Ackerman.
On Sunday, he is scheduled to attend men's and women's swimming and the men's basketball game against China, after squeezing in a bit of work: meetings with President Hu Jintao and other Chinese leaders.
NBC GETS HIGH RATINGS NBC can feel satisfied that it carried Friday's opening ceremony on a 12-hour tape delay rather than streaming or broadcasting it live. 
The 21.5 overnight rating was the best on record for a nondomestic Summer Games opener, with the closest being an 18.5 from Sydney in 2000.
Twelve years ago, the ceremony that opened the Atlanta Games produced a 27.2 overnight rating for NBC. 
In other foreign-based Summer Games, NBC's overnights were an 18.0 in Athens in 2004, a 16.5 for Barcelona in 1992 and an 18.3 for Seoul in 1988.
Each overnight rating point currently equals 787,659 television households. 
But overnight ratings, a quick snapshot from urban metered markets, usually go down when the national ratings are calculated. 
So the 21.5 rating from Beijing may fall 2 or 3 points.
NBC also reported that its Web site, NBCOlympics.com, had 70 million page views on Friday, 10 times the figure for Athens's opening ceremony, with 4.2 million unique users, nearly 500 percent above Athens. 
NBC will subsequently announce how long each unique user stayed on the site.
