file: Internet-Age Detective on the Trail of Gymnasts.txt
text:
ï»¿
Mike Walker does not care much about gymnastics, and he did not pay much attention to the Olympics.
But when he heard stories about electronic records reportedly bearing the disputed ages of Chinese gymnasts vanishing from the Internet, he saw an opportunity to test his computer hacking skills.
''I didn't get excited until I read about documents being available and then blocked,'' said Walker, a 32-year-old computer security specialist who lives near Washington. 
''That set all kinds of alarm bells in my head in terms of going and finding records. 
It is something I like doing.''
After about three days of on-and-off cyber-sleuthing last week, Walker found copies of a spreadsheet that had previously been posted on a Chinese government Web site. 
It listed the age of the Chinese gold-medal gymnast He Kexin as 14, not 16, as it says on her passport.
Walker promptly started a blog, and his first post was titled ''Hack the Olympics!''
It included copies of his find and details of how he uncovered the information. 
The attention his post garnered -- it received a total of 1,500 comments on his blog and on the technology news site Slashdot -- helped revive the debate over whether He, who won an individual gold medal on the uneven bars, and other Chinese gymnasts were old enough to participate in the Olympics. 
Since 1997, rules have required that a gymnast turn 16 in the year of the Olympics to compete in those Games.
Chinese officials have insisted that all the country's gymnasts were the appropriate age. 
On Sunday, they blamed a paperwork error for the conflicting records of He's age. 
The International Olympic Committee has asked the international gymnastics federation to investigate.
Giselle Davies, a spokeswoman for the I.O.C., said in a phone interview Thursday that the federation had not yet completed its inquiry. 
She would not go into details about the documents involved in the analysis.
Federation officials said last week that they had asked the Chinese Gymnastics Federation for passports, birth papers, national identity cards and family residence permits for five of the six members of the Chinese women's team. 
Four Olympic medals, including the team gold in women's gymnastics, are at stake.
''I don't think there's any update just yet because they got documents that were in Chinese and they were seeking to verify them,'' Davies said of the international federation's investigation of the Chinese women's team. 
''We don't have a specific time limit or timeline set for it.''
Phone calls to the federation's headquarters in Switzerland went unanswered Thursday.
Walker said he believed that the documents he found belied the latest claims of Chinese government officials. 
And for the last 10 days, he said he had been playing a sort of cat-and-mouse game with people he believes are trying to erase digital tracks that may point to further evidence that some Chinese gymnasts were under age.
On Sunday, Walker posted a link to another file that suggested that the Chinese gymnast Jiang Yuyuan was also under age. 
Suspecting that the file would disappear, he titled the post ''Ready, Set, Censor!'' and challenged readers to be ''faster than the delete button.''
By Wednesday, the file had disappeared, but not before Walker and others made copies on sites that included the Internet Archive, a San Francisco-based nonprofit, which takes periodic snapshots of the Internet and stores them.
Walker is not the only blogger to have found documents raising questions about the ages of China's Olympic gymnasts. 
Others in the United States and China have uncovered news articles and government documents suggesting that He, Yuyuan and another gymnast, Yang Yilin, did not meet the minimum age requirements. 
The New York Times first found and reported on July 27 about the existence of online documents suggesting that He and Yuyuan were under age.
But Walker's painstaking documentation of his cyber-sleuthing efforts have thrust him into the spotlight, especially in the United States. 
He has appeared on Fox News and been interviewed by other television networks and major American and foreign newspapers. 
Other hackers, some in China, have continued to send him tips on where to dig for further evidence that the gymnasts may be under age.
Somewhat sheepishly, Walker, whose blogging name, Stryde Hax, is a playful reference to his last name and his hacker chops, said he did not mean to steal the spotlight from others. 
''It was not my intention to rebreak a story,'' he said.
The efforts of people like Walker are the latest sign that a new generation of individuals see ''information gathering as a participatory contact sport,'' said Jonathan Zittrain, a law professor at the Harvard Law School and a co-founder of its Berkman Center for Internet and Society. 
''I think that is a positive sign.''
Despite the work of the Internet Archive, the lack of a complete and authoritative Web archive makes it possible for digital information to disappear forever, Zittrain said. 
At the same time, he added, the debate about the age of the gymnasts shows that it is increasingly difficult to erase files, especially those that begin in relative obscurity and quickly end up in the public eye, like the various spreadsheets containing the registration of Chinese athletes with sports agencies.
Walker and others owe their discoveries in large part to Internet search engines like Google and Baidu. 
Search engines visit, or crawl, sites across the Internet periodically to build an index that users can search. 
Most search engines also keep a copy, or cache, of the pages they index. 
Because some Web sites are crawled infrequently, say every few weeks, a file may remain in cached form long after it has been removed from the Web site where it originally appeared.
That is what happened with the documents that Walker and others found. 
But it took some digging. 
After much trial and error, Walker conducted a search on Google for spreadsheets on Chinese Web sites that contained He's name and the year 1994. 
Walker got one result, a registry of athletes from the General Administration of Sport of China. 
When he clicked on the link, the file was no longer on the site. 
Walker was able to view the cached version, but He's name was not listed.
That raised suspicions for Walker and other bloggers that Google could have modified the cached file, perhaps at the request of Chinese authorities. 
Google denied it. 
The company said that it caches only the first few hundred kilobytes of a spreadsheet. 
The file in question was large, and He's name did not appear in the portion that Google had cached. 
(Walker said he was satisfied with that explanation.)
Walker had better luck with Baidu, a Chinese search engine, whose cached copy of the athletes registry included the entire spreadsheet. 
It listed He's birthday as Jan. 
1, 1994, which would make her 14. 
The cached page has since vanished from Baidu, probably because Baidu has crawled the site again and updated its cache accordingly.
By Walker's account, bloggers have uncovered at least four other official documents that show He's age as 14.
Not everyone believes the evidence. 
Comments on Walker's blog point to other information suggesting the Chinese Olympic gymnasts are all 16 or older. 
And many in China are contemptuous of the claims that the gymnasts could be under age.
Zittrain said it may be difficult to resolve the matter definitively. 
For documents that were born in digital form, like those hackers and bloggers found online, ''it may be harder to know what is authoritative especially if it has changed,'' he said.
For Walker, the experience has shed new light into the challenge of concealing information in the digital age.
''If you look at an adversarial relationship between people trying to control the distribution of information and people trying to seek the information, both sides have new tools,'' he said. 
One side ''can modify and remove information, leaving almost no trace. 
But the people who are seeking the information have global reach, anonymity and infinite distribution.''

file: Living With Cancer, and Swimming in Its Shadow.txt
text:
ï»¿
Eric Shanteau knows himself.
''I have a history of thinking myself crazy,'' he said Wednesday. 
''A lot of people don't know that.''
He now has something to focus on -- the diagnosis of testicular cancer he received in mid-June. 
As he swims his practice laps, training for the Games, he lives with the reality that the cancer is there, waiting for the surgery that must take place.
But first, he will swim in the Olympics. 
Waiting was his decision, backed up by his doctors and his parents. 
He swims and he rests, and he talks about survival rates the way other swimmers obsess about fractions of seconds and the number of laps and all the other minutiae of this sport.
Shanteau dwells more on the figures 95 percent and 5 percent. 
The ratio for testicular cancer used to be the other way around, he has been told, but now a vast majority of people who come down with it are cured.
''Normally, you get to the Olympics, you put pressure on yourself,'' he said, adding that his illness had given him a different perspective.
He would not normally be getting this kind of attention, as a marginal member of the United States squad who narrowly missed making the last two Games in Sydney and Athens. 
But now he is in Beijing, and he draws a crowd.
On Wednesday, select American swimmers gave a news conference in the main auditorium of the press center, the one reserved for the biggest stars. 
The room was nearly packed with perhaps 500 journalists for Michael Phelps, the man who will try to win eight gold medals, and Dara Torres, the 41-year-old who is a medal contender again. 
On this day, Shanteau was the best story because, as he sat on the stage, everybody knew he was bearing a disease.
''You have to take ownership of it,'' Shanteau said. 
He is 24 years old, from the Atlanta area, slender and restrained -- not a presence, a mass of power, like Phelps and Torres. 
This was his year to make one more try for the Games, in relative anonymity. 
In mid-June, he felt a small lump that had not been there days before. 
His girlfriend told him to get it checked, and in short order, a specialist told him he had cancer.
''It will be a defining day in my life,'' he said Wednesday, admitting that his first reaction was, ''Why me?'' and ''I've got the trials.''
The doctors gave him the options -- surgery right away, or wait. 
They assured him that his kind of testicular cancer is slow-growing, so he felt comfortable in putting off the surgery, accompanied by weekly testing.
''If certain tests had come back elevated, my parents would have stepped in,'' he said.
He went to the trials in Omaha and finished second in the 200-meter breaststroke, qualifying for the Games. 
His teammates thought he was behaving a bit blase about finally getting to the Olympics, but they had no idea what was really on his mind. 
A couple of weeks later, when the team assembled in California to prepare for the trip to China, Shanteau decided to tell his teammates in a group.
''If you guys knew how the swimming world works,'' Shanteau said to reporters, adding that he thought it was pretty good he kept his frightening secret for more than three weeks.
''We thought he was acting coy,'' said Aaron Peirsol, a teammate.
''Many rumors were flying around. 
We started a few.''
Peirsol added that the way Shanteau had handled his illness ''gives you a different perspective.''
Brendan Hansen, who failed to qualify in the 200 breaststroke at the trials but who made the team in the 100 breaststroke, said Wednesday, ''The Olympics look smaller when you're dealing with cancer.''
Shanteau has had a role model through his crisis. 
He had moved to Austin, Tex., the home base of Lance Armstrong, who recovered from an advanced stage of testicular cancer that had reached his brain, and later won the Tour de France seven straight times.
''I looked up to that guy long before I got cancer,'' Shanteau said.
Armstrong, who is an inspiration to thousands of cancer survivors, has let Shanteau know that he considers him a kindred soul. 
Shanteau can take solace that his cancer was diagnosed at an earlier stage than Armstrong's was.
Shanteau hopes to be competing for a medal in the finals on Aug. 
14. No matter what happens in the pool, he will hang out in China for about five days before heading home to Atlanta around Aug. 
20. He expects to have the surgery about a week later at Emory University Hospital. 
He does not mind admitting that his mind wanders to cancer when he is not in the pool.
''I am human,'' he said. 
''This isn't just the flu, it's cancer. 
When I am in my downtime, I look to the people around me. 
It is on my mind. 
I can't help it. 
That's just the way it's got to be.''

file: Morgan Hamm Receives Final Clearance.txt
text:
ï»¿
Morgan Hamm can rest easy now, knowing that his spot on the United States Olympic men's gymnastics team is safe.
The International Gymnastics Federation announced Tuesday that it would not appeal the United States Anti-Doping Agency's decision to give Hamm a public warning -- and not a suspension -- for receiving a cortisone-like shot without obtaining clearance.
Hamm, who will be competing in his third Olympics, received the warning July 3 after failing a drug test in May at the United States championships. 
Under a physician's care, Hamm was given an anti-inflammatory shot in his injured left ankle in early May, but he never filed the necessary paperwork with the antidoping agency. 
The medication triggered the positive test several weeks later.
The antidoping agency and the United States Olympic Committee cleared Hamm to compete in the Olympics. 
They said the public warning and the nullification of scores from the day he tested positive at the championships did not affect his status on the Olympic team.
But the international federation, known as the F.I.G., had yet to review Hamm's case and make a decision. 
It took three and a half weeks to do so.
''Although this is the result we anticipated, we are glad to have the final ruling so we can focus on final preparations for Beijing,'' Steve Penny, president of USA Gymnastics, said in a statement. 
''We appreciate the F.I.G.'s handling this case in a timely manner so the matter was resolved prior to the start of the competition in Beijing.''
Hamm, 25, is set to travel with the team to China, where he will compete in his first Olympics without Paul, his twin.
Paul Hamm withdrew from the team Monday, saying he was not healthy enough to compete.
INTERNET CENSORSHIP Olympic organizers are backtracking on another promise about coverage of the Beijing Games, keeping in place blocks on Internet sites in the main press center and other locations where reporters will work.
The blocked sites will make it difficult for journalists to retrieve information, particularly for articles about political and human rights. 
On Tuesday, the sites for organizations like Amnesty International or any search for a site with Tibet in the address could not be opened at the main press center, which will house about 5,000 print journalists when the Games open Aug. 
8.
''This type of censorship would have been unthinkable in Athens, but China seems to have more formalities,'' said Mihai Mironica, a journalist with ProTV in Romania. 
''If journalists cannot fully access the Internet here, it will definitely be a problem.''
The censoring of access to the Internet is the latest broken promise on press freedoms. 
When they were bidding for the Games seven years ago, Chinese officials said the news media would have ''complete freedom to report.''
In April, the senior members of the International Olympic Committee who are overseeing the Games, Hein Verbruggen and Kevan Gosper, said they had received assurances from Chinese officials that Internet censorship would be lifted for journalists during the Games.
China routinely blocks Internet access for its citizens.
Gosper, however, issued a clarification Tuesday. 
He said the open Internet extended only to sites that related to Olympic competitions.
''My preoccupation and responsibility is to ensure that the Games competitions are reported openly to the world,'' Gosper said.
He noted that the changes the I.O.C. negotiated with the Beijing Olympic organizers, ''which required Chinese legislative changes,'' had do with reporting on the Games. 
Gosper said, ''This didn't necessarily extend to free access and reporting on everything that relates to China.''
Journalists trying to use the Internet on Tuesday expressed frustration. 
(AP)
RADCLIFFE TO JOIN BRITISH TEAM The marathon world-record holder Paula Radcliffe will join the British Olympic team this weekend in a bid to recover from an injury in time to compete in the race Aug.

The 34-year-old Radcliffe, who has a stress fracture in her femur, will travel Sunday to the British training camp in Macau.

file: OLYMPICS_ TV_MARKETING_You_ll Be Looking Live At Some Morning Events.txt
text:
ï»¿
The choice of Beijing to be the host city for the 2008 Summer Olympics might initially appear to give NBC the time zone problem it had last year in Sydney when 15 hours separated Australia from the Eastern time zone of the United States. 
NBC showed only one Olympic event live in prime time.
Paris and Toronto, which finished second and third to Beijing in yesterday's vote by the International Olympic Committee, offered greater chances for some live coverage.
But Dick Ebersol, the chairman of NBC Sports, said that the Eastern time zone's 12-hour difference from Beijing will be easier for the network to cope with. 
"There are plenty of events we can carry live," he said in a telephone interview from Beijing. 
"A fair amount of good events will take place in the morning."
Although schedules will not be determined for three years, it is possible that some indoor events, like gymnastics, swimming or diving, could take place in the Beijing morning to be shown live in the United States.
Neal Pilson, an industry consultant, said NBC's coverage of the men's finals of Wimbledon last Monday -- carried live on its cable channel, MSNBC, and then followed on tape on NBC -- offers a model for Beijing eight years after viewer discontent over the taped Sydney broadcasts. 
"We may be ready for live events at 9 a.m. on cable followed by a full prime-time kaleidoscope on NBC," Pilson said. 
"I think they will have that in mind as they ponder their options for Beijing."
Ebersol said the tape-or-live equation is less important than scheduling the 2008 Games in July, unlike the last two weeks of September, when the Sydney Games were held.
"I'm convinced that the most important reason that our ratings were not at the levels we expected in Sydney was because we were dealing with children back in school and adults back to work," he said.
NBC's prime-time rating for its telecasts from Sydney fell by 36 percent from the 1996 Summer Games in Atlanta and 21 percent from the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona, Spain.
NBC is the largest financial contributor to the Olympics. 
The 2008 Games will be the last in a cycle of five Olympics that NBC acquired in a 1995 deal for $3.5 billion.
NBC is paying $894 million to carry the first Olympics in China, where its parent company, General Electric, sells aircraft engines, medical equipment and steam turbines, and has investments in joint ventures or subsidiaries totaling $1.5 billion.
Forty-nine percent of NBC's payment will go to Beijing's Olympic committee and the rest to the I.O.C., to give to international federations and national Olympic committees.
Unlike NBC, worldwide sponsors have fewer worries about time differences between the United States and Beijing. 
Their aim is to expand existing business in China or break into its vast market.
For that reason, Beijing's selection is the sponsor's pot of gold, an opportunity that is viewed with more corporate glee than if the I.O.C. had made Paris, Toronto, Istanbul or Osaka, Japan, the host in 2008.
"For existing and potential sponsors, China was the first choice, which the I.O.C. probably knew," said Jim Andrews, the editorial director of IEG Sponsorship Report, an industry newsletter in Chicago. 
"It's the market everyone wants to go after."
There are 10 global sponsors in the I.O.C.'s TOP Program for the 2002 and 2004 Olympics. 
Two of them, Coca-Cola and Kodak, have extended their contracts to cover the 2006 to 2008 period.
In 1998 and 2000, IEG said, the 11 TOP sponsors paid a total of more than $600 million. 
Andrews said the sponsors for 2002 and 2004 will pay an average $60 million each, while those for the 2006 Winter Games in Turin, Italy, and the 2008 Beijing Olympics may pay much more.
"Olympic sponsorship values will soar in the next quadrennium," said John Krimsky, the former chief marketer of the United States Olympic Committee. 
"For sponsors who are primarily American companies, to ride the Olympic rings to China will be a totally unique opportunity."
Visa views the Beijing Games in a similar vein to the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul. 
Credit-card payment systems were new to South Korea then, as they are to China now. 
Visa's sponsorship greatly accelerated its Korean business.
"Business is growing relatively slowly for us in China," said Tom Shepard, the executive vice president of global sponsorships for Visa. 
"There's been some activity with the government and how they plan to handle cards. 
I think they're looking to us for our expertise."
Coca-Cola, with 33 bottling plants in China that showed 10 percent sales growth last year, is looking to further expand its business there.
Kelly Brooks, a spokesman for Coca-Cola, said, "We're happy Beijing is chosen, but we would have been happy with any of the five."
But Xerox, which is signed through the 2004 Summer Games in Athens, has been reducing its involvement in China. 
Last year it sold its Hong Kong and mainland China operations to Fuji Xerox, its Japan-based joint printer venture with Fuji Photo Film, and later sold half its stake in Fuji Xerox to Fuji. 
Xerox is focused on its 2002 Winter Olympics sponsorship in Salt Lake City.

file: ON PRO BASKETBALL_Seeking an Epiphany at Center.txt
text:
ï»¿
They filed into the rickety old brick gymnasium one at a time, like a caravan of fans at an Indiana high school game in 1950. 
By the time Yao Ming stepped on the court he was not merely a Chinese national treasure. 
In a Webcam world, he had become a piece of basketball folklore more talked about than seen.
From Pat Riley to "News at 11" anchors, they all heard about this big kid from far away, even saw him on TV a couple of times. 
But they had to see for themselves what all the fuss was about -- a 7-foot-5 center who runs like a deer and whose shot is silkier than Hugh Hefner's bathrobe.
One of the first to weigh in was Zeke from Cabin Creek, W.Va.
"This guy is big, but he's a more of a finesse player at this point and time," declared Jerry West, the Memphis Grizzles' new president for basketball operations. 
He said he thought Yao, expected to be among the top three picks, would be drafted in the "top five or six players" this June.
When asked if he thought Yao is the kind of player franchises could be built around, West, architect of the Los Angeles Lakers for the past two-plus decades, replied, "I don't know about that."
Quentin Richardson then disrespected Yao's game. 
Everybody was huddling around Richardson, the Clippers guard and Chicago native, as if he could distill what all the politically correct general managers could not.
"I don't think he'll be a big concern," Richardson said. 
"I'm used to seeing big guys like that get dunked on. 
If we play, we'll be making bets on who's going to get him."
Nice. Beautiful. 
A 22-year-old travels halfway across the world, braves annoying team doctors pulling on his limbs, hits a bevy of jump shots and shows he has a bit of a drop-step move, and we say, "Now go home."
You wanted to take Richardson aside and say, "Yo, Q, you guys finished behind the Jazz, and you're watching the playoffs from your couch, right?"
Or explain to West that Shaquille O'Neal is not your average N.B.A. center.
But you knew what was happening in their reluctance to embrace Yao. 
After all, the Grizzlies had been denied permission to work out Yao privately, even though the Grizzlies will have one of the top picks. 
Why pump up a player who will never be yours?
And Richardson is probably like a lot of N.B.A. players who grew up honing his game on a playground. 
With Dirk Nowitzki, Peja Stojakovic and 19-year-old Tony Parker leading a cast of talented foreigners running some of them out of the league, he needs to stand up for his country's sagging hoop reputation.
No, why were 65 team executives, 150 credentialed journalists and another 100 or so onlookers really there at Loyola University's Alumni Hall yesterday?
They were longing for a big man to change the game or at least match up with O'Neal.
P. J. Carlesimo ran the workout, putting Yao through a round-the-horn shooting drill. 
Yao dropped in four of five shots from the baseline, four of five off the glass from 18 feet. 
His touch was pillowy soft. 
At times, he made so many in a row he looked like he was playing Pop-a-Shot at a sports bar.
He ran sprints, went end to end, handling the ball well before laying it in. 
He converted drop-step moves into powerful dunks. 
On the flip side, Yao looked tired and a little thin in the upper body. 
Will he be a serviceable pivot his first two seasons?
Yes. Can he be an All-Star?
Definitely. Is he a future Hall of Famer?
Probably not, but then what center besides O'Neal is?
Yao did not speak to the news media. 
Privately, Chinese and N.B.A. officials were worried that he or his entourage could say something that would be perceived as hurtful to the goal of having him play abroad.
Before the workout ended, a five-paragraph statement from Yao was released.
"It's been a dream of mine to play in the N.B.A. ever since the first time I saw a game on TV many years ago," it began. 
"To almost touch that dream today fills me with a sense of joy that words simply cannot describe."
He humbly thanked everyone, mentioning, "I hope I have not disappointed you with my performance today."
Proving he and his handlers have been well schooled in marketing, he also said he planned to take every member of the news media out to dinner, adding, "But the check is on you if your reporting makes me look bad."
The scene around Yao could have been taken from a bad "Rocky" sequel. 
The foreigner with the crew cut and mysterious past comes to America to show off his wares before hyperbolic journalists hanging over a running track in the gym's upper level, pointing their cameras at his head. 
The stone-faced executives sit below, taking stock of his every movement and mannerism.
Even Yao's entrance -- he walked in from the far corner of the gymnasium -- looked scripted. 
Remember the Russian fighter in "Rocky IV," Ivan Drago?
The only element from the plot missing was a semidecent American to challenge him.
His combatant for the day finally made his way across the court to shake hands with Yao. 
His name was Chris Christoffersen, the 7-2 center from Oregon, who was not invited to the league's predraft camp. 
Christoffersen is Danish.
"There's some good American-born centers," he said. 
"Look at Shaq."
He was asked to name another. 
"Uh, Patrick. 
He's good."
Patrick Ewing is from Jamaica.
When you think Yao, think somewhere between Jack Sikma and Rik Smits, with a little Bob Lanier mixed in. 
He will not change the game, but he will make it better. 
And at his position, that's a step in the right direction.
Hey, he beats Marcus Camby in a designer suit -- or Frederic Weis in Spain.

file: Out of Thin Air, Nigel Short Conjures Up a Crushing Attack.txt
text:
ï»¿
Nigel Short of England won the Sanjin Hotel Cup in Taiyuan, China, with a 6 1/2-2 1/2 score. 
The tournament, played from July 17 to 26, featured an all-grandmaster invited field of 10. 
Second place was captured by Ni Hua of China, who scored 5 1/2-3 1/2.
Joel Lautier of France and Alexey Dreev of Russia shared third and fourth places with 5-4 each.
Short showed his marvelous knack for attack in his eighth-round game with Ye Jiangchuan. 
The latter did his best by choosing a conservative defense that squelches the sort of explosive tactics that Short is famous for. 
Accordingly, the game started on a quiet track up to the 15th move, but then Ye could not keep Short from sacrificing a pawn to shake up the play and advance a mating attack.
There were rook sacrifices in the offing, but the final blow was Short's queen sacrifice on the 27th move. 
Ye gave up. 
There were alternative modes of defense, but nothing that could withstand the Englishman's onslaught.
One thing Short has going for him is the creation of attacks for what appear to be routine formations. 
He produces threats from anywhere, and they often catch his adversaries napping.
After 5 Qc7, the opening took the form of the Taimanov Variation of the Sicilian Defense. 
Black holds back most of the development of his pieces so he can retain maximum mobility and deny his opponent a clear target for attack. 
Moreover, White cannot gain anything by playing 6 Bg5 or 6 Bc4. 
He can play 6 g3 and 7 Bg2, but this line does not lead to a promising attacking formation. 
After 6 a6, the two squares for a knight invasion, b5 and d5, are covered, so White has nothing better to do than finish his mobilization.
Short clarifies the central pawn situation with 10 Nc6 bc so that he can bring his queen to the king's wing with 11 Qd3 to be followed eventually by 15 Qh3. 
His objective is the black king. 
If Black had played 10 Qc6, then 11 Bf3 Qc7 12 a4 Nd7 13 a5, and White would have had a slight advantage in space on an open board and a lead in mobilization. 
Overall, there would be a slight superiority for White.
There is now a question as to how Ye should handle his future defensive problems. 
After 14 Rae1, his 14 Rae8 is too committing. 
Perhaps 14 Rad8 might have given him more flexibility.
After 15 Qh3!?, Short sacrifices a pawn to open lines of attack to the black king. 
It does not look as though Ye has any obvious weaknesses on his kingside, but Short can often see what others fail to see. 
After 16 Nf6 17 Re3 g6 18 Nd1 c4 19 bxc4 Qc5, Short followed with 20 f5!, which is a tremendous breakthrough into the black king's defenses. 
If Black had answered with 20 ef, then 21 Rf5! gf 22 Rg3 Kh8 23 Qh6, and Black will be mated.
After 26 Nd5, Ye blundered with 26 Nd5? overlooking 27 Qh7!
As soon as he observed that 27 Kh7 28 Rh3 Kg7 29 Bh6 Kh7 is followed by 30 Bf8 Bh4 31 Rh4mate, he gave up.

file: Patchwork Team Wears Its Bronze With Pride.txt
text:
ï»¿
Sometimes, bronze feels just like gold.
''It's kind of heavy, actually,'' said the American gymnast Joey Hagerty, just off the victory stand, as he lifted the medal from his chest after the men's team final.
This strange Olympian alchemy is based on low expectations, on the mediocrity predicted for a team whose two stalwarts had dropped out because of injuries.
For a powerful nation, the United States has a love affair with underdogs. 
America celebrates the little guys, the Hoosiers from the little town in Indiana who win the state championship, the miracle hockey team that beat the Soviets. 
Loves them more than Dream Teams.
And this bronze-medal team -- take it from the bouncy little guys, displaying their bronze medals and their hyperactive smiles -- was no Dream Team. 
This was a bunch of recruits slapped together, the starting lineup from Class AAA baseball that somehow qualified for the playoffs, the outsider that reaches the Final Four in college basketball.
Not only that, but this was a team right out of the old movies, the platoon with the youngster from Brooklyn and the youngster from the plains and the kid from the South, one from Column A, one from Column B. An all-American team. 
And it won a bronze medal in the team finals of gymnastics on Tuesday, behind China and Japan, and celebrated as if some magician had waved a wand and turned their bronze into gold.
They live in the shadow of the munchkins, the young women who draw the ratings back home, who win more medals, who get young girls into the gymnasiums with their parents and a checkbook. 
These smallish young men, muscles and all, are the warm-up act. 
And yesterday, they could have lighted all of Beijing with their energy.
''I just get hyped up,'' said Jonathan Horton, a mainstay of this patchwork team, the most emotional, bouncing around on the sideline. 
His enthusiasm was infectious, as he exhorted his teammates after he had hit his own routines.
They were not expected to win a medal here, not without Paul Hamm, who won the gold in the all-around in Athens in 2004; and not without Morgan Hamm, his twin, who had deep Olympic experience. 
Paul had to withdraw at the end of July because the broken bone in his right hand did not heal, and Morgan had to pull out two days before the Games because of an injured left ankle.
''Those guys contributed the most of anybody in history,'' Horton said. 
''The Hamms are irreplaceable athletes, but we had to say, 'Get off it.'
''
They could not put Paul's gold medal out there to compete, and they could not put Morgan's dossier in a uniform. 
They had to regroup, like in the old movies that America used to make before it became an ironic nation. 
You, you and you, front and center.
The last men standing included Kevin Tan, whose family is originally from China; and Raj Bhavsar, whose parents emigrated from the Gujarat region of India in the '60s; and Sasha Artemev, who was born in Russia. 
And by some bizarre coincidence, these were the three best Americans on the pommel horse, the last of the six disciplines on Tuesday. 
Only in America.
Chinese people listen politely when Americans talk about ourselves as a nation built on immigrants, some of them Chinese, of course. 
We can talk about our tangled family histories, the races and colors and ethnic groups all blending in a lot of family trees these days, united under something we call America. 
But here it was, the American dream, flipping around atop a pommel horse. 
Tan got hung up and received low grades. 
Bhavsar did not score well, either. 
But Artemev scored 15.350, just enough to hold off Germany.
''I'm just thinking about his routine, and let the math take care of itself,'' Kevin Mazeika, the head coach, said.
And as the figures flickered on the scoreboard, before they allowed themselves to celebrate, the Americans went over and hugged their friends and colleagues on the German team, who did not win a medal. 
They won their bronze with grace. 
They made their country proud.
''It's been a roller-coaster ride,'' said Tan, who stopped to include the Hamm brothers and David Durante, the last alternate, who did not get to compete.
''Morgan, Paul and Dave were out there today,'' he added.
Tan was listed as Kai Wen Tan on the scoreboard -- ''that's my name,'' he said, meaning he adopted Kevin the way so many young people in China are now Wendy or Steve. 
Tan understood how good the Chinese men are. 
He also understood what it meant for his team to be on the victory stand, and for him to be in China with a medal.
''I never thought, in my wildest dreams, I would be here,'' he said. 
''This is my heritage. 
To be able to do it in China is fantastic.''
He said it with the unaccented English of a Penn State grad, the all-American boy, albeit with a medal hanging around his neck. 
The medal had a bronze hue to it, but it glowed like a more precious metal.

file: PRO BASKETBALL_Record of Defeat Doesn_t Matter to Knicks.txt
text:

Scott Layden smiled and spoke as if he had just secured a genius for the Knicks' bench next season. 
Without a hint of doubt or regret, he talked of his decision to extend Don Chaney's contract as if no defense was necessary.
"Having the opportunity to work with Coach Chaney since December -- we work together every day -- and seeing what a great communicator he is, seeing how he prepares his team, I felt it was the right decision," Layden said. 
"I believe that Don Chaney is the right person to coach this team. 
I believe in Coach Chaney and I'm very excited that this day is here."
Knicks fans can only hope that Layden, the Knicks president and general manager, has seen something in Chaney that has not been evident to most of them during his three-month tenure as coach. 
Since replacing Jeff Van Gundy, who stunningly resigned on Dec. 
8, Chaney has guided the Knicks to a 12-27 record chock full of humiliating, exasperating and almost unbelievable losses.
Still, the Knicks gave Chaney a one-year contract extension yesterday with a team option for a second year. 
Including the unguaranteed second year, the package is worth about $3 million.
James L. Dolan, the chairman of Madison Square Garden, joined Layden and Chaney at the news conference, and Dolan made it clear that it was Layden's decision to extend Chaney's contract. 
He said Layden made the decision before embarking on a scouting trip to China last Wednesday.
"We have great confidence in Don's ability to lead the Knicks," Dolan said. 
"We appreciate Don's willingness to step into a challenging position in December and believe that he deserves the chance to return as head coach for a full season."
The Knicks' decision seems an admission that the club is ready to rebuild. 
Why bring in a high-priced head coach to oversee what will be a season or two of struggle?
Layden did not go that far yesterday, but he said the timing of the announcement had a lot to do with the draft. 
With the Knicks likely to have a high lottery pick, Layden felt it was necessary to have a head coach in place to help make what could be one of the franchise's most important decisions of the past decade.
Despite speculation that the Knicks had talked to other coaches, including Doc Rivers, a team official said that the team had not considered anyone else.
Layden also said -- without using the word rebuilding -- that the Knicks were committed to doing whatever it took to improve the team over the off-season. 
Both he and Dolan said it was important to have a man of character and integrity -- which, by all accounts, Chaney is -- out front during such a period of transition.
"While everyone would like us to reveal the plan and put a plan out on the table, I don't think it's wise to discuss those strategies publicly," Layden said.
Layden and Chaney, who has a 277-409 career record that includes coaching positions with four teams, believe the Knicks will improve by simply going through a training camp with Chaney. 
They believe it was difficult for the players to adjust from the demanding ways of Van Gundy to the calm and reserved Chaney in midseason.
"Training camp makes a season because that's the biggest juncture of the N.B.A. where you have your players in an isolated situation and you get their mind-set together so they know exactly where we're headed and how we're going to play. 
It's very difficult to do that midway through the season."
The players, all of whom are relieved to be on the team after the trading deadline, realize that some of them may not be around for Chaney's first training camp.
"I don't know if I'm going to be back here," Latrell Sprewell said, referring to the possibility of a trade. 
"I don't know what the situation's going to be. 
I think that's just where you're at when you're going through a tough season. 
I don't know anything about what the roster is going to be like. 
Not saying that I don't want to be here. 
I just don't know what management's going to do. 
Who knows?"
And in regard to Chaney's future: Who knew?
REBOUNDS
During his 72 hours in China, SCOTT LAYDEN was one of many N.B.A. executives who watched YAO MING, the 7-foot-6 center, dominate a game. 
"Yao Ming is a very talented guy who has a lot of potential," Layden said. 
"It was a very positive scouting trip. 
He's got a lot of skills, a lot of talent, and I was impressed with him."
Yao is expected to be the first or second pick in the draft.

file: Racial _Handicaps_ and a Great Sprint Forward.txt
text:
ï»¿
He is now nicknamed ''the Yellow Bullet.''
His gold medal is said to be ''the heaviest,'' or most significant, of the 32 that China won in the Athens Olympics. 
He carried the Chinese flag in the closing ceremonies and has returned home to riches and glory.
All of this adulation because Liu Xiang, a high hurdler, has proved what many Chinese have long felt was not possible: that yellow men can jump, and sprint, too.
''It is a kind of miracle,'' Mr. Liu, 21, exulted at a post-race news conference after tying the world record and winning gold in the 110-meter high hurdles. 
''It is unbelievable -- a Chinese, an Asian, has won this event.''
He added: ''It is a proud moment not only for China, but for Asia and all people who share the same yellow skin color.''
In many countries, particularly the United States, this kind of racial stereotyping often touches a raw nerve in society. 
But among Chinese, the proposition that genetic differences have made Asian athletes slower in sprinting than their American, African or European rivals is a widely accepted maxim, if an unproven one.
The Communist Party apparently thinks so, too. 
At the midway point of the Athens Games, with China in a surprisingly tight competition with the United States for the lead in gold medals, the party's chief newspaper, People's Daily, cautioned that track and field events were about to begin.
While Chinese are ''suited'' to sports like Ping-Pong, badminton and gymnastics that require agility and technique, the newspaper noted, purely athletic events are different. 
Chinese had ''congenital shortcomings'' and ''genetic differences'' that created disadvantages against black and white athletes.
In an effort to give this halftime pep talk a positive spin, the commentary urged Chinese athletes to work harder. 
''If Chinese people want to make their mark in the major Olympic competitions, they have to break through the fatalism that race determines everything,'' the newspaper advised.
Mr. Liu's victory has not fully erased this ingrained belief. 
Chinese sports officials have explained his win, in part, by noting that hurdles also require technique, not just raw speed, an observation that invokes another, more positive, stereotype -- that Chinese are disciplined and smart. 
His coach has been credited with developing special training methods to overcome any racial deficiencies.
But by becoming the first Chinese man to win a sprinting event in modern Olympics history, Mr. Liu's victory has been particularly embraced by a younger generation of upwardly mobile, urban Chinese who themselves are eager to shatter stereotypes. 
Handsome, with thick, styled hair, Mr. Liu is 6 feet 2. 
His playful smile on the medal stand, with his tongue sticking out, offered a far different image from that of the reserved Chinese medalists of the past.
''Glory Belongs to the New Generation of the 1980's,'' proclaimed China Newsweek magazine, with a picture of a determined Mr. Liu striding over a hurdle.
Yao Ming, the Chinese basketball star, was one of the first athletes to touch this chord in the national psyche. 
His stardom with the Houston Rockets has made him the most famous athlete in China. 
He is popular not just because he is a good player, but because he is tall. 
At 7 feet 5, he helped dispel the Western stereotype that all Chinese are short.
But if Mr. Yao was chosen to carry the Chinese flag at the opening ceremony, it was Mr. Liu who was selected to carry it at the closing. 
He is already being deluged with endorsement and entertainment offers. 
A record company reportedly offered him $600,000.
Like many Chinese, Feng Jue, 32, a marketing executive for the Chinese Web site, Tom.com, stayed up late to watch the live telecast of Mr. Liu's race. 
She had not even heard of him until the day before the finals. 
But when he won, she was overjoyed.
She thought his victory represented a significant and positive change in Chinese society. 
''The new generation, I think, is more civilized,'' she said of people in their 20's. 
''They think of themselves as human beings first, not the country and the party's interest.''
The Communist Party has been quick to take advantage of the popularity of Mr. Liu and the other Olympic athletes. 
This week, the country's gold medal winners have been on a tour of Hong Kong, a thinly disguised attempt by the government to generate good will before Hong Kong's critical coming elections.
Mr. Liu's victory has Chinese sports officials looking at other athletic events that might produce gold when Beijing plays host to the Summer Olympics in 2008. 
Li Aidong, a researcher with the China Institute of Sports Science, said coaches believe Chinese athletes could be successful in long jumping, high jumping and speed walking. 
They have already had some success in distance running, including a gold in the women's 10,000 meters this year.
There are no credible scientific studies to underpin the idea that Asians are physically inferior to other athletes in sprinting. 
Nor are Chinese alone in succumbing to ingrained racial beliefs: the Olympics victory of the white American sprinter Jeremy Wariner in the 400-meter dash startled a fair number of people in the United States. 
He was the first white winner of the event in 40 years.
But Ms. Li said she doubted China could compete in events like pure sprinting.
''Short distance races are physically intensive,'' Ms. Li said. 
''They require a lot of physical abilities, like speed and sudden strength. 
Although we have no research data, it has been an open fact that Asians and Chinese are disadvantaged when compared to Europeans and Americans.''
Mr. Liu had been very modest before the Olympics, hoping for a top six finish, perhaps a bit of bluffing from a man who finished second at the world championships. 
He sounded very different by the time he spoke with reporters after his victory in Athens.
He said he was looking toward Beijing in 2008 and he predicted more ''miracles''' -- not just from himself, but also from other Chinese track athletes.
''Please pay attention to Chinese track and field,'' he told a Chinese newspaper. 
''I think we Chinese can unleash a yellow tornado on the world.''

file: SALT LAKE CITY 2002_ THE 19TH OLYMPIC WINTER GAMES_SHORT-TRACK SPEEDSKATING.txt
text:
ï»¿
FORGET ABOUT roller derby on ice. 
This sport is more like "Survivor" on ice. 
Competitors race counterclockwise in a pack, jockey for position at speeds up to 40 miles an hour and inevitably crash, always in danger of being gashed by another skater's blade. 
First one to complete the requisite number of laps wins. 
Unlike long track speedskating, the athletes compete against one another and not the clock.
THE SETUP -- They skate around a 111.12-meter oval on an indoor rink, at the Salt Lake Ice Center (better known as the Delta Center). 
Turns are marked by seven cones, although there are no lane delineations. 
Four skaters race in a heat, with the top two advancing. 
Depending on disqualifications, however, more than four skaters can line up in subsequent rounds. 
There are eight different races. 
Men and women compete in the 500 meters (4 1/2 laps), 1,000 (9 laps), and 1,500 (13 1/2 laps). 
The women also compete in a 3,000-meter relay (27 laps), and the men in a 5,000-meter relay (45 laps).
THE NAMES -- If the on-ice drama is not enough, this sport has already enjoyed pre-Olympic controversy within the United States team. 
Tommy O'Hare went to arbitration charging that Rusty Smith and Apolo Anton Ohno, the sport's superstar, conspired to exclude him from the team during the trials. 
But O'Hare eventually dropped the arbitration and the 19-year-old Ohno emerged relatively unscathed. 
Last season Ohno captured the World Cup title, bringing the Americans into prominence they had never seen. 
Ohno is favored in all four events. 
His four medals in one Olympics would be the most of any speedskater since Eric Heiden won five golds in 1980.
Also watch the teams from China, South Korea and Italy. 
Amy Peterson is the top female skater for the United States. 
Evgenia Radanova of Bulgaria has been rising in the world. 
Kim Dong-Sung of South Korea is the defending Olympic champion and World Cup champion.
China boasts two top competitors in the 500 meters who share the same Anglicized name: Yang Yang. 
The unrelated skaters are designated Yang Yang (A) the older, and Yang Yang (S) the younger. 
LIZ ROBBINS

file: Security for 2008 Olympic Equestrian Events Is Questioned.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was a device worthy of Rube Goldberg, or perhaps Wile E. Coyote. A remote-controlled mechanism with a dozen launching tubes was found buried in the turf at Hong Kong's most famous horse racing track last week; it was rigged with compressed air to fire tiny, liquid-filled darts into the bellies of horses at the starting gate.
No horses were injured because the supervisor at the Happy Valley Racecourse, where horses have been racing since 1846, noticed something on the turf before racing started Wednesday. 
He discovered the mechanism concealed by grass-colored tape and called in a police bomb squad to remove it.
The discovery of the device, which was equipped with elaborate electronic controls, has raised concerns about security for the six Olympic equestrian events to be held in Hong Kong next year.
Security experts tend to say that the risk of a terrorist incident during the 2008 Summer Games is lower than at other recent Olympics. 
But Hong Kong is a far more open, less-controlled city than Beijing, where most of the Olympic events will be held.
The equestrian events will not be held at Happy Valley, but at Hong Kong's other racetrack, in Sha Tin, just north of the Kowloon peninsula.
Most of the Sha Tin site has been closed to the public since July for the construction of special facilities. 
It will remain closed until the Olympics begin.
''There will be a full lockdown period of the entire Olympic venue'' and a thorough police inspection before the Games begin, said Lam Woon-kwong, the chief executive of a company set up by the Hong Kong government to organize the Olympics here.
Police officials refused to discuss the device found at Happy Valley, except to say that it was under investigation. 
One popular theory is that gamblers installed it in an attempt to fix the outcome of races.
The liquid in the darts was being analyzed at a laboratory to determine whether it was a tranquilizer, poison or something else entirely. 
A long trench was dug underneath where the starting gate stands during a race, and the footlong launching tubes were placed in the trench and concealed under the locations where each horse would stand at the beginning of a race.
Donald Tsang, who was re-elected Sunday as the chief executive of Hong Kong, said in an interview that he believed gamblers were responsible.
''We'll bring these guys to the book,'' he said, adding that Olympic events like dressage were far less likely to draw the attention or interest of gamblers.
Tsang tends to be well informed about police investigations in Hong Kong. 
He not only heads the territory's government, but his brother was also the police commissioner until retiring in 2003; their father was a police sergeant for many years.
In a sign that the case of the mysterious device at Happy Valley may prove tough to solve, a person close to the investigation said Monday that the police would probably offer a reward as soon as Tuesday for information that would help them find the culprits.
Stephen G. Chandler, the executive director of security and corporate legal services at the Hong Kong Jockey Club, said that the motives and identity of whoever built the device remain a mystery. 
The jockey club manages the city's racetracks and has been working closely with the police.
''We've contacted our counterparts around the world -- it's never been seen before,'' said Chandler, a former Hong Kong police official.
He declined to speculate further on motives. 
Other theories include terrorism, extortion and insurance fraud. 
Chandler said that no one contacted the club before the device was found.
Horse racing experts said it might be hard for gamblers to profit by silently firing darts into one or more horses and betting on others to win. 
They said that any horses that were pierced, and possibly horses near them in the starting gate, might react violently, which would probably lead to the discovery of the darts and the cancellation of the race.
Happy Valley Racecourse is unlike most racetracks because the infield is a public park, equipped with ball fields and operated by the government. 
A public jogging trail lies next to the track's inside rail. 
Three tunnels under the track provide public access.
Soccer balls, badminton birdies and other sports equipment periodically land on the turf on days when there is no racing, and people at the park sometimes stray onto the racetrack. 
As a result, Jockey Club officials inspect the track before races are held.
The track has security cameras, but the trench was dug in a blind spot for the cameras. 
Chandler said that because the Jockey Club had more than 5,000 full-time employees and nearly 20,000 part-time employees, it was possible that someone at the club participated in the scheme.
Video cameras are nearly useless at night because the track is nearly surrounded by apartment towers whose residents object to having floodlights used on the site more often than necessary. 
The club considered installing infrared cameras but decided against it.
But since the discovery of the dart-firing device, guards have begun patrolling the track with dogs at night.
Sha Tin Racecourse has a public park in its infield, but it was closed when the construction project began last summer. 
In 2001, a cleaner found a nail bomb under a seat there. 
A 27-year-old electrician later pleaded guilty to putting the bomb there in an attempt to draw government attention to his personal-financial difficulties; he was sentenced to five years in prison.
A spokeswoman for the International Olympic Committee in Lausanne, Switzerland, said the group was not concerned about the device at the Happy Valley Racecourse because it had not been planted at an Olympic site.
The I.O.C. decided in July 2005, at a meeting in Singapore, to transfer all six equestrian events to Hong Kong from Beijing. 
The Beijing Organizing Committee had new stables built and special fields planted in an unsuccessful attempt to convince international veterinary groups that it could protect horses during the Olympics from 17 equine diseases that are endemic to China.
If the events had been held in mainland China, other countries would have required the Olympic horses to spend months in quarantine before being allowed to return to their home stables. 
Hong Kong, however, meets international veterinary standards.
The I.O.C.'s decision to transfer the events to Hong Kong attracted little attention at the time because it was made at the same meeting in which the 2012 Games were awarded to London, passing over New York, Paris, Madrid and Moscow.
The six equestrian events are individual and team competitions in dressage, jumping and eventing. 
For eventing, a three-day competition, riders seek the best combination score for dressage, jumping and a cross-country race.
Dressage and jumping will be held at Sha Tin Racecourse. 
The cross-country event will be held at a luxury golf course that already has a high fence around it for security and has few trees inside that could be used for cover.
Trying to attack horses at the Olympics would be much harder because the riders have considerable choice about where their horses should stand at the start of each event. 
''Greater variability makes it a harder target,'' said Chandler, of the jockey club.
Stephen G. Vickers, a former Hong Kong police intelligence official who is now the president and chief executive of International Risk, a security consulting company, said that any possible incidents at the Olympic events in Hong Kong would probably be peaceful. 
They may include demonstrations by followers of the Falun Gong spiritual sect, which has been banned and sometimes repressed in mainland China.
Strenuous efforts against triads, which are Chinese organized crime syndicates, have made horse races here less likely to be fixed than anywhere else in Asia, Vickers said.
But the device found at Happy Valley is certain to make security even tighter during the Olympics next year, he said, adding, ''I think they're going to quadruple whatever they were going to do before.''

file: SOCCER_Chinese Goalkeeper Stands With U.S. Women_s Stars.txt
text:
ï»¿
One of the indelible images in women's soccer history is Brandi Chastain's left-footed penalty kick past the Chinese goalkeeper Gao Hong to win the 1999 World Cup for the United States.
The goal was followed by a brouhaha about a doffed jersey and an exposed sports bra.
Now, less than two years later, Gao is tending goal for the New York Power, one of eight teams in the new Women's United Soccer Association, which opens next month and features nearly all of Chastain's teammates and four of Gao's from the Chinese national team.
Among Gao's new teammates for the 21-game W.U.S.A. season are Tiffeny Milbrett, Christie Pearce and Sara Whalen, all United States World Cup veterans, plus the elite Norwegian national team players Gro Espeseth and Ann Kristin Aarones.
"She never thought of the U.S. players as enemies, but she always tried her best to play a good game against them," Heike Chan, who translated for Gao, said yesterday at a W.U.S.A. news conference in Manhattan. 
"She likes the U.S. team. 
She's excited to be on the same team as Tiffeny. 
She sees her role is to promote soccer."
Gao has met the United States players on occasion, but her inability to speak English got in the way. 
"They could only smile at each other or pat each other on the shoulder," Chan said. 
"But even that she felt good about."
Milbrett said: "I have incredible respect for her. 
I hope to learn a lot more about her. 
We may not learn a lot soccer-wise, but to get inside her brain, to learn how she grew up and how she views life."
Gao knows a little English, but she will be taking language classes after the W.U.S.A. teams finish training next month in San Diego. 
Chan said that Gao knew of the league's startup plans well before she was signed last fall. 
"Her only surprise in coming here is in how well developed it is," Chan said.
W.U.S.A. officials have enormous confidence that they have produced an attractive, marketable mix by allocating United States team stars like Chastain, Milbrett, Mia Hamm, Brian Scurry and Julie Foudy to the eight teams, then adding elite international players and rising college stars.
They believe the W.U.S.A. is more immediately attractive than Major League Soccer, largely because of the United States team's success.
Power Coach Pat Farmer said that while there are other women's professional leagues, "This is the premier league for women."
The league also plans to inject its players into communities to build upon the large interest in their sport among soccer-playing girls and young women and their families.
"We have to get involved, do what we love to do," Milbrett said, "and show that we're not here just to play awesome soccer, but for the betterment of people around us."
The Power opens in Atlanta on April 21. 
The first home game, against the San Diego Spirit, will be played April 29 at Mitchel Athletic Complex in Uniondale, N.Y.

file: SOCCER_The Questions Are Fading After Hamm_s 2 Goals.txt
text:
ï»¿
For all her accomplishments as soccer's leading scorer and the biggest superstar in women's team sports, Mia Hamm has never sustained her brilliance consistently throughout a major tournament like the World Cup or the Olympics.
That may soon change. 
At 31, as she nears retirement after the 2004 Summer Games in Athens, Hamm is playing the most complete soccer of her career. 
She delivered a pair of goals and an assist tonight in a 5-0 victory over Nigeria before a crowd of 31,553 at Lincoln Financial Field, matching her goal output for the entire 1999 Women's World Cup and placing the United States on the verge of qualifying for this tournament's quarterfinals.
In the past, Hamm's confidence has been mercurial, rising or falling with her ability to put the ball into the net. 
She has scored only twice in the knockout phase of a World Cup or an Olympics. 
But she has become more assured, versatile and resilient -- no longer consumed by defeat or a failure to score -- during three seasons with the Washington Freedom in the Women's United Soccer Association.
As her teammates on the national team have become more accomplished and better known, Hamm no longer has an urgent obligation to carry the team on the field, or to shoulder the burden of media attention off it. 
Freed of the responsibility to take control, she seems more willing to do it.
In tonight's rugged game, Hamm tackled fiercely, tracked back to retrieve balls, dropped into midfield on occasion and seemed intently driven from the beginning.
"She wants the responsibility on her shoulders," Coach April Heinrichs said. 
"I believe this will be her best World Cup."
A reluctant superstar, Hamm now seems more comfortable with her celebrity and more relaxed in the way she plays. 
She has scored a pair of goals and collected four assists in two matches of this World Cup, her fourth. 
With 8 career goals and 12 assists, she has surpassed Michelle Akers of the United States and Sun Wen of China as the leading all-time scorer in the women's world championship.
"There's not a reluctance to take over games," the captain, Julie Foudy, said of Hamm. 
"Before, she wasn't reluctant, but she was content with others' taking the stage. 
Now, she's saying, 'I can do it.'
She's playing with an intensity that is inspiring all of us."
The United States (2-0) can advance to the quarterfinals with a draw or narrow defeat on Sunday against North Korea in Columbus, Ohio. 
In the first game of tonight's doubleheader, Sweden (1-1) defeated North Korea (1-1) by 1-0 as forward Victoria Svensson scored on a volley in the seventh minute.
The United States had defeated Nigeria by 7-1 in the 1999 World Cup as the match grew edgy and scabrous. 
The Americans expected a similar game tonight, and Nigeria quickly fell into trouble with its fierce tackling.
In the fifth minute, the Nigerian captain, Florence Omagbemi, took down forward Cindy Parlow from behind in the penalty area, and the Argentine referee, Florencia Romano, signaled a penalty kick.
As the game moved into the sixth minute, Hamm called for the kick, which was a departure from the 1999 World Cup final, when she had not wanted to take one -- then did reluctantly -- in the penalty kick shootout against China. 
Tonight, she assuredly placed a low shot inside the right post. 
The Nigerian goalkeeper, Precious Dede, guessed incorrectly, shuffling to her left, and Hamm pumped her fist in celebration at the 1-0 lead.
In the 12th minute, Parlow was fouled a second time, giving the United States a free kick from 32 yards. 
Again, Hamm stepped forward to take the kick. 
Playing in the W.U.S.A., she has refined her playmaking skills and fashioned herself into a dangerous threat on set pieces. 
Hamm intended to make a pass from the left flank as Parlow made a run toward the far post, but the ball kept floating inexorably toward the goal. 
Dede seemed frozen off her line and reached up with both hands but could not control the ball, allowing the United States to take a 2-0 lead.
Two minutes into the second half, Hamm placed a corner kick perfectly onto the head of Parlow, who was left unmarked from six yards out. 
Abby Wambach scored in the 65th minute, and Foudy delivered a penalty kick in the 89th minute, but the game was dominated by Hamm.
"It's more consistent than in the past," Hamm said. 
"I credit the W.U.S.A. for putting you under pressure week in and week out. 
I'm trying to enjoy this. 
I'm definitely a lot looser than in previous World Cups. 
I'm an intense, emotional person. 
Sometimes, stopping to smell the roses isn't a bad thing."
RUSSIA 3, GHANA 0
Marina Saenko got one goal and started another scoring play as Russia beat Ghana in Carson, Calif.
Saenko scored on a free kick in the 36th minute, Natalia Barbachina made the score 2-0 in the 54th minute, and Olga Letyushova capped the scoring with a close-range volley in the 80th minute.
Russia goalkeeper Alla Volkova, sometimes rushing to the top of the box to turn away scoring threats, was particularly effective when Ghana had breakaways.
CHINA 1, AUSTRALIA 1
Bai Jie scored in the 46th minute as heavily favored China settled for a tie with Australia in Carson, Calif.
Heather Garriock scored in the 28th minute to give the upstart Australians (1-0-1) a short-lived lead.
China (1-0-1), ranked fourth in the world to Australia's 15th, kept the pressure on most of the second half, but Australia's defense crowded back into its own zone to turn back repeated threats.

file: SOCCOR_ NOTEBOOK_MetroStars_ Rookie Makes an Impact.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was only 24 minutes into BRAD DAVIS'S Major League Soccer career, but he quickly had the look of a grizzled, confident veteran.
Davis was inserted into Saturday's game in the 81st minute by MetroStars Coach OCTAVIO ZAMBRANO, replacing ROSS PAULE on the left side of the midfield. 
Davis scored the game-winning goal in overtime as the MetroStars defeated the Columbus Crew, 2-1.
"He obviously wanted me to take care of my role defensively," Davis said, referring to Zambrano. 
But he mostly wanted me to go forward and make things happen. 
I'm an offensive player. 
I had a couple of chances but couldn't put them away until the overtime.
Davis, who is 20 and played at St. Louis University, was picked by the MetroStars No. 3 over all in the recent M.L.S. draft. 
He showed his offensive prowess last year, scoring 10 goals and adding 14 assists as the Billikens advanced to the quarterfinals of the N.C.A.A. tournament.
Against the Crew (he had also been a late sub in a 1-0 loss to Columbus at Giants Stadium on April 3), Davis went immediately forward, forcing Columbus to scramble. 
Early in the second five-minute overtime period, Davis drifted into the left side of the penalty area as the MetroStars attacked on the right side.
"I don't remember who made the original run, but I do know I was calling for the ball because I was open on the opposite side from the get-go," Davis said. 
There were a couple of shots that were deflected. 
I held my position and, as it rolled to me, my eyes felt like they opened up real big. 
I put my head down and struck it well.
The game-winner, however, is no guarantee of more playing time.
"Hopefully, I will get more playing time," Davis said. 
"I feel I can play. 
It's just a matter of time."
WORLD CUP
BORA MILUTINOVIC, the peripatetic Serb who is the coach of China's national team, said that he might stay in China after the World Cup, but that he would definitely retire from coaching. 
"I'll be 60 when the World Cup is over," Milutinovic told a daily newspaper in Sichuan. 
"The places where I prefer to stay most are the United States and China, not Mexico, where my family lives now."
As the start of the tournament nears, Chinese officials have told the nation's clubs that 11 injured national team players will not be allowed to play in remaining league games, even if they are fit. 
Striker HAO HAIDONG (toe) and the captain and veteran midfielder MA MINGYU (knee) top the list of injured players. 
"If all the players are injured, I would go to the World Cup alone," Milutinovic said.
China has scheduled five warm-up matches -- the first is against South Korea on April 27 -- before it begins play on June 4 against Costa Rica in a first-round group that also includes Brazil and Turkey.
The Manchester United and Ireland midfielder ROY KEANE tore a hamstring in last week's Champions League match in Spain and will be out for at least six weeks. 
The Irish defender STEPHEN CARR, who plays in England for Tottenham Hotspur, has been slow to recover from a knee injury.
"The World Cup's gone, and it's now about getting myself fit and playing football again," Carr said on the club's Web site. 
"I found out last week, and it's a massive disappointment."
Portugal, which opens World Cup play against the United States on June 5, will be without the 22-year-old Benfica wing SIMAO SABROSA. 
Sabrosa, who has played 12 times for the Portuguese national team, underwent surgery on his left knee after he was injured in last week's exhibition loss to Finland. 
Arsenal of the English Premier League said it was prepared to allow its Japanese midfielder, JUNICHI INAMOTO, to leave the club and join his national team at the end of April. 
Arsenal signed Inamoto for $5.7 million from Gamba Osaka last summer, but he has been unable to win a spot in the Gunners' starting lineup.
Japan is scheduled to play host to Costa Rica (April 17), Honduras (April 29) and Slovakia (May 4) in warm-up matches.
A poll of 442 college students conducted by the South Korean magazine Vox found that the American short-track speedskater APOLO ANTON OHNO was the most unwelcome at the World Cup. 
Ohno was followed by OSAMA BIN LADEN, JAY LENO and BRIGITTE BARDOT.
Ohno won a gold medal at the Salt Lake Games when a South Korean skater was disqualified; Leno and Bardot have ridiculed South Koreans for their custom of eating dog.
CORNER KICKS
The New York Power of the Women's United Soccer League will play a benefit match at 7 tonight at Baker Field in Upper Manhattan against the Columbia University's women's team. 
The match will be preceded by a clinic at 5 p.m.
On Sunday, the Power defeated the Philadelphia Charge, 2-1, in an exhibition match at Indian Hills High School in Oakland, N.J.
The Power opens its second season on Saturday night in Washington against the Freedom. 
JACK BELL
