BEIJING -- The Chinese Communist Party has long cherished competitive sports as a conduit for geopolitical detente. 
For decades, the slogan ''Friendship First, Competition Second,'' guided the nation's approach to international sporting events. 
It was dueling table tennis teams, after all, that 40 years ago paved the way for the historic thaw in relations with the United States.
But even if Beijing has since come to believe that gold medals are lovelier than bronze, senior leaders are clearly displeased that players from its most popular men's basketball team got into an ugly, full-court brawl Thursday night with the Georgetown University Hoyas.
It does not help that the melee took place on the second day of Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.'s first official visit to China.
The violence, captured by amateur video cameras and broadcast around the world, occurred during the final minutes of a ''good will'' match between the Hoyas and the Bayi Rockets, a team whose members are drawn from the People's Liberation Army.
In the video, a Rockets player can be seen ramming the guard Aaron Bowen through a partition and pounding on him with fists as he sat on his chest. 
Before the Georgetown coach pulled his men off the floor and called the game quits, Chinese players and spectators threw punches, folding chairs and full bottles of water. 
With that, the game officially ended in a tie, 64-64.
But even as members of both teams met Friday morning at a Beijing hotel to make peace, the country's propaganda maestros were trying to ensure that the brouhaha did not find its way into the national psyche. 
Censors quickly deleted videos and chat room comments, although by evening, the restrictions appeared to be easing.
In a country prone to nationalistic sentiment, most microblog remarks were surprisingly critical of the home team, a once-reliable champion that has fallen off its pedestal after losing some of its best players to retirement.
''Aren't Bayi players soldiers?
Why would they beat up a bunch of college students?'' asked one posting. 
''What a loss of face for the people's army!''
Others made light of the situation. 
''The Bayi team sure is lousy at basketball and should try some other sport -- like boxing.''
One of the few newspapers to cover the fight, The Beijing News, blamed the referee for poorly officiating the game and security guards for inaction during the fisticuffs. 
The paper, however, suggested that the Hoya coach, John Thompson III, had a hand in the skirmish, and that Georgetown was known for its aggressive defensive tactics.
But one member of the Hoya entourage, in an anonymous posting on a chat board for Georgetown fans, blamed the Chinese referee for overzealously calling fouls on the visiting team -- the Bayi Rockets were awarded 57 free throws, and Georgetown just 15.
Mr. Thompson could not be reached for comment, but in a statement posted on Georgetown's Web site Thursday night, he took a decidedly diplomatic tack. 
''Tonight, two great teams played a very competitive game that unfortunately ended after heated exchanges with both teams,'' he wrote.
Despite the sport's soaring popularity, the reputation of the Chinese basketball league has taken a beating in recent years. 
Game fixing and bribery scandals have fueled widespread cynicism, and on-court fisticuffs have been a perennial problem. 
Last year, a friendly warm-up match between the Brazilian and Chinese teams turned into a kicking-and-punching fracas just one minute into the game. 
Officials suspended the team and issued an apology.
The Bayi Rockets, despite their military provenance, are not especially known as brawlers. 
Lin Kunyi, a veteran reporter for Basketball News China, said the team -- the first part of its name refers to the founding date of the People's Liberation Army -- is better known for endurance. 
''The team is celebrated for what people call 'the Bayi spirit,' which means you are tough, you eat bitterness and you don't leave the court even if injured,'' he said.
After watching footage of the brawl, Mr. Lin, too, blamed poor officiating and suggested the whole matter was best forgotten.
By Friday afternoon, many of the players seemed to agree. 
After flying to Shanghai, members of the Hoyas and the Rockets shared the lobby of the Portman Ritz Carlton without any palpable tension. 
One Georgetown player shrugged off the contretemps. 
''Man, it's just a game,'' he said.
Online Correction: August 19, 2011, Friday
This article has been revised to reflect the following correction: An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that an anonymous comment on the basketball brawl was posted on the university Web site. 
It was posted in a chat room on a Hoya fans Web site.

file: Australian National Team Seeks Competition in Asia.txt
text:
ï»¿
SEOUL -- As Australia was chasing shadows last weekend in Seoul, desperately trying to keep the South Korean team at bay on a hot and humid evening at the 2013 East Asian Cup, there may have been a twinge of nostalgia for the days before the country joined the Asian Football Confederation. 
Life was easier in Oceania.
Australia's former confederation is the smallest and weakest of the six that fall under the auspices of the world governing body FIFA. 
Victories were frequent but too comfortable. 
The 31-0 slaughter of American Samoa in 2001, still an international record, did not help anyone.
Even what seemed to be a relatively straightforward World Cup qualification route often was not. 
It involved becoming Oceania's representative, which was usually easy, and then a two-legged playoff against a battle-hardened team from South America or Asia, which was not. 
It was a short, sharp shock of frantic competition and intense pressure after 3 years and 11 months of mostly gentle tests in the South Pacific.
On Jan. 
1, 2006, Australia became the 46th member of the Asian Football Confederation in a bid to become a stronger soccer nation. 
This means it gets to participate in the quadrennial continent-wide A.F.C Asian Cup and will be host to the next edition of that tournament in 2015. 
It has also given the country access to the 2013 East Asian Cup, a smaller regional four-team tournament currently taking place in South Korea that includes the host, China and Japan. 
It has no effect on qualification for the World Cup but is a useful testing ground.
''Being in Asia means we play a lot more competitive games against good teams, and that has been the biggest thing for the senior national team,'' said Australia assistant coach Aurelio Vidmar. 
''With qualification for the World Cup, we don't go through the old path of Oceania. 
We have lots of tough games, and that helps us improve,'' he added.
In June 2013, Australia qualified for the 2014 World Cup through Asia for the second successive time.
But Australian clubs have been participating in the Asian Champions League since 2007, and almost 50 Australian players now play professionally in Asian leagues.
A new rule introduced in 2008 by the A.F.C. was the catalyst. 
The so-called Asian quota rule allowed clubs around the continent to sign an extra foreign player outside of the usual limit of three, provided he came from a fellow A.F.C. member nation.
It is changing the makeup of Australia's national team. 
At the 2006 World Cup, 20 of the 23 players on the roster were playing for European teams. 
But this year, when coach Holger Osieck named his 26 players for a series of vital World Cup qualifiers in June, only 10 were Europe-based, with 7 active in various Asian leagues and the rest either in Australia or North America.
'We have a lot of players now playing in Asia, and if you go to a decent league then it's O.K., and quite competitive,'' Vidmar said.
Vidmar used Robbie Cornthwaite, now playing club soccer in South Korea, as an example of how playing in Asia can benefit a player's development.
''After he went, I didn't see him for a year, but now everything is a little bit different,'' Vidmar said. 
''His touch is better and he looks a lot sharper, all because they train a lot harder than we do. 
We've got so many more things happening in Australia for young players -- outdoor activities and so many other sports, but here in Asia, it is the No. 1 sport.''
Matt McKay made his 39th appearance for Australia at the East Asian Cup opener against South Korea, a country where he spent a successful season in 2012 with the K-league club Busan I'Park. 
He then signed a two- year deal to play with the Chinese Super League club Changchun Yatai, although he was released by the team this week.
''I've played in two Asian leagues and they are good,'' McKay said. 
''Technically, we can learn a lot from playing there, and off the pitch, too, it is a very good experience. 
Being in Asia and having lots of players in Asia is changing Australian football.''
But Australia's transformation from a nation that has traditionally looked toward England, in soccer terms, into one that looks toward Asia may be a long one.
The Socceroos' games in South Korea for the East Asian Cup were somewhat overshadowed by the recent visits of English clubs to Australia for exhibition games. 
A combined total of 178,000 fans saw Manchester United in Sydney, and Liverpool in Melbourne.
The influence of the old country can still be felt in the team's physical and direct style of play under Osieck, a German.
Gary White, the coach of Guam, who acted as a technical observer while watching Australia play South Korea to a 0-0 tie last weekend, said that ''Australia's football looked like the English league of the early '90s, with not a lot of thought about what they were doing, and they played the ball long.''
He added: ''Australia couldn't cope with the Korean speed, touches and combination play, but that is why these games are necessary. 
Playing teams like South Korea and Japan is good for their development.''
Australia improved against Japan later in the week, although it lost the game, 3-2. 
It next plays China on Sunday.
More than the results however, the tournament is a welcome opportunity for Australia, as well as Japan and Korea, to field experimental squads with the 2014 World Cup less than a year away.
''This tournament is really useful for us,'' McKay said. 
''It is the first time to be involved and it gives a lot of our younger players an opportunity to show what we can do.
''To play three games in a week against tough opposition is exactly what we need, and it shows the benefits for Australian football to being in Asia,'' he said.

file: Biles Has One Peer in Rio. Or Maybe Ever.txt
text:
ï»¿
RIO DE JANEIRO -- In the hours before the preliminary round of Olympic gymnastics, members of the United States women's team were at the cafeteria in the athletes' village, goofing around. 
Telling jokes. 
Making funny faces. 
Laughing so hard that Martha Karolyi, the women's national team coordinator, approached Aly Raisman, the team captain, to tell them to quiet down.
''Today is the Olympics,'' Karolyi said. 
''You have to be more serious.''
Karolyi, of course, was right. 
The team should have been more focused. 
But when a squad's star is Simone Biles -- the best gymnast in the world and the best in history, for that matter -- that team can afford to relax. 
Biles has set the tone for that.
She is good at what she does, so good that she won the last three world championships in the all-around, collecting 10 gold medals at the worlds along the way. 
That's the most ever won by a female gymnast.
So incredibly good that Biles finished first on Sunday in the preliminary round here at the Olympics, 1.76 points ahead of the No. 2 gymnast, Raisman. 
She also finished first in three of the four events: floor exercise, vault and balance beam.
''Obviously, as expected,'' said Raisman, who added that she would be happy to finish second to Biles in Thursday's all-around final because that's the first spot up for grabs.
The United States team won qualifying by nearly 10 points, over China -- a chasm in a sport in which top competitors are often separated by tenths, or even hundredths.
You can guess what the United States gymnasts did to celebrate. 
Yes, they hugged. 
Certainly, they laughed.
Biles's joy is contagious. 
To end the team's qualifying, she performed on the balance beam, then ran off to embrace her teammates in a happy, sparkly huddle.
''She's a huge role model of mine, honestly,'' Danell Leyva, who is on the United States men's team, said of Biles. 
''Like, huge. 
I've been trying to emulate the way she goes about her gymnastics. 
She enjoys it. 
The last two years, just watching her really helped me enjoy my gymnastics more.''
Biles, 19, is not unique in the sport. 
At least when it comes to dominating it. 
And that's what makes the gymnastics at these Rio Games such a massive draw. 
It is one of the Olympic sports I've been looking forward to seeing for months and months now.
Here in Rio, there are two gymnasts who are the best ever. 
Biles is one. 
Kohei Uchimura, of Japan's men's team, is the other.
Even people who don't know a thing about the sport can appreciate the uniqueness of Biles and Uchimura. 
They perform exceptionally difficult skills while making those dangerous skills look so simple, and even fun.
Uchimura's rÃ©sumÃ© is even more impressive than Biles's. 
At 27, he is the defending Olympic gold medalist in the all-around and a six-time world champion. 
He is a 10-time world gold medalist, too.
''You don't see two gymnasts like this very often, if ever, so this Olympics is pretty amazing,'' said Mark Williams, the gymnastics coach at the University of Oklahoma, who is the United States men's Olympic team coach in Rio. 
''It's some of the best gymnastics you'll ever see in your lifetime.''
In men's qualifying, Uchimura uncharacteristically fell off the high bar. 
Yet he still finished second in the all-around, about 1.5 points back from first. 
No matter. 
Other top gymnasts are still in awe of him.
Louis Smith, a British pommel horse specialist, called Uchimura ''the perfect gymnast'' and said he made magic.
''It's a privilege to watch him,'' Smith said.
Kristian Thomas, also of Britain, said he based some of his training on how Uchimura performs. 
That means Thomas makes sure to put on a show when he does his sport, and not just go through the motions. 
He makes an effort to play to the crowd and make gymnastics beautiful.
''Uchimura always looks relaxed and seems to enjoy every minute of being in front of the crowd,'' Thomas said. 
''But his gymnastics is so clean, so amazing. 
He's so good that you can't really describe it.
During qualifying, Uchimura smacked the ground hard when he fell during his high bar routine. 
But he calmly rose, walked away to rechalk his hands, walked back to the bar and started again. 
Ho, hum. 
Seemed like no problem.
Biles admires Uchimura's carefree attitude. 
It's alluring, but she knows he is fierce somewhere deep inside. 
Could be that she considers herself the same type of gymnast. 
But she is careful not to go too far with the comparison.
''He's a legend, and it's awesome seeing him around the village, because he's just so chill,'' Biles said, explaining that the women's team calls out, ''Hey, Kohei!'' when it sees him, and he just nods in return.
''Literally everyone knows who he is,'' she said. 
''We just all look up to him. 
But he's a normal human being just like the rest of us.''
When asked if she was the Uchimura of women's gymnastics, or Uchimura was the Biles of men's gymnastics, Biles smiled.
''Gosh, no, I haven't accomplished as much as he has,'' she said.
Yet.
In her red, white and blue leotard covered with bling, Biles walked onto the floor for her floor exercise on Sunday. 
Her Olympics would now, finally, begin.
Thousands of fans in the Rio Olympic Arena snapped to attention. 
Smartphones rose and pointed her way. 
Cameras began clicking away. 
Fans moved to the edge of their red plastic seats.
What they saw was Biles leaping higher and twisting and tumbling in such dynamic, unique ways that other gymnasts can only envy her. 
(Including one tumbling pass that is called the Biles, which is a double flip with a half turn.) Then, as she moved from event to event, those countless sets of eyes followed her.
Just another day for this newest Olympic star.
The team final is Tuesday. 
The all-around final is Thursday. 
Event finals are next week. 
Plenty of reasons for Biles and her team to stay serious and focused. 
Yet on Sunday, she spoke with reporters and joked and laughed.
When Karolyi saw it, she frowned.
''Come on, this is Simone, and this is the Olympics,'' she said to Biles's handler from U.S.A. 
Gymnastics. ''So, Simone, you have to go now.''

file: Chinese Champ Back To Defend Her Title.txt
text:
ï»¿
PITTSFORD, N.Y. 
-- Shanshan Feng of China says she has always chased Yani Tseng of Taiwan, since the two were 13-year-olds competing in Asia. 
Tseng was always better when they were juniors, and that didn't change years later when the two women found themselves half a world away competing on the L.P.G.A. 
Tour.
But after last year's L.P.G.A. 
Championship, Feng was the one holding the trophy. 
It was her first L.P.G.A. win and her first major championship, and Feng was the first woman from China to win an L.P.G.A. tournament. 
This time, Tseng got to watch.
The 23-year-old Feng acknowledged that Tseng had always been her target. 
''She was always ahead,'' Feng said, ''but now I'm getting closer. 
I still haven't caught her. 
Well, I'm still trying.''
When Feng arrived at Locust Hill Country Club earlier this week, she said her memories of last year's win came flooding back. 
She is coming off a runner-up finish last week at the ShopRite L.P.G.A. 
Classic in New Jersey and has risen to No. 7 in the Women's World Golf Rankings, two spots behind Tseng.
Feng did not cause a nation to suddenly embrace the game, as Tseng did when she ascended to the world's top ranking and dominated the L.P.G.A. in 2010 and 2011, becoming the youngest player to win five major championships. 
But Feng's win last June raised awareness about golf in China.
Feng's countrymen noticed, but instead of parades, fanfare and a crush of autograph seekers wanting time with her, she was named China's best non-Olympic athlete last year. 
It was the first time a golfer had been nominated for the award.
She was surprised to be greeted by fans and members of the news media when she arrived at the airport after her win, and she said she was happy to sit through news conferences in Beijing and her hometown, Guangzhou, carefully explaining golf to anyone who would listen.
''People don't know much about golf in China, so we had a great chance to promote it,'' Feng said. 
''They didn't really know what a major was or what it means, so it wasn't like a big deal.''
Her countrymen knew that she had won, that she had defeated Tseng and that she had done it in the United States. 
But her homecoming did not significantly alter Feng's stature as a sports figure back home.
''I would say that my life hasn't really been changed,'' she said. 
''But with golf in the 2016 Olympics, if somebody from China can do well, I'm sure it's going to change everybody.''
That needle of enthusiasm for golf moved a little more this spring when the 14-year-old amateur Guan Tianlang made the cut at the Masters. 
He is from the same city as Feng, and she watched him play as a junior.
Feng's 2013 season has featured four top-10 finishes, as well as a bit of a roller-coaster ride. 
Throughout the season, she found herself trying to please her club sponsor while trying to play consistently with her new equipment.
Two weeks ago she switched to Honma, a Japanese brand she had used once before, and competed with them at the New Jersey tournament. 
The runner-up finish kept the clubs in her bag.
It was a solid return to the tour after Feng had skipped the two L.P.G.A. tournaments leading to last week's ShopRite L.P.G.A. 
Classic. Rather than playing the tour's event in Mobile, Ala., she flew to Asia and played a tournament in Japan.
Feng had planned to fly to the Bahamas for the L.P.G.A.'s event the next week but unexpectedly ran into trouble with her visa and decided to skip it.
She learned to roll with the punches long ago. 
A tour rookie in 2008, she did a lot of listening that first year.
As her English improved, she said she began to ''feel more comfortable.''
As the years passed, she added some words and phrases in Korean and Japanese.
''No Spanish yet, because I can't really roll my tongue,'' Feng said.
But Feng can roll her putts, and she hits 72.3 percent of her fairways and nearly 73 percent of her greens in regulation.
She says she likes the narrow fairways and high rough she will see at the L.P.G.A. 
Championship. It is a major championship, and what she taught her compatriots last year was that majors take the measure of the best in the world.

file: Chinese Club Team Thrives as National Squad Sputters.txt
text:
ï»¿
A victory by Guangzhou Evergrande in the A.F.C. 
Champions League, the biggest competition for club soccer in Asia, offered a quick hangover cure for Chinese fans reeling from the continuing struggles of their country's national team.
The 1-0 win in the second leg of the finals against the United Arab Emirates' Al Ahli on Saturday gave Guangzhou its second Asian Champions League title in three years. 
Its 2013 title was the first by a Chinese club.
Last week, China's men's national team drew, 0-0, with Hong Kong in a match colored by domestic rivalry and political discontent. 
The tie made it unlikely that China will advance to qualify for the 2018 World Cup, which provoked angry reactions from Chinese fans and demands that the team's coach, Alain Perrin, be fired.
The long-running travails of China's national team are a source of endless distress to Chinese soccer enthusiasts, and Guangzhou's recent success has prompted further head-scratching. 
Many sports pages have asked what the vastly different fate of the national team says about the state of soccer in China. 
''Evergrande's Victory Confirms the Strength of Chinese Players, So Why Is the National Team No Good?'' read the headline on an article on Sunday by the state-run China News Service.
While the rules differ by league, the lineups of professional teams are mostly limited by checkbooks, not nationalities. 
Evergrande has three Brazilian attackers in its starting lineup, including the forward Elkeson, who scored the winning goal on Saturday.
Some national teams rely on naturalized players. 
Against China, Hong Kong fielded players born in Cameroon, England, Ghana, Nigeria and mainland China. 
China, however, uses only homegrown players. 
An official in Wuhan has proposed lifting the restrictions that prevent foreign-born players from participating on the national team. 
But for many fans, such a solution would sidestep the question of why a nation of 1.4 billion, which has managed to dominate global competition in sports like badminton and diving, cannot do the same in soccer.
While Evergrande has strong foreign talent, it also has a core of Chinese players, an indication that other problems are at play. 
Several commentators have argued that China's national team still suffers from unwieldy state-run management. 
It could benefit from the streamlined, ''capitalist'' model of Evergrande, they say, which is owned by a real estate company and the e-commerce giant Alibaba and this month became the first listed club in Asia.
''Evergrande's ability to succeed confirms that if the government gets out of Chinese soccer and gives it over to the market and society, there will be quick results,'' the sports commentator Huang Jianxiang wrote. 
''They don't only rely on money, but also the most professional skill levels and methods to improve their game.''
President Xi Jinping of China has made no secret of his love for soccer. 
On a trip to England in October, he visited Manchester City's training ground and had a photo taken with the team's Argentine star, Sergio AgÃ¼ero, and Prime Minister David Cameron. 
In March, China announced a plan to overhaul the sport, including increasing youth participation levels and moving the soccer federation from the national sports administration to give it more autonomy.
Still, not everyone is confident that Evergrande's success will mean much to anyone besides Evergrande.
''The national team is now under Uncle Xi's watch, and the main points of reform have come out, including removing the soccer federation from under the sports administration,'' said a column on the website of the Southern Media Group, based in Guangzhou. 
''But what will the national side learn from Evergrande?
That's still a question.''

text:

A 26-year-old Chinese cyclist is set to be the first person from his country to participate in the Tour de France when the sport's biggest race begins next week.
Team Giant-Shimano announced on Wednesday that Ji Cheng had made its list of nine riders expected to participate in the 21-stage, 2,272-mile race. 
The 101st edition of the race begins in Leeds, England, on July 5.
Mr. Ji has competed in professional cycling's two other grand tours, the Vuelta a EspaÃ±a in 2012 and the Giro d'Italia in 2013.
Although China was once famous for its streets clogged with bicycles, it has lagged in competitive road cycling. 
The state sports system has focused on track cycling, which sees smaller fields competing for more medals at the Olympics. 
At the 2012 London Olympics, Chinese track cyclists won two silvers and a bronze.
Mr. Ji, from the northern city of Harbin, attended a Chinese sports school as a runner before moving to track cycling and then road cycling.
While most professional cyclists come from Europe, the Americas and Australia, the sport is making inroads in Africa and Asia. 
"Having Cheng in the team as the first Chinese rider ever to ride the Tour de France will be huge for him and his country, and we look forward to seeing the impact this has on the globalization of the sport," the Team Giant-Shimano coach, Rudi Kemna, said in a statement announcing the team selection.
Although Mr. Ji's inclusion in Giant-Shimano's Tour de France team marks a high point for Chinese cycling, his role in the race will be decidedly humble. 
In previous races he has been known for his tireless work chasing breakaways to help position his team's talented sprinters for wins on flat stages.

file: For Georgetown, a Peaceful Win in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
SHANGHAI -- Three days after an ugly brawl ended an exhibition basketball game between Georgetown and a Chinese professional team, the Hoyas played another game here on Sunday without incident.
The game was tinged with geopolitics. 
Georgetown is on a good-will tour of China, and the brawl took place on the second day of Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.'s first official visit to China.
The game's public setting seemed as if it might invite further trouble. 
It was held outdoors, on a court set up under a giant tent, with free admission as part of a promotional event called the Nike Festival of Sport.
But Georgetown looked poised in a 92-69 victory over the Liaoning Dinosaurs, who play in the professional Chinese Basketball League.
The game was sloppy in the early going, but the Hoyas' trapping defense and accurate outside shooting from its guards turned it into a rout late in the second half.
Georgetown Coach John Thompson III said he was pleased with how the team played and how his players kept their focus.
He also said he met with members of the Bayi Rockets, the team the Hoyas brawled with, on Saturday in Beijing.
''We got together the following morning in the airport and sat down and talked,'' Thompson said at a news conference, adding, ''We're going to move on; it's time to move on.''
The fight, captured on amateur video, was a full-court melee that broke out at the end of Thursday's exhibition game in Beijing, with a group of Bayi players chasing a Georgetown player down under the basket and then one Chinese player repeatedly hitting him.
The images stunned many in China, some of whom criticized the behavior of the host team, whose players are drawn from China's People's Liberation Army.
Some in the crowd threw water bottles and folding chairs at the Georgetown team after the fight.
The game ended in a 64-64 tie after Thompson pulled his players off the court.

file: Former Nets Try to Put Dark Season Behind Them.txt
text:
ï»¿
Avery Johnson, the new Nets coach, approached Courtney Lee after one of the most painful seasons in N.B.A. history had finally concluded. 
Johnson gave Lee an option: he could have a significant role with the Nets while the organization rebuilt, or he could seek a fresh start with another team through a trade.
Lee took option No. 2. So off he went to the Houston Rockets last August in a four-team deal as the Nets essentially wiped clean a roster that produced just 12 victories last season, the fourth fewest since the N.B.A. expanded its regular season to 82 games in 1967-68.
As an organization, the Nets now have new ownership, new management and even a new, if temporary, home in Newark as they get ready for their big move to Brooklyn in two years. 
And only four players remain from last season's fiasco.
But although it is relatively easy for the Nets to pretend last season is gone and forgotten, and to unveil a new slogan that proclaims that ''It's all new,'' it is not that simple for the players who have moved on. 
They are trying to jump-start their careers while trying to shake off the indignities of 2009-10.
Some have new jobs playing basketball, and some do not. 
All of them were on the wrong side of history. 
All of them are trying to deal with it.
''There's definitely a stigma that comes along with that,'' said Keyon Dooling, now a member of the Milwaukee Bucks, as he looked to the 12-70 record that is a permanent part of his resume. 
He added, ''A lot of good players are without jobs because of that whole stigma.''
The four players who remain on the Nets from last season are Devin Harris, Brook Lopez, Kris Humphries and Terrence Williams. 
Harris and Lopez are cornerstone players; Williams has already run afoul of Johnson for repeated violations of team rules this season and on Friday was assigned to the team's Development League affiliate in Springfield, Mass.
But of the 13 others who wore a Nets uniform at some point last season, one is in China, at least one is in the minor leagues and others have a foot teetering in retirement.
Seven players -- Tony Battie, Yi Jianlian, Eduardo Najera, Chris-Douglas Roberts, Chris Quinn, Dooling and Lee -- have latched on with other N.B.A. teams. 
Dooling and Roberts are teammates in Milwaukee. 
Quinn got a job with the San Antonio Spurs after another 2009-10 Net -- Bobby Simmons -- was waived.
''It's quite the contrast,'' Quinn said recently of a Nets team that won 12 games last season and a Spurs club that has won 14 of its first 16 in 2010-11.
''It's good to be part of a winner,'' he said. 
''That's everyone's goal in this league, to be part of a winning organization, and it's clear that things are done the right way here.''
Josh Boone, who toiled for the Nets last season, is playing for Zhejiang Chouzhou of the Chinese Basketball Association. 
Sean Williams, a former first-round draft selection of the Nets, suits up for the D-League's Texas Legends. 
He finished last season in China after starting it with the Nets. 
Rafer Alston, Jarvis Hayes and Trenton Hassell did not find any N.B.A. takers over the summer, although Alston could end up in China, too.
No matter where they are, they remain linked by last season's ordeal.
''When you win 12, there's always a lot of talk about players, no matter how good they are,'' said Rod Thorn, who was the Nets' president last season and now holds the same position with the Philadelphia 76ers. 
''There are questions from the league, from other coaches, G.M.'s and so forth,'' he added.
The catalyst for last season's futility came in the cost-saving trade the Nets made before the first regular-season game. 
Vince Carter went to the Orlando Magic in exchange for Battie, Lee and Alston. 
The move opened up cap room for the Nets, who were looking ahead to the summer pursuit of LeBron James, Chris Bosh and others, futile as it turned out to be.
But meanwhile, they would have to do without Carter. 
They began the season by losing 18 straight games, an N.B.A. record. 
In the midst of the streak, the Nets fired Coach Lawrence Frank, now an assistant with the Boston Celtics. 
Kiki Vandeweghe, who was the organization's general manager, reluctantly took on the job of interim coach. 
He and Thorn decided to give preference to the team's younger players.
On an already bad team, some veterans took another hit.
''That was a business decision that they made, and I understand that,'' Battie said. 
''You have to do that, especially at that point when we had no chance of making the playoffs and no chance of even having a somewhat O.K. record.''
The losses continued to pile up. 
Still, the Nets played a little better toward the end of the season, and the record for the fewest victories in a regular season -- nine, by the Philadelphia 76ers, in 1972-73 -- remained safe.
''Just losing those games and trying to run away from that record and when you go to the games and you see people with trash bags on their heads and people holding signs like, 'Worst team in the N.B.A.'
-- that's definitely one of the toughest things I've ever been through,'' Lee said. 
''But that made me who I am today. 
It made me tougher.''
Dooling recalled: ''It was a tough situation, but it wasn't all bad. 
I met a lot of nice people when I was in New Jersey, I enjoyed my time there. 
It wasn't all bad there. 
I got all my money, you know what I mean?''
Still, modest veterans like Dooling and Battie needed to stay in the league.
''Players make a good salary,'' Thorn said, ''but it's not like if you're a lawyer or a doctor or some other professional, that your career can span decades.''
Vandeweghe, who moved back to California after the season and is not working for any N.B.A. team, said he did not agree that a stigma was attached to last season's players. 
If an organization needed a player with certain needs and that player fit, he said, the player would be signed no matter how bad his team was.
''All the G.M.'s and coaches understand and they've been through rebuilding themselves,'' Vandeweghe said in a recent telephone interview. 
''They're going into it thinking Keyon Dooling was hurt all year. 
He got hired right away. 
We all knew he could play.''
This season's Nets team is off to a 6-11 start, not very good, but nothing like 0-18. 
Derrick Favors, the third overall draft pick last June, is full of potential. 
Off in the distance, Brooklyn awaits. 
But in the rearview mirror remains the wreckage from last season. 
Even Thorn, who has been in the N.B.A. for nearly five decades, feels its lingering sting.
''It's something that I don't know that you ever forget,'' he said. 
''If you dwell on something, whether it's really good or really bad, you get yourself in a bad spot. 
For me, it happened. 
It wasn't fun, but it happened.''
Rebounds
Devin Harris had 25 points, including a clutch 3-pointer with 1 minute 11 left, and 8 assists to lead the Nets to a 98-96 win over the visiting Portland Trail Blazers. 
The teams traded the lead five times during the fourth quarter, before Harris made the long jumper from beyond the top of the key. 
Portland turned the ball over on its next possession.

file: In Basketball, a Different and More Literal Globetrotter.txt
text:
ï»¿
LONDON -- The traveling basketball coach, now on gig No. 12 and in country No. 3, looked across the scorer's table as ''The Star-Spangled Banner'' played Sunday. 
He recognized the faces of the opposition, all American, all familiar.
The coach, Bo Overton, sat opposite them, an American surrounded by Chinese. 
How he ended up there, an assistant with the Chinese women's national team, even Overton is not exactly sure. 
There was the forced resignation in Chicago. 
The stint in the Bahamas. 
The rock from Italy.
The years and milestones, they blend now, a mishmash of small towns and big cities and foreign lands.
Overton played basketball in college for Oklahoma. 
He coached men and women, in college and the pros. 
He never wanted to be a lifer, the stereotypical old ball coach, someone who settled in one place for decades and became an institution.
Overton always liked life better in transit, his passport filled with stamps. 
Even if that meant his old friends pounded China on Sunday, 114-66, as both teams advanced to the quarterfinals in women's basketball. 
The United States tied its highest ever Olympic score and earned Group A's top seed.
''I don't know if I ever came to, like, that moment,'' Overton said last week, outside a coffee shop, as the local traffic zipped past. 
His kind of people, on the move. 
He continued: ''That moment where you say, 'Now this is what I'm going to do.'
''
His father, Claudell Overton, played minor league baseball, minor league basketball and 15 games in the N.B.A. 
For one season, he toured with and played against the Harlem Globetrotters.
The lessons his father imparted gave Overton his first glimpse of the world outside Oklahoma. 
Pictures showed his father playing basketball on a battleship, or with Globetrotters like Marques Haynes in France. 
After one trip, Claudell brought home a rock from Italy, dated it and displayed it in the living room.
Funny how it all worked out, Overton said. 
Here the father played against the Globetrotters and later settled into coaching. 
The son never wanted to coach but did so anyway. 
And now, ''I'm an actual globetrotter,'' Overton said.
The latest adventure in the Overton Chronicles took him to China, where he took over the Liaoning Hengye of the Women's Chinese Basketball Association. 
Overton sent e-mails of some of the funnier lost-in-translation moments to friends, who forwarded the messages, until Overton's e-mail list grew to more than 200.
He wrote about trying to decipher the ''language of honking one's horn in Shenyang'' and watching table tennis in prime time. 
He wrote about his adventures in finding a cable box, eating with the consulate general of the United States, hot milk, no ovens and facial scans.
A sample: ''This one I love, it's the guy riding the bike with cart in front. 
I'm saying, he's in trouble no horn. 
No problem, he carries a can with rocks in it. 
As he strolls thru the intersection he shakes his rocks. 
I want to tell him, 'For God's sake, go buy a bullhorn!'
''
Overton learned small, pertinent portions of Chinese, how to say ''rebound'' and ''get back quick.''
He named plays after common words, like pizza or Adidas. 
An interpreter assisted with practices and games. 
Tone and inflection took care of the rest.
Early on, Overton learned what would not change. 
His players, regardless of instruction, still practiced three hours in the morning and three hours in the afternoon, six days a week, 12 months a year. 
They did not take vacations.
Liaoning doubled the salary he had in the W.N.B.A. 
But such riches ratcheted up the pressure, too. 
''The owners are crazy,'' he said. 
''They want to win.''
Three weeks into the season, the team's 4-3 record apparently unacceptable, Overton said he was instructed to win the next game or pack his bags and head home.
Overton eventually adjusted to the showers that doubled as bathrooms in hotel rooms, the patrons at the next table who ate the heads of fish. 
He purchased the N.F.L. 
Sunday Ticket to watch his beloved Dallas Cowboys. 
He ate Subway every day for lunch.
As many as 5,000 fans turned out for games. 
As few as 200 did, too. 
The style of cheering took a while to get used to. 
A short ''Whoa!'' usually followed a great play, then silence. 
Overton could not read newspapers or watch TV, so he saw zero reviews of his performance.
Ruth Riley played for Overton in China, and she said in an e-mail that the moment she met him at the airport, Overton struck her as a traveler's spirit, a storyteller, like a ''good ol' country boy back home.''
She said they made friends at the pizza parlor near where they lived and relied on hand signals to communicate with the rest of the team.
''I'm pretty sure Bo and I would win a charades tournament,'' she wrote.
Overton never expected he would end up here. 
He played point guard at Oklahoma for Dave Bliss and Billy Tubbs. 
Phoenix drafted him in 1983 but cut him quickly. 
He became a coach.
First, he worked with men, an assistant at times and head coach at others, at Oklahoma as a graduate assistant, then with a C.B.A. team in Pensacola, Fla., then at Oral Roberts, Murray State Junior College, Southwest Texas State and Louisiana Tech.
In his final year at Louisiana Tech, his boss left and his father died. 
Overton returned home to be near his mother. 
Sherri Coale, the Oklahoma women's coach, asked Overton if he ever thought about coaching women.
He started in 1998, and in his six seasons as an assistant at his alma mater, the Sooners won 143 games and 3 Big 12 regular-season titles and made the N.C.A.A. title game in 2002. 
Attendance, Overton said, soared to 5,000 from 200. 
Salaries increased. 
He saw a future in the women's game.
Overton left for the University of Missouri-Kansas City, then jumped to the W.N.B.A. with the Chicago Sky. 
In 2008, an anonymous poster on a message board accused Overton of sexual harassment toward his players. 
The Sky's management forced him to resign; it also said its internal investigation did not uncover any examples of harassment. 
Overton said he signed a nondisclosure agreement and cannot discuss the resignation.
Next, Overton went to the Bahamas, where he assisted with the national team. 
That period gave him international experience, which led to the job in China, which led him to the national team, which led him to the basketball arena and the game against the Americans on Sunday.
Through his travels, Overton never married. 
He said he always thought: ''I'm going to settle down in a year or two. 
I'll stay in one place. 
I've got plenty of time.''
So said the traveling basketball coach.
2012 LONDON

text:

The first SportAccord World Mind Games, which ended on Friday in Beijing, brought together competitors in five disciplines: bridge, checkers, chess, Chinese chess and go.
In bridge, 24 players from four countries competed in team, pair and individual events in both open and women's categories.
The concluding three-session individuals were won by Americans. 
The women's was captured by Janice Seamon-Molson and the open by Chris Willenken.
Seamon-Molson won $6,000 by finishing 0.6 of a board ahead of Nicola Smith from Britain ($4,000), with Tobi Sokolow from the United States third ($3,000).
Willenken, who received $8,000, finished 0.8 of a board in front of Jie Li from China ($6,000), with Brad Moss from the United States ($5,000) only 1 match point behind in third.
Given that the results were that close, several boards could have changed the rankings. 
The diagramed deal occurred during the final session.
At Jie Li's table, North opened two diamonds; Jie (East) passed; South bid three hearts; West jumped to four spades; South competed with five diamonds; and West's five spades ended the auction.
North led a heart, South winning with his jack and shifting to a diamond. 
Xu Hou from China (West) won with his ace and ruffed both of his heart losers in the dummy to take 12 tricks.
Note that neither a spade lead nor a Trick 2 trump shift would have defeated six spades. 
Even if declarer were not willing to risk the club finesse, he could have played a club to the ace and ruffed a club, bringing down the king. 
Then he would have crossed to dummy's spade nine to run the clubs.
In the given auction, Willenken (South) ended in six hearts doubled. 
It looked as if this might be expensive, the defense going (in some sequence) diamond ace, club to East's queen, club ace, diamond ruff, spade ace for down four, minus 1,100. 
(Yes, it could have been 1,400 with two diamond ruffs, but no West was going to underlead his spade honors, playing partner for the nine.)
At the table, though, West led the spade king. 
He then cashed the diamond ace. 
Now a club switch was needed, but West led a second high spade. 
Declarer ruffed, drew trumps and ran the diamonds to escape for down one, 8 match points out of 10 and first place.

26 to 30.

file: Japan Exults as Kohei Uchimura, Gymnast Called _the King,_ Expands His Empire.txt
text:
ï»¿
TOKYO â By the time most Japanese were sipping their morning coffee on Thursday, the gymnast known as "the king" already had another crown.
On Wednesday night in Rio de Janeiro, Kohei Uchimura, 27, won the men's all-around gymnastics title for the second straight Olympic Games, the first time anyone has accomplished that feat since 1972.
Japanese newspapers printed special editions, and television news programs replayed highlights nonstop.
Mr. Uchimura has lifted Japanese men's gymnastics to a level of glory not experienced in generations. 
Described as "magic," "perfect" and "a machine," he has not lost an individual competition since taking silver at the Beijing Games eight years ago.
And with the next Summer Olympics scheduled to take place in Tokyo in 2020, the pressure on him to keep going will be huge. 
"I'm exhausted," he said after his latest victory.
"I put everything out there, until there was nothing left," he added. 
"More than happiness, I'd say I feel contentment."
If American television networks have dedicated a lot of airtime to Simone Biles, the dominant female gymnast at the Games, Japanese television has been focused on its own Â  national hero.
Ms. Biles has been barely a blip in the coverage here. 
Mr. Uchimura gets the gauzy profiles: of his childhood in the countryside, training under his gymnast parents; of the birth of his daughters, in 2013 and 2015; of his struggles to give up junk food and smoking.
A gymnastics-themed comic he devoured as a child â "Gamba!
Fly High," written by a Japanese gold medalist from the 1984 Games in Los Angeles â has gone into reprints.
He has appeared in advertisements for Toyota, frozen noodles and gyms. 
When the news media reported on his favorite snack a few years ago â a chocolate cookie called Black Thunder â its sales surged. 
(He has since learned to love vegetables, word has it.)
Tabloids reported that he racked up nearly $5,000 in cellphone roaming fees after downloading PokÃ©mon Go in Rio. 
His provider has reportedly waived the charges.
Mr. Uchimura did not have the Olympics news cycle here to himself on Thursday. 
Two gold medals won the day before by Japanese athletes in judo â a sport in which the Japanese team had been disappointing during these Games â drew extensive attention, too. 
Like gymnastics, judo is beloved in Japan, albeit in the sort of way that brings its stars wide popular attention only every four years.
In Isahaya, Mr. Uchimura's hometown on the island of Kyushu, a crowd of about 250 gathered before dawn on Thursday at a sports center nicknamed Uchimura Arena.
More fans assembled at the headquarters of Konami Sports Club, the chain of gyms that sponsors him, along with a number of other Japanese Olympians. 
In one of Konami's commercials, Mr. Uchimura spins on a pommel horse in the middle of an office full of presumably exercise-deprived workers.
In interviews before the Games, Mr. Uchimura said he wanted to exorcise the "demons" of past Olympics. 
Though he won individual gold in London in 2012, the Japanese team finished second to China, the dominant power in men's gymnastics in recent years and a regional rival of Japan.
In Rio, it initially looked as if the demons might get the better of him. 
He fell off the horizontal bar in the qualifying round, and the Japanese team started behind China, the United States and Russia. 
But in the end, Mr. Uchimura led Japan to a team gold, a prelude to his individual victory.
On Thursday, early risers watched as he took the gold on the last of the event's six apparatuses, nailing a difficult routine on the horizontal bar. 
Before the bar, he trailed Oleg Verniaiev, 22, of Ukraine by more than nine-tenths of a point, a gap large enough that headlines called his comeback a miracle. 
He won by less than a tenth of a point.
Japan has not enjoyed this kind of success in gymnastics since the 1960s and '70s, when it was known as the kingdom of gymnastics. 
Bolstered by an intense government-sponsored training effort that started in the lead-up to the 1964 Tokyo Games, its men won five consecutive team golds in the Olympics and five consecutive world championships from 1960 to 1978.
It was a Japanese, Sawao Kato, who won the last consecutive all-around golds, 48 and 44 years ago.
On social media, speculation about whether Mr. Uchimura would compete in 2020 has ranged from resigned to hopeful. 
By then, he will be 31. 
Japan has other skilled gymnasts, but none with his talent.
"Uchimura, please stay until 2020. 
I know 31 will be tough," read one typical Twitter post. 
"He's saving his best performance for Tokyo 2020 â I believe it," read another.
After his victory, Mr. Uchimura seemed both tempted and daunted by the prospect. 
He said he wanted to take time off to think. 
He said that if he did compete, his fans should not expect more miracles.
"I won't be able to match Oleg in the all-around event," he said of the man he beat on Wednesday.
"I'd be happy if I could somehow make the team," he added. 
"My kids would be at an age when they would remember it."

file: Leap Forward for China_ Setbacks for United States.txt
text:
ï»¿
BEIJING -- Randy Huntington's laugh boomed through the hallways of the Bird's Nest stadium after the long jump competition, making him something of a rarity at the world track and field championships on Tuesday: an American with something to celebrate.
Huntington, who hails from Walled Lake, Mich., coached Mike Powell when Powell jumped 8.95 meters (29 feet 4 Â¼ inches) in Tokyo in 1991 -- setting a world record that has now endured a year longer than the ethereal Bob Beamon mark it broke.
Huntington has worked with many fellow Americans through the years, but he is now coaching Chinese athletes. 
Though his arrival in 2013 is not the only explanation for the buzz in the stands on Tuesday night, it is certainly a big part of why China now has its first medal in the long jump at the world championships.
''We brought him here because he is good, simply because he's good,'' said Feng Shuyong, the Chinese team leader.
China's first long jump medal at a global championships turned out to be bronze, which Wang Jianan, just 18 years old, secured with an 8.18-meter leap -- all of which seemed auspicious given China's talismanic attachment to the number 8. 
Chinese jumpers also finished fourth and fifth, a signal that an event long dominated by the West may soon see a boost in its global profile similar to the one that Liu Xiang brought to the 110-meter hurdles a decade ago.
The gold went to Greg Rutherford of Britain -- already the Olympic, European and Commonwealth Games champion -- with a leap of 8.41 meters and the silver to Rutherford's training partner, the Australian Fabrice Lapierre (8.24). 
They, too, train under an American coach, Dan Pfaff, at a high-performance center in Phoenix.
Those looking for the Americans, whose legacy remains the richest in this event, needed to keep moving briskly down the results list.
The two who did make the final -- Jeff Henderson and Mike Hartfield -- failed to advance past the first phase of three jumps. 
Hartfield, who had jumped 8.27 meters this season, fouled on all three of his attempts. 
Henderson, who had jumped 8.52 meters, fouled on his first and third attempts and could go only 7.95 meters on his second.
''There are no words I can say about how disappointed I am,'' Henderson said.
It was that sort of evening in general for the United States team, the sport's powerhouse, as it failed to win a medal in any event. 
Those included its traditional stomping ground of the men's 400 hurdles, which was won by Nicholas Bett of Kenya in 47.79 seconds.
It was Kenya's first victory in the event at the world championships, and given its dominance of the 3,000-meter steeplechase (which also has hurdles), perhaps it was only a matter of time. 
The other medalists on Tuesday were Denis Kudryavtsev of Russia in 48.05 and Jeffery Gibson of the Bahamas in 48.17. 
Gibson finished a hundredth of a second ahead of the former world champion Kerron Clement of the United States.
Another former world champion from the United States, Jenny Simpson, lost her left shoe in the 1,500 meters and finished 11th in a 12-woman race that was won -- to the surprise of no one -- by Genzebe Dibaba, the latest Dibaba sister to win gold for Ethiopia.
Her older sibling Tirunesh swept the 5,000 and the 10,000 at the 2008 Olympics and has won three Olympic gold medals and five world titles over all. 
Now 30, she is taking a break from the sport after giving birth to a son, Nathan, in March. 
Another Dibaba sister, Ejegayehu, now 33, was a silver medalist in the 10,000 meters at the 2004 Olympics and won bronze in the 5,000 and 10,000 at the 2005 world championships.
But Genzebe Dibaba, 24, is the sister making headlines now. 
She set the world record in the 1,500 last month in Monaco in 3 minutes 50.07 seconds, prompting her to add the event to her world championship program. 
She is now in strong position to complete her own double in Beijing when she runs the 5,000 later this week.
''A new queen Dibaba is arriving,'' she said through a translator.
After four days, Kenya leads the medal count with four gold medals and nine medals over all. 
The United States has just one gold and six medals, below its customary and anticipated strike rate.
''US team need to turn it around quick!''
Michael Johnson, the former American sprint star, wrote on Twitter. 
''Competition management has been atrocious with multiple event favorites failing to advance to final!''
But it was a better night for American long-jump coaches, even if Huntington was not entirely satisfied.
''I think they really had more in them,'' he said of his three Chinese jumpers. 
''But when you put the pressure on kids like this, it is quite something for them to handle.''
The Chinese entries' runway sprints generated the biggest roars of the night in the stadium. 
And as it turned out, Wang, the youngest, handled the pressure best. 
Nicknamed Eddie, Wang is a former world junior long-jump champion as well as a former decathlete.
''Eddie is just steady Eddie,'' Huntington said. 
''He's only 18, but he has the mental capacity of a 30-year-old in the way he approaches things.''
He is also the least flashy of the three and the only one without a tattoo. 
The others are more challenging to coach, Huntington said.
Gao Xinglong, 21, who finished fourth, thrusts his chin far back when he jumps. 
''A real exuberant personality, but he gets really wired real fast, so bad that there would be times he'd be at a competition and would start at the wrong check mark because he'd get just so whacked out,'' Huntington said.
Li Jinzhe, the 25-year-old Asian Games champion who finished fifth on Tuesday, is an even bigger challenge. 
''He and I are at tremendous odds all the time,'' Huntington said. 
''He's a gamer, but he doesn't want to train. 
He's like an old basketball player. 
They want to play, but they don't want to train.''
This is not Huntington's first expatriate assignment in Asia. 
He worked with the South Korean national team before returning to the United States and rejoining the private sector.
In dire need of a vacation in early 2013, he said, he decided to go to the airport in Portland, Ore., that March and fly to the first city that appeared on the departure board. 
It was Beijing, and as he already had a valid multiple-entry visa for China, he stayed true to his word. 
There, he dined with Feng, who invited him to attend a meet outside of Beijing.
Four months later, Huntington, back in the United States, received a job offer from the Chinese track and field federation. 
Two years later, the Bird's Nest was atwitter over -- of all things -- the men's long jump.

Last February, when Jeremy Lin emerged as a unique and unlikely N.B.A. star, he exuded a striking mix of confidence and composure.
But it was not as if he did so without support, and Lin said he got much of that from Yao Ming, the N.B.A.'s first Asian superstar. 
Lin, as he struggled in his first season and a half to stay in the league, became close to Yao, playing in charity events with him and exchanging text messages. 
As Lin tried to both enjoy and endure his sudden celebrity last season, he talked with Yao nightly.
''He's a role model and a mentor to me,'' Lin said at the time.
So it was no surprise that as Lin figured out his future, seeking millions on the free-agent market while trying to remain loyal to the Knicks, he consulted with Yao.
This time, Yao said, he was of only limited help.
''Only he knew what he needed most,'' Yao said in a telephone interview from China. 
''He had to make the decision on his own. 
I didn't want to affect him too much.''
Lin's decision to sign an offer sheet from the Houston Rockets, Yao's former team, and the Knicks' decision to let Lin go, set off a fierce debate in New York.

''I'm so glad the Knicks didn't match the contract,'' Yao said. 
''Houston is a good place for Jeremy to come to. 
It's a good fit because both sides can provide the best opportunity for each other.''
Yao recalled that the environment in a smaller market helped make him a better player. 
In eight seasons, all with the Rockets, the 7-foot-6 Yao averaged 19 points, 9.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks as a center.
''In Houston, we have a very good community and great fans,'' Yao said. 
''With less media coverage, I think it made me focus more on basketball. 
I think that's one reason I played so well.''
The Rockets hope that Lin, who is of both Chinese and Taiwanese descent, can continue the franchise's popularity in China, for which Yao was responsible.
''The people in China are very familiar with Houston,'' said Yao, who, since retiring from the N.B.A. because of chronic injuries, has become the owner of the Shanghai Sharks of the Chinese Basketball Association. 
''The Rockets have been a symbol here for the last 10 years, and now that can be continued.

China announced a partnership with Yao to help raise basketball participation among youths in China while also holding an annual camp intended to develop elite Chinese players.

China. ''The interest in basketball has matured to where it goes beyond any player or one team.''

file: Lin Narrows His Focus in Lakers Move.txt
text:
ï»¿
EL SEGUNDO, Calif. 
-- Jeremy Lin was in Shanghai this month on a marketing tour, surrounded by adoring throngs in Houston Rockets red. 
Then he got word that he was being traded to the Los Angeles Lakers. 
He made a quick trip to Los Angeles for a physical and returned immediately to China to finish his obligations.
Word had traveled quickly.
''Everybody was wearing only yellow,'' Lin said Thursday at an introductory news conference with the Lakers. 
''I was like, 'Wow, that was fast.'
''
Lin is hoping for an equally rapid transformation after the Rockets sent him to the Lakers to clear cap space in an ultimately failed attempt to lure the free agent Chris Bosh away from the Miami Heat.
Lin, in the final year of a contract that will pay him $15 million -- about half of which will count against the salary cap -- is hoping that after being replaced in Houston's starting lineup last season he can establish himself as something more than the crossover cultural sensation that hit New York two years ago.
''I'm not trying to recreate Linsanity,'' Lin said. 
''I'm not trying to be that phenomenon that happened in New York. 
I think I just want to be myself, more than ever.''
And so Lin, dressed in a blue suit, did not shrink when Lakers General Manager Mitch Kupchak, wearing slacks and a polo shirt, chided him for being overdressed by Los Angeles's casual standards. 
He stood, smiled and relaxed.
Just what the Lakers have in mind for Lin is unclear. 
They have yet to hire a coach, though Byron Scott has been interviewed three times.
They also have a remade roster built on short-term contracts. 
The Lakers picked up Carlos Boozer on an amnesty waiver claim, drafted Julius Randle and brought back Nick Young and four other free agents who were on the worst team in franchise history.
With Kobe Bryant -- soon to be 36 and coming off Achilles' tendon and knee surgeries -- and the Lakers starting their third consecutive season with a new coach, expectations have been tempered.
Given Los Angeles's sizable Chinese population, Lin is expected to remain a popular figure. 
A sign came recently when a 72-year-old retired Chinese-American schoolteacher, who happens to be an avid Lakers fan, went on Craigslist to offer Lin a spare room, according to The Daily Breeze, of Torrance. 
The Lakers are also gearing up for a substantial increase in media interest from China, where Bryant is quite likely the N.B.A.'s best-known player.
That sort of following recalled Lin's early days with the Knicks, when Lin, one of the few Asian-Americans to play in the N.B.A., became a national sensation after he was picked up off waivers from Houston, dropped into the moribund Knicks' lineup and transformed into a nearly unstoppable offensive force -- all while sleeping on his brother's couch on the Lower East Side.
The highlight was Lin's 38-point performance in a nationally televised victory over the Lakers at Madison Square Garden.
Asked if the trade prompted any memories of that game, Lin said: ''It hasn't until I got asked 500 questions about it in Asia. 
I didn't think of that at all when I first heard of it, but I've replayed that game in my head a few times in the past couple weeks.''
Lin parlayed that brief period into a three-year, $25.1 million free-agent contract with the Rockets -- and a photo shoot in GQ. 
Though Lin continued to improve his 3-point shooting -- he shot a career-best 35.8 percent last season -- and his ability to play without the ball, he was replaced as a starter by Patrick Beverley, a superior defender on a team with few good ones.
Lin suffered another indignity earlier this summer when the Rockets, in a free-agent pitch to Carmelo Anthony, showed Anthony in a display in a No. 7 Rockets uniform, which at the time happened to belong to Lin. 
(He will wear No. 17 with the Lakers.)
Lin said his roller coaster ride -- from being a fringe player to a sudden star to one searching for his niche in the N.B.A. 
-- had seasoned him. 
Yes, he would like to start -- just like anyone. 
But what is important, he said, is making the most of his opportunities, in whatever form they arrive.
''After my year in New York, I wanted to stay on that path; I wanted to be a starter, and that was something I really kind of cherished,'' Lin said. 
''I really appreciated it because I was on the other end of being cut and getting waived, and maybe held on to it a little too tightly.''
He relishes the possibility of learning from Steve Nash, who is 40 and coming off two injury-plagued seasons with the Lakers. 
One of Lin's regrets about leaving New York was not getting the chance to play with Nash, who considered approving a trade to the Knicks two years ago, or Jason Kidd, two likely Hall of Fame point guards.
Lin does not have many of those regrets. 
He is about to turn 26, an age when most players -- for better or worse -- have established an identity. 
He will be a free agent again next summer, and he is on a team that is rife with uncertainties of its own.
Pressure?
''Coming back to L.A. where there will be a bigger market, a much bigger spotlight, hopefully I'm able to handle it better with each and every passing year,'' Lin said.
''I'm not trying to relive that banner season. 
I think that's been a big weight off my shoulders.''

file: Long Way for a Snub in a Qualifying Match.txt
text:
ï»¿
Justin Meram apologized in advance for any yawns that might occur during the interview. 
He had just endured a 27-hour journey from Chinese Taipei that had included two layovers, 13 time zones and one very troublesome, existential question:
Why had Meram bothered to join the Iraqi national soccer team on the other side of the globe right in the middle of the Major League Soccer postseason to play in a World Cup qualifying match -- or, as it turned out, not to play?
''I was down, I'm not going to lie,'' Meram said. 
''I was extremely upset. 
Not everyone who travels far should play, but not even to be on the selection?
''I know it's something not related to soccer,'' added Meram, the only American-born player on Iraq's team. 
''From previous games, I did everything right to be in the starting 11. 
I was playing well with Columbus. 
I'm trying to figure it out, something between the fans and the federation. 
We're baffled by this. 
I can't tell you why. 
I'm making phone calls. 
Maybe I'll be able to tell you in a few months.''
One game in which he is sure to see action arrives straight away: Meram, 26, will most likely be in the starting lineup when his Columbus Crew face the Red Bulls on Sunday in the first leg of the Eastern Conference finals. 
His path to that game had its own quirks -- lightly recruited out of high school, he went to junior college before he starred at the University of Michigan and was drafted by the Crew -- but it was nothing compared with his journey into international soccer.
Discovered online by an Iraqi supporter trawling for national team prospects, Meram made his debut for Iraq in November 2014. 
He had started two of Iraq's three previous matches in the current round of Asian World Cup qualifiers and was brought in as a substitute in the third. 
He had scored two goals -- one after he was chosen to take a penalty kick in the first match against Taipei.
Meram showed up for the return match in Taipei last week in time for four of the team's six training sessions, expecting more minutes. 
But he was snubbed by Yahya Alwan, the Iraqi coach, a cruel reminder to Meram and others that the Iraqi national team remains very much a work in progress, steeped in the vagaries of politics, religion and enigmatic grudges.
Only 15 years ago, Uday Hussein, the son of Saddam, ruled brutally over the soccer team, reportedly imprisoning or torturing players who faltered on the field. 
A remade Iraqi team won the Asian Cup in 2007, yet conditions remain far from ideal. 
FIFA has mandated that no matches can be played inside volatile Iraq, so the team stages home qualifying games in Iran.
''The organization and the logistics are much better than they were, but nowhere near where they should be,'' Meram said. 
''The resources, the field, the ability to train at home. 
Sometimes, when I come from America, I feel for them. 
Even the small things -- the taping, the massages, the treatment -- we don't have what Japan or the Emirates have.''
Meram has never visited Iraq. 
His father, Sam, and mother, Lamia, are Chaldean Catholics who met in the Detroit area after immigrating to the United States separately from Mosul, more than a decade before Justin was born. 
His parents' families all escaped Mosul, now under ISIS control, yet his mother and father remain deeply concerned about the city's fate.
''They're devastated,'' Meram said. 
''My mom feels it a lot. 
When all the museums of the Chaldean culture in Northern Iraq are being destroyed, where they grew up, that's hard on them. 
Ancient statues are getting destroyed. 
It's devastating seeing that.''
Meram, 26, a dual citizen, finally became eligible to play for Iraq late last year. 
His technical skill was evident early in his youth, when he excelled at Eisenhower High School in Shelby, Mich., in both soccer and as the kicker for the football team. 
Major colleges at first failed to recognize his talents, but Maurice Hughes, a graduate of Yavapai College in Arizona, a top junior college power, recommended him to the coach there.
''We knew we'd discovered a diamond in the rough the very first training session,'' Yavapai Coach Michael Pantalione said. 
''In the first preseason training session, we had seven-a-side matches. 
Three groups. 
When the session was finished, Justin had a dozen goals. 
He had a brilliant career. 
Then the same schools that said no to him, two years later, were extremely interested in the junior college player of the year.''
Yavapai won two national titles with Meram before he headed to the University of Michigan and then to Columbus, as the 15th pick in the 2011 M.L.S. draft. 
Pantalione praised his ability to run at defenders, putting them on their heels. 
In 33 regular-season and playoff games this year, Meram has six goals, five assists and 78 shots on goal, while establishing himself as a complementary threat to the team's top scorer, Kei Kamara, whose 22 goals this season tied him for the league lead.
''Give him a window, he'll get a good shot on goal,'' Crew Coach Gregg Berhalter said. 
''He was always a strong 1v1 finisher,'' he added, referring to one versus one. 
''Now, his work defensively is outstanding, his ability to take the ball in transition, his passing, they're much better.''
Iraq defeated Chinese Taipei, 2-0, without Meram on Tuesday, and now must beat both Thailand and Vietnam next March, most likely in Tehran, in order to advance to the next round of Asian World Cup qualifying.
Meram, though, is confused and uncertain about whether he will rejoin the Iraqi team if it calls again, until he figures out why a federation with such limited resources flew him business class to Taipei only to ignore him once he arrived.
''It's not like this has happened many times, just this once,'' Meram said. 
''I'm waiting to hear some answers. 
Right now, I'm looking forward to Sunday. 
At least I'm fresh.''

text:

Tim Hardaway Jr. experienced the less glamorous side of the N.B.A. this month when the Knicks went on a barnstorming tour of New England and beyond.
The team played three games in four nights, starting in Providence, R.I., where the visitors' locker room seemed to be the size of a cubicle. 
It continued to Toronto, where a video of a Hardaway dunk went viral. 
It wrapped up in Manchester, N.H., where the road took its toll and the team looked sluggish.
''It was a learning experience,'' said Hardaway, a first-year shooting guard.
With renovations continuing at Madison Square Garden, the Knicks have become vagabonds once again this preseason. 
On Monday, the team will make its second trip to Toronto for an exhibition against the Raptors before heading to Green Bay, Wis., for a game on Wednesday against the Milwaukee Bucks. 
The Knicks' lone preseason appearance at the Garden will not come until Friday, when they host the Charlotte Bobcats.
It might not be an ideal situation -- ''It's O.K.,'' Coach Mike Woodson said -- but at least the Knicks have company. 
In fact, N.B.A. teams are collectively logging more than 200,000 miles of preseason travel to destinations as diverse as Biloxi, Miss., and Istanbul.
All that traveling can create challenges for coaching staffs that would prefer to focus on evaluating personnel and devising offenses. 
But the league increasingly sees the preseason as vital for spreading the N.B.A. gospel at home and abroad.
Consider that 28 percent of the N.B.A.'s games this preseason are being played at nonleague locations. 
For example, the Knicks' appearances in New Hampshire and in Rhode Island were home games for the Boston Celtics. 
Just two of the Celtics' eight preseason games are being staged at TD Garden.
At the same time, the Knicks' peripatetic schedule, covering about 3,070 miles, has been a breeze compared with the globe-trotting of other teams. 
The Oklahoma City Thunder played two games in Europe this month. 
The Houston Rockets and the Indiana Pacers faced each other in the Philippines and in Taiwan. 
Most recently, the Golden State Warriors and the Los Angeles Lakers had a two-game swing through China.
Those exhibitions were all part of what the league has branded the N.B.A. 
Global Games: eight preseason and two regular-season games featuring 12 teams in seven countries. 
Commissioner David Stern said the league's overseas adventures required an extraordinary amount of planning.
''But they're our attempt to grow the game,'' said Stern, who added that the league was ''serious about bringing this sport to the greatest number of people.''
League officials seem well aware that the travel can be a drain. 
Upon arriving in China last week, Adam Silver, the league's deputy commissioner and chief operating officer, reflected on his 24-hour trip from Rio de Janeiro, where the Washington Wizards played the Chicago Bulls on Oct. 
12. ''I look forward to the next generation of airplanes,'' he said.
Wizards Coach Randy Wittman said his team enjoyed its trip to Brazil. 
Many of the players took their families along.
''We were basically together 24/7,'' Wittman said. 
''It was a good time to sit down and get to know families, which we don't have an opportunity to do that often.''
No team will wind up traveling more during the preseason than the Pacers: roughly 19,770 miles, based on an analysis of their schedule. 
The Celtics (2,060) and the Nets (2,310) have the lightest schedules. 
It is all relative, of course.
As for the Knicks, they dealt with the same issue last year, playing all six of their preseason games on the road, though it did not seem to have an adverse effect on their preparation for the regular season. 
They won 54 games and advanced past the opening round of the playoffs for the first time since 2000.
Their preseason excursions have also been a boon for arenas -- and secondary markets -- that seldom have the opportunity to host N.B.A. games. 
The Knicks' game on Thursday against the Wizards had an announced attendance of 12,376, a sellout, at Baltimore Arena, a 51-year-old building that has seen brighter days.
The game required substantial preparations by the arena's staff. 
Frank Remesch, the arena's general manager, said his crew had refurbished the court, installed new backboards and replaced both 45-second clocks. 
On game day, Remesch approached Woodson after the Knicks' morning shootaround and asked if the accommodations were suitable.
''He said it was perfect, so that meant a lot,'' Remesch said.
